                        Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 3
INTRODUCTION
For the first time in nearly 2 decades, the United States is seeing rapid growth in electricity demand, driven by
the data center boom as well as expanding electrification. Total electricity use in the United States reached a
record high of 4,430 terawatt hours (TWh) in 2025—almost 3 percent above 2024 levels1—and is expected to
continue growing at a similar rate through 2050.2 Meeting this increased demand, while continuing to advance
action on climate change, will require a massive ramp up in renewable energy development. Notable progress
was made in 2025, with utility-scale solar generation in the United States growing by a record 34 percent, and
wind generation by 3 percent.3 The 2 technologies together accounted for 17 percent of total generation in
2025, another record high, but still well below what is needed to achieve climate goals.4 This highlights the
extent of the challenge ahead: if the United States is to meet increasing electricity demand while continuing to
drive down greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy facilities must be developed at faster rates than ever
before. But such development faces increasing headwinds.
This report documents legal obstacles and challenges to renewable energy siting at the state- and local-levels
in the United States. In particular, the report focuses on: (a) state laws and local ordinances that impede the
siting of utility-scale solar, wind, battery storage, and related transmission projects (referred to as “state and
local restrictions”); and (b) instances of organized opposition to individual projects (referred to as “contested
projects”). The report updates and significantly expands 5 previous editions, which were published annually
from 2021 to 2025.5 This 6th edition of the report details state and local restrictions and contested projects
through December 31, 2025. The many restrictions on renewables imposed at the federal level by the Trump
administration have been amply documented elsewhere and are beyond the scope of this report.

By the end of 2025, at least 888 state and local restrictions that were so severe they could have the effect of
blocking renewable energy projects had been adopted. The great bulk of these were local restrictions, with at
least 865 local restrictions across 46 states identified (see Figure 1 below). Florida, New Mexico, New Jersey,
and West Virginia were the only states nationwide in which no local restrictions were identified. However,
Florida and West Virginia were among the 19 states that had adopted state-level restrictions as of December
31, 2025. New Mexico and New Jersey were the only states where no restrictions—either local or state-level—
were identified. But even they, like most other states, had renewable energy projects that encountered
significant opposition. There were at least 567 contested projects across 48 states through the end of 2025.

significantly higher than the totals in the previous edition published in June 2025. These increases reflect not

only recent developments (i.e., restrictions adopted and projects contested in 2025), but also earlier
restrictions and contested projects that were not previously identified. In compiling this edition, we made use
of new data sources published by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR; formerly the National
Renewable Energy Laboratory) in 2025.7 NLR used advanced machine learning tools to compile a list of 23,712
local ordinances applicable to wind and solar energy development.8 The Sabin Center, with assistance from
Columbia’s Data Science Institute, used AI tools to identify a subset of ordinances from the NLR list that qualify
as “restrictive” according to our criteria (described below).9 To maximize accuracy, each ordinance in the
subset was manually reviewed by Sabin Center researchers before it was included in our data set. Sabin Center
researchers also identified additional state and local restrictions and contested projects from other sources,
including government websites, academic studies, and news reports. As such, this 6th edition of the report
provides a more comprehensive picture of the extent of state and local opposition to renewable energy
development, which is even more widespread and significant than our previous reports suggested.

Our Criteria for Determining if a State Law or Local Ordinance Is “Restrictive”
This report only includes state laws and local ordinances that are so severe that they either (a) scuttle a
specific project or (b) could have the effect of barring or significantly curtailing renewable energy development
within the relevant jurisdiction, either permanently or temporarily. More specifically, for the purposes of this
report, a state law or local ordinance is considered “restrictive” if it includes:
     1.      any ban on renewable energy facilities, whether permanent or temporary, and whether complete
             or partial (e.g., no solar on agricultural land) (“Rule 1”);

     2.      any cap on renewable energy facilities (e.g., no more than 1,000 acres or 1% of county land can be
             used for wind or solar) (“Rule 2”);

     3.      any restrictions on the use of energy generated from renewable energy facilities (e.g., ordinances
             that allow production for on-site use only) (“Rule 3”);

     4.      any restriction designed to block a particular project (“Rule 4”);

     5.      any viewshed limitation that is not feasible (e.g., facility must not be visible from roads) (“Rule 5”);

     6.      any requirement that wind turbines be set back (a) more than 1,000 feet (305 meters) or more
             than 2x maximum blade tip height from property lines or roads (“Rule 6a”); or (b) more than 1,500
             feet (457 meters) or more than 3x maximum blade tip height from off-site structures (“Rule 6b”);

     7.      any requirement that noise from wind turbines be limited to less than 45 dBA (“Rule 7”);

     8.      any requirement that shadow flicker from wind turbines be limited to less than 30 hours per year
             (“Rule 8”);

     9.      any requirement that the height of wind turbines be limited to less than 500 feet (“Rule 9”); and/or

     10.     any requirement that solar energy projects be set back (a) 300 feet (91 meters) or more from
             property lines or roads (“Rule 10a”) or (b) 500 feet (152 meters) or more from offsite structures
             (“Rule 10b”).10

In the chapters that follow, we present tallies indicating the number of state and local restrictions that fall
within each category above, referred to by the applicable rule number. Because this report focuses on
obstacles to siting renewable energy facilities, policies related to other issues that affect renewable energy—
e.g., net metering, renewable energy standards, tax credits, etc.—are not discussed.

Our Criteria for Determining Whether a Project Is a “Contested Project”
For the purposes of this report, “contested projects” are defined as those that have faced significant
opposition from individual residents, community-based groups, or other organizations. Significant opposition
is defined to include the organization of one or more opposition groups, the circulation of a petition,
intervention in administrative procedures, and/or the filing of lawsuits to block the contested project at issue.
In many cases, opponents have succeeded in delaying a contested project’s approval, scaling down its size, or
securing its cancellation (see Figure 3 below).

Key Findings
State and local restrictions, as well as controversies over individual projects, are numerous and widespread
across the United States. By the end of 2025, at least 888 state and local restrictions on renewable energy
development had been adopted in 48 states, and at least 567 renewable energy projects in 48 states had
been contested.11 There was not a single state where renewable energy development had not been affected

developers have indicated is feasible to comply with. For example, wind energy developers have indicated that a 1,000-foot setback
from occupied structures represents the upper limit of what is typically workable for designing a utility-scale wind project.

by restrictive laws or local opposition. Only New Mexico and New Jersey had no identified state or local
restrictions, but both had seen their share of contested projects. Conversely, the only states where no
contested projects were identified—Alaska and Utah—both had local restrictions on renewable energy
development.
The 888 identified restrictions included 23 state-level restrictions adopted in 19 states and 865 local
restrictions adopted in 46 states. Wind was the technology most commonly targeted in state and local
restrictions. Of the 865 identified local restrictions, at least 416 were directed solely at restricting wind
energy development, 294 specifically targeted solar energy projects, and 123 covered both technologies
(sometimes also together with storage and/or transmission projects). In addition, we identified 35 local
restrictions targeting battery storage projects, either alone or together with other technologies.12 This is likely
an underestimate of the total number of local restrictions on battery storage projects. Ordinances targeting
battery storage projects were not captured in the NLR datasets and thus had to be identified through manual
searches of local government meeting records, local news reports, and other similar sources.
The 567 contested projects included 217 with a wind component, 322 with a solar component, 41 with a
battery storage component, and 17 with a transmission component (see Figure 1).13 As indicated in Figure 3
and explained further in the chapters that follow, at least 227 contested projects (approximately 40 percent
of the total recorded) have been cancelled, though this may not be solely due to local opposition.

State and local restrictions and contested projects are more prevalent in some states than others. Figure 4 and
Figure 5 below show the top 10 states with the highest cumulative tallies of restrictions and contested
projects, respectively.14 These top 10 lists are somewhat different from those that appeared in the previous
edition of this report published in June 2025. For example, Texas and Kansas are no longer among the top 10
states with the most restrictions; Texas has moved to 11th position and Kansas to 13th. They have been
replaced by Pennsylvania (now in 3rd place) and Minnesota (now in equal 6th place with Virginia). These shifts
are due to a combination of factors. Both Pennsylvania and Minnesota were among the states with the most
new restrictions adopted in 2025—7 in Pennsylvania and 6 in Minnesota15—but that does not fully explain
their addition to the top 10 list. With the new data collection processes instituted for this edition, we were
able to identify additional restrictions adopted in earlier years in Pennsylvania and Minnesota, which were not
captured in our previous reports. This, together with the large number of new restrictions adopted in 2025,
explains their inclusion on the list of top 10 states with the largest cumulative number of restrictions.

Nationwide, the total number of state and local restrictions on renewable energy development has grown
significantly over the last decade (see Figure 6), but our data suggests that the rate of adoption of new
restrictions may be slowing. We identified 70 new state and local restrictions adopted in 2025, compared to
112 restrictions adopted in 2024, and 165 in 2023.16 Focusing on the 10 states with the most restrictions (see
Figure 7), 8 saw declines in the number of new restrictions adopted in 2024, compared to 2023 levels. In 7 of
those states, the decline continued into 2025, with fewer restrictions adopted in that year than 2024. In some
cases, the decline may reflect the impact of new state legislation, aimed at limiting local governments’ ability
to block renewable energy projects. For example, in 2023, Michigan enacted Public Act 233 which transfers
authority for the siting of certain large renewable energy projects from local governments to the state Public
Service Commission. Under the law, local governments only retain siting authority over covered projects if
they have adopted a “compatible renewable energy ordinance” (“CREO”), which imposes restrictions no more
severe than those allowed under state law. Since Public Act 233 was enacted, the number of new local
restrictions adopted in Michigan has declined from a high of 15 in 2023 to 8 in 2024 and 6 in 2025.

Ohio has also seen a similar decline in the number of new local restrictions adopted in recent years. However,
rather than signaling a positive shift in local governments’ approach to renewable energy projects, the
slowdown may simply reflect the fact that Ohio was already saturated with local restrictions by 2023. This is
primarily due to the state legislature’s decision to enact Senate Bill 52 of 2021, which authorizes counties in
Ohio to designate restricted areas where wind and solar energy projects are prohibited. Many counties moved
quickly to designate restricted areas, with 11 doing so in 2022 and another 13 in 2023. Since then, the rate at
which new restrictions are being adopted has slowed, with just 4 in 2024 and 3 in 2025. Even so, 30 of the 88
counties in Ohio (i.e., over 34 percent) have now designated restricted areas, putting large swaths of land in
the state off-limits to renewable energy projects.
Other states have also recently sought to restrict renewable energy. Indeed, while state level restrictions
continue to account for a small share of total restrictions in our database, they have grown in number over the
last 5 years. At least 3 new state restrictions were adopted in 2025 alone: (1) The Arkansas state legislature
enacted the Wind Energy Development Act of 2025,19 establishing restrictive setback requirements for wind
energy facilities (i.e., facilities must be at least 3.5 times the turbine height from private property lines), which

industry groups say will “ban or significantly impede wind energy development” in many areas of the state.20
(2) In Louisiana, House Bill 459 of 202521 was passed, requiring solar energy facilities to comply with onerous
setback requirements (i.e., at least 300 feet from residential properly lines) and strict noise limits (i.e., 10 dBA
above ambient noise at the property line) that would effectively prevent facilities being “louder than a
whisper or rustling leaves. This may block many projects or require relocating inverter infrastructure to the
middle of a parcel.”22 (3) The Renewable Energy Certainty Act of 202523 was enacted in Maryland, imposing an
acreage cap for solar energy development on certain farmland classified as “priority preservation areas.”
There is reason to think that state-level restrictions on renewable energy development may become more
widespread in coming years. One recent study found that, in 2025, at least 148 bills that would make
renewable energy development more difficult were introduced into state legislatures across the United
States.24 While only a small proportion of these bills passed, the study concluded that “[r]estrictive policy
approaches are gaining momentum,” especially in states that have already seen significant renewable energy
development.25 For example, thanks to highly permissive permitting structures, Texas has added more wind
energy capacity over the last 10 years than any other state. But, in 2025, the Texas legislature considered at
least 24 bills aimed at restricting wind and other renewable energy development.26 Many of these bills were
reportedly advanced by “a group called Stewards for Texas, which is linked to billionaire Daniel Friedkin,” who
had previously opposed construction of a transmission line through his ranch.27 This highlights a larger
phenomenon: concerns about a single project can, and often do, motivate broader efforts to restrict
renewable energy development more generally.
This scenario is currently playing out at the federal level. President Trump, whose animosity towards
renewable energy reportedly stems in part from the development of an offshore wind farm that was visible
from one of his Scottish golf courses, has directed many harmful changes in federal clean energy siting
policy.28 Among other things, the second Trump administration has moved to end all new leasing for offshore

wind projects in federal waters off the U.S. coast29 and sought to block the construction of projects for which
leases had already been finalized, including by revoking previously issued permits (e.g., for the Atlantic Shores
Offshore Wind Project),30 issuing stop work orders (e.g., to the Empire Wind Project),31 and even paying
developers to surrender their leases and redirect investments earmarked for offshore wind to fossil fuel
projects.32 Similarly, onshore, the administration has promoted fossil fuels while restricting renewables. The
Department of the Interior, for example, has implemented emergency permitting procedures to accelerate the
review and approval of new oil and gas projects33 while simultaneously requiring wind and solar projects to
undergo additional rounds of review and be personally approved by the Secretary of the Interior.34 Both the
Department of the Interior and Army Corps of Engineers have also instituted new permitting procedures that
require consideration of projects’ “energy density” (i.e., the amount of energy produced per acre) and thus
preference oil and gas projects over renewables.35 Many of these actions have been blocked by the courts but,
even so, a number of projects have been delayed and others cancelled as a result of the change in federal
siting policy.36

                               Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 13
These impacts have been compounded by the rollback of federal tax credits for renewable energy projects.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law by President Trump in July 2025, accelerated the phase out of
tax credits for wind and solar projects. Now, to qualify for the credits, projects must have begun construction
by July 6, 2026, or be placed into service by December 31, 2027. It is estimated that the changes have already
resulted in over $26 billion in lost capital investments in wind and solar energy projects, with further losses
expected in coming years.37
Overall, these shifts in the federal policy landscape, together with the growing number of state and local
restrictions and contested projects documented in this report, indicate a challenging path ahead for the
renewable energy sector. There are some reasons for hope, however. Renewable energy generation has
tripled over the last decade and, even now, solar deployment continues to grow at record rates.38 States can,
and increasingly are, supporting the industry to push back against anti-renewables actions at the federal
level.39 Several states have also recently enacted, and more are considering, legislation to accelerate
renewable energy development.40 These actions reflect a growing recognition among states and many other
groups – from local landowners to environmental groups to large technology and other companies – that
renewables are the cheapest and fastest way to meet rising energy demand while advancing action on climate
change.

1.1 State Siting Framework43
Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. State legislation expressly
grants 4 counties – Baldwin, Cherokee, Dekalb, and Etowah – zoning authority over wind projects. The
legislation specifies that a county permit is required for any wind project in Cherokee, Dekalb, and Etowah
counties. In Baldwin County, the county commissioner can choose whether or not to require county permits
for wind energy projects. State legislation does not expressly address solar energy project siting but, in
practice, siting decisions are made at the local level.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no
deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

     Ala. Admin. Code §§ 45-2-262 (Baldwin), 45-10-260.02 (Cherokee), 45-25-260.02 (Dekalb), 45-28-260.02 (Etowah).

1.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Alabama. Of the 67
counties in Alabama, at least 4 – Baldwin, Cherokee, Dekalb, and Etowah counties – have adopted restrictive
ordinances. All 4 ordinances limit wind energy development, either by banning it entirely or by imposing
onerous setback and noise restrictions.

     ● Total number of state restrictions: 0
     ● Total number of local restrictions: 4
     ● Technology targeted:
          ○ 4 (wind)
     ● Type of restrictions:
          ○ Baldwin County: Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (wind)
          ○ Cherokee County: Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
          ○ Dekalb County: Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)
          ○ Etowah County: Rule 6a: Setback Restriction (wind) | Rule 7: Noise Restriction (wind)

1.3 Contested Projects
     ● Noccalula Wind Energy Center (Etowah County): In August 2014, Pioneer Green Energy, a Texas-based
       developer, abandoned plans to construct a $160 million wind project comprising 35 to 40 turbines
       after local residents filed a lawsuit challenging the project and after the state enacted onerous
       restrictions on wind energy in Etowah County.44

     ● Origis Energy Solar Farm (Covington County): Local residents expressed strong opposition to a
       proposed solar farm at an August 21, 2023 meeting reviewing the possible construction of a 160
       megawatt (MW), 1,000-acre solar panel array. The residents opposed the farm for several reasons,
       including that the farm would be powering communities “over an hour away” and not their own; that
       the solar farm might encroach on family properties that have existed for generations; and that
       potential road runoff might impact their well water supplies. Residents also expressed frustration that
       surveyors had entered their property without their permission. An online petition created by the group
       “Concerned Citizens of Covington County Alabama” urged Origis Energy to relocate the project to a
       more remote or industrial area of Covington County. As of December 31, 2023, the petition had 80
       signatures.45

     ● Shinbone Ridge Wind (Cherokee County): In August 2014, Pioneer Green Energy abandoned plans to
       construct a $40 million wind project comprising 7 to 8 wind turbines in Cherokee County after local
       residents filed a lawsuit challenging the project and after the state enacted onerous restrictions on
       wind energy in Cherokee County.46

     ● Stockton I and Stockton II Solar (Baldwin County): In October 2025, Alabama Power submitted its
       proposal for 2 solar projects, the 80-MW Stockton I and the 180-MW Stockton II, to be located on
       approximately 2,000 acres of land in Stockton. The projects were designed to power a Meta-affiliated
       data center under construction in Montgomery. Local residents have voiced concerns about the
       projects, including the impacts on the community’s rural character and wetlands as well as its
       proximity to the Mobile-Tensaw Delta and the potential environmental risks posed by hurricanes and
       flooding. The opponents created a Facebook page titled “Stop Solar in Stockton,” where residents have
       raised concerns about land use, environmental impacts, and the lack of public notice. In December
       2025, the Alabama Public Service Commission unanimously approved the projects. Construction is
       expected to begin in 2026, with commercial operation by the end of 2028.47

     ● Turkey Heaven Mountain Wind (Cleburne County): In October 2015, Native Energy Solutions, an
       Oklahoma-based developer, announced that it was no longer planning to build a wind project in
       Cleburne County. The project faced opposition from local residents who, in June 2014, filed a lawsuit
       seeking a permanent injunction that would bar the developer from constructing wind turbines in the
       County, citing concerns about “wind turbine syndrome” among other things. The developer filed a
       motion to dismiss, but the motion was denied.48

2.1 State Siting Framework49
Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects less than 65 megawatts
(MW) in size. The state has principal authority over larger projects (65 MW or larger). These larger projects
require a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Regulatory Commission of Alaska.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no
deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

restrictions on certain wind facilities.

3.1 State Siting Framework50
Local governments have principal siting authority over wind energy projects of any size and solar energy
projects less than 100 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over larger solar energy
projects (100 MW or more). A certificate of environmental compatibility (CEC) from the Arizona Power Plant
and Transmission Line Siting Committee is required for these larger solar projects.

One or more public hearings are required as part of the CEC application process and the Arizona Power Plant
and Transmission Line Siting Committee is required to grant or deny a CEC within 180 days of an application
being filed.

3.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Alabama. There are at
least 5 local restrictions – adopted by Apache County, Coolidge City in Pinal County, Navajo County, Mohave
County, and Yavapai – in the state. All 5 local restrictions apply to solar energy development and 2 also restrict
wind energy development. Most involve temporary moratoria or permanent bans on solar, and sometimes
wind, projects.

          ■ Navajo County: Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (wind) | Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (solar) | Rule 6a
              and 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)
          ■ Mohave County: Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (solar)
          ■ Yavapai County: Rule 10a and 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)

3.3 Contested Projects
     ● Black Mesa Pumped Storage Project (Apache and Navajo Counties): The developer Nature and People
       First has sought to develop a 6,000-MW, utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project on
       approximately 400 acres of land. In July 2023, 3 organizations—Tó Nizhóní Ání, Diné Citizens Against
       Ruining our Environment, and Center for Biological Diversity—submitted a letter to FERC attaching
       resolutions against the project from 18 Navajo Nation chapters and agencies. Nearby residents had
       expressed concerns that the project could damage underground water supplies and sacred lands and
       that the developer had not sufficiently involved nearby residents. In February 2024, FERC denied
       applications for a preliminary permit for the project, stating that “[t]he Commission will not issue
       preliminary permits for projects proposing to use Tribal lands if the Tribes on whose land the project is
       to be located opposes the permit.” 51

4.1 State Siting Framework57
Local governments in Arkansas have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects less than 50
megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting of larger wind and solar projects (50
MW or more in size). A certificate of environmental compatibility and public need (CECPN) must be obtained
from the Arkansas Public Service Commission for these larger projects. The Commission must hold a public
hearing on an application for a CECPN at least 40, and not more than 180, days after receipt of the application.
The Commission must issue a decision within 60 days after the public hearing.

4.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction has been adopted in Arkansas. In 2025, the state legislature enacted the
Arkansas Wind Energy Development Act, which establishes restrictive setback and noise limits for wind energy
facilities. Additionally, local restrictions have been adopted by at least 2 counties: (1) Carroll County imposed a
5 year moratorium on commercial wind and solar energy development in 2025; and (2) Madison County
imposed a 1 year moratorium on wind development in 2024. The Madison County moratorium has now
expired.58

4.3 Contested Projects
     ● Nimbus Wind Farm (Carroll County): In 2016, Scout Clean Energy began negotiating contracts with
       landowners for the 180-MW Nimbus Wind Farm, which would cover 14 square miles of land atop the
       Ozark Mountains. In 2023, a group called Stop Wind Farms was formed to oppose this development
       and collected over 1,000 verified signatures in opposition, raising concerns about disturbances to the
       aesthetic value of the Ozark ridgeline and decreased property values. Nevertheless, on September 17,
       2024, the Carroll County Quorum Court approved Scout to use county roads for installation, so long as
       Scout covered the cost for road maintenance around the wind farm. The project is expected to
       commence construction in 2025.59

5.1 State Siting Framework61
Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. However, developers of
projects meeting certain size thresholds may opt-in to a state siting process, which is administered by the
California Energy Commission (CEC). The CEC has jurisdiction to issue a certificate for any: (a) photovoltaic
solar facility, on-shore wind facility, or thermal energy facility not powered by fossil fuels or nuclear fuels, with
a generating capacity of at least 50 megawatts (MW); (b) energy storage system with a storage capacity of
least 200 MW hours (MWh); (c) electric transmission line from any such generating or storage facility to an
interconnected transmission system; and (d) facility that manufactures, produces, or assembles wind, solar, or
storage systems with a capital investment of at least $250,000,000 over a period of 5 years. The issuance of a
certificate by the CEC eliminates the need for “any permit, certificate, or similar document required by any
state, local, or regional agency,” and “supersede any applicable statute, ordinance, or regulation of any state,
local, or regional agency.”

The CEC must conduct multiple public hearings of differing scope and scale before issuing a certificate. The
CEC must make a final decision on the certificate within 270 days of an application being filed.

5.2 Restrictive Local Ordinances and State Statutes
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in California. However, at
least 16 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by 15 counties in the state. One county – Yolo – has
adopted 2 separate ordinances restricting renewable energy development. Most of the local restrictions
target wind energy development, but some cover solar projects (either alone or in addition to wind). Several
of the local restrictions involve either temporary moratoria or permanent bans on wind and/or solar projects.

5.3 Contested Projects
     ● Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area First-Generation Wind Farms (Alameda and Contra Costa
       Counties): In 2004, the Center for Biological Diversity brought a lawsuit against the operators of wind
       turbines in the Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, alleging that
       the “obsolete, first-generation wind turbine generators” being used at the site were killing and injuring
       birds in violation of the public trust doctrine. The lawsuit was dismissed, and the dismissal was upheld
       on appeal.62

     ● Aramis Solar Project (Alameda County): Opponents of 2 North Livermore Valley solar projects, Aramis
       (410 acres) and Sunwalker (70 acres), led by a group called Save North Livermore Valley, argued that
       the proposed locations of the projects impinge on agriculture, natural wildlife habitat, open space, and
       visual and scenic resources. In October 2020, 2 candidates running for election to the Alameda County
       Board of Supervisors issued a joint statement urging the board to place a moratorium on solar
       development on agricultural land. After the East County Board of Zoning Adjustments approved both
       projects, local groups appealed both decisions. By December 2020, 3 local organizations had filed
       appeals challenging the approval of the Aramis project. In May 2022, the Alameda County Superior
       Court upheld the county’s approval of the Aramis project, dismissing a lawsuit by project opponents. In
       July 2023, Save North Livermore Valley appealed the Superior Court’s decision. California’s First District
       Court of Appeals denied the appeal in August 2023.63

    ● Aratina Solar Center (Kern County): In October 2021, the Kern County Board of Supervisors
      unanimously approved the Aratina Solar Center, a solar-plus-storage project including 530 MW of solar
      capacity and 600 MW of battery energy storage capacity. Shortly thereafter, local community members
      organized a petition that received 51,000 signatures. A primary concern driving local opposition to the
      project is the potential impact on local wildlife and on Joshua Trees. In compliance with the California
      Western Joshua Tree Conservation Act, the developer received an Incidental Take Permit, which
      authorized the developer to remove trees with an option to pay a standard mitigation fee rather than
      complete mitigation fee.64

    ● Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project (Riverside County): The Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project is a 465-

      The Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) sued the Department of Interior in 2014 in the U.S. District Court
      for the Central District of California, claiming that BLM’s lack of government-to-government
      consultation violated the NHPA; the lawsuit also included claims under NEPA and the Federal Land
      Policy and Management Act. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the Department
      of Interior in July 2015.65

        wildlife and groundwater and the effects of noise disruptions. In March 2024, the Fourth District Court of Appeal

       Santa Barbara County, encountered opposition from local conservation groups and members of the
       Northern Chumash Tribe in 2022. The project site is in an area the Northern Chumash Tribe have

       developer entered into a community benefits agreement with the Santa Ynez Chumash to resolve
       opposition to the project.68

     ● Calico Solar Project (San Bernardino County): In 2005, Stirling Energy Systems signed a contract with a
       utility to sell up to 850 MW of energy from a concentrating solar-thermal power plant that would
       involve 30,000 solar dishes standing up to 40 feet high in the Mojave Desert. Due to concerns about
       impacts on the desert tortoise, project plans were reduced to 663.5 MW. In 2012, the Sierra Club,
       Natural Resources Defense Council, and Defenders of Wildlife filed a lawsuit to stop the project,
       arguing that the project was “wrong from the start,” due to impacts on wild lands and wildlife. By
       2013, the project was dead.69

     ● Coyote Creek Agrivoltaics Farm (Sacramento County): In 2025, D.E. Shaw Renewables proposed the
       200-MW Coyote Creek Solar project which will have an additional 100 MW of battery energy storage
       and incorporate sheep grazing. The project is to be located on approximately 2,700 acres. In November
       2025, the Sacramento Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the project after 5 hours of debate
       and testimony from over 150 speakers. Dozens of attendees spoke in opposition and raised concerns
       about the project’s impact on the region’s native oak tree forests, grasslands, and wetlands. The
       developer estimated that the project would generate approximately $76 million in tax revenue over
       the next 20 years and made conservation commitments including at least 1,150 acres of oak woodland,
       riparian habitat and wildlife corridors.70

     ● E-Group Solar (San Bernardino County): In December 2025, E-Group PS proposed the 50-MW E-Group
       Solar project to be located on 477 acres of land in the City of Twentynine Palms. The City enacted a ban
       on commercial solar facilities, which was preempted by Assembly Bill 205 (AB 205), a state law that
       went into effect in June 2022. AB 205 allows the developer of a solar project at least 50 MW or more to
       seek approval from the California Energy Commission (CEC) and bypass any local approval process. The
       developer opted to seek approval from the City. [Note: At a public meeting on February 17, 2026, the
       City of Twentynine Palms’ Planning Commission considered adopting a resolution recommending the
       City Council approve a number of amendments to the General and Development Plans to establish the
       renewable energy land use designation that would allow the construction of the project. During the
       meeting, 18 of 22 local residents in attendance voiced opposition to the project, citing concerns about
       potential damage to the city’s vistas, excessive dust caused by grading, and impacts to the quality of
       life for residents and tourists. The Planning Commission moved to continue the discussion at a future
       meeting and ultimately decided to transfer its decision-making authority to the City Council. On March
       23, 2026, the City Council held a public hearing and after a lengthy public comment session and
       discussion, it denied the project in a 3-1 vote, with one abstention.]71

     ● Fort Ross Pumped Storage Project (Sonoma County): Hydro Green Energy proposed the Fort Ross
       Pumped Storage Project in September 2022, a project expected to be built about 1.5 miles northwest
       of the historic Fort Ross. In July 2023, California Senate Majority Leader Mike McGuire stated, “there is
       no chance a project of this size, with this scope, will ever get approval in such an environmentally
       sensitive region like the Sonoma Coast . . . This project will not see the light of day.” Others quickly
       rallied in opposition to the proposal, including Richard Charter, director of the coastal coordination
       program for The Ocean Foundation, citing concerns about the project’s scale, impacts to the marine
       sanctuary, the lack of reliable power transmission in the area, and numerous indigenous archaeological
       sites in the area. At an August 2023 meeting planned by project advocates to answer community
       questions, local political and environmental leaders expressed strong opposition to the project. FERC
       denied Hydro Green Energy’s preliminary permit application in December 2023.72

     ● Fountain Wind Project (Shasta County): In October 2021, the Shasta County Board of Supervisors
       upheld the Shasta County Planning Commission’s rejection of a permit application for the Fountain
       Wind Project, a 4,500-acre, 200-MW wind farm proposed by Repsol. The project has faced significant
       opposition from the community and from the Pit River Tribe, whose ancestral homelands are within
       the project area. In denying the appeal, supervisors emphasized (a) the height and visibility of the
       turbines and (b) the potential that the presence of turbines could exacerbate the challenge of fighting
       wildfires. In June 2022, Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 205 into law, which allowed the developer
       to revive the application and the California Energy Commission to consider overruling the decision. In
       November 2023, Shasta County and the Pit River Tribe filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the
       Commission from approving the project. The California Attorney General moved for a change of venue,
       citing possible prejudice against the California Energy Commission in the County. In April 2024, a Shasta
       County Superior Court judge denied the request for a change of venue but ruled that a judge from
       another county would preside over the lawsuit. In October 2024, the litigation was stayed. In March
       2025, the California Energy Commission’s staff assessment concluded that the benefits of the project
       did not outweigh its environmental costs. In November 2025, the Executive Director of the California
       Energy Commission recommended that the state reject the approval of the project. In December 2025,
       the California Energy Commission unanimously denied approval of the project.73

    ● Genesis Solar Energy Project (Riverside County): The Genesis Solar Energy Project is a 250-MW
      concentrated solar project developed by NextEra on 1,800 acres of land near the town of Blythe in
      Riverside County, California. In 2010, BLM briefly halted construction on a 125-acre portion of the site
      that the Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) asserted was a historic crematorium, burial ground, and
      village for the Mojave Tribes. After the BLM found no conclusive evidence of habitation, human
      remains, or funerals, BLM allowed construction to resume. This led CRIT to sue NextEra in May 2012 in
      the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, seeking to halt construction on the 125-acre
      portion. The court denied the tribe’s request for an injunction, and construction continued. Many
      cultural artifacts were destroyed during construction, compelling BLM to order NextEra to pay $3
      million for an ethnographic study of the site and scholarship for Indigenous students.74

    ● Granite Mountain Wind Energy Project (San Bernardino County): The Granite Mountain Wind Energy
      Project was a proposed 84-MW, 100-acre project that Renewable Energy Systems would have built on
      BLM land. The Apple Valley town council and nearby rural communities both expressed opposition to
      the project, based on concerns including impacts to sightlines, property values, and community values.
      A flyer organized by Lucerne Valley residents expressed similar concerns and encouraged individuals to
      submit comments against the project to BLM. In August 2013, the developer withdrew its application
      due to proximity to golden eagle nests.75

    ● Grant Line Solar Project (Alameda County): On September 18, 2022, a local group called Friends of

     ● Morro Bay Wind Area (San Luis Obispo County): In February 2024, 2 commercial fishing organizations
       filed a lawsuit in San Luis Obispo Superior Court seeking to block state agencies from issuing permits
       for site surveys for 3 proposed projects (Atlas Wind, Even Keel Wind, and Golden State Wind) in the
       376-square-mile Morro Bay Wind Energy Area. The lawsuit named the California Coastal Commission,
       the State Lands Commission, the developers of 3 offshore wind projects, and an offshore wind survey
       company as defendants, and it alleged that issuance of the permits would violate the California Coastal
       Act and the California Constitution.82

     ● Mount Signal Solar Farm (Imperial County): The Mount Signal Solar Farm, also known as the Imperial
       Valley Solar Project, is an 800-MW solar project built by 8minutenergy in Imperial Valley. The project
       was built in 3 phases beginning in 2011. In November 2010, a 3-day protest against the project
       occurred, which included members of Desert Survivors, Basin and Range Watch, Solar Done Right, the
       Quechan Tribe, Cocopah Tribe, Imperial Valley Environmental Justice Task Force, Comite Civico del
       Valle, Seeley Citizens United, and nearby residents. The project was temporarily paused in December
       2010 by a preliminary injunction issued by a judge in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of
       California, in response to a lawsuit filed by the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation. The
       Quechan Tribe’s lawsuit raised claims under NEPA, the NHPA, and the FLPMA.83

     ● Mulqueeney Ranch Wind Repowering Project (Alameda County): In November 2021, the National
       Audubon Society and local affiliates filed a lawsuit in Alameda County Superior Court challenging the
       county’s October 2021 approval of a new 80-MW wind project by Brookfield Renewables in the
       Altamont Pass. The lawsuit alleged insufficient environmental review and failure to adequately assess
       impacts to birds and bats. The lawsuit was eventually resolved by settlement agreement. In March
       2024, the county approved the conditional use permit for the project.84

     ● Napa Sanitation District Solar Farm (Napa County): In May 2024, the Napa Planning Commission voted
       to delay taking action on a proposal to build a 56-acre, 25-MW floating solar farm by Laketricity, at the
       recommendation of county staff. The delay would allow time for the commission to review the public
       comments and deliberate on the proposal. Several groups, including California Unions for Reliable
       Energy, as well as Citizens for Responsible Energy, oppose the project. Opponents have raised concerns
       about wildfire risks and impacts on biological resources. On the other side, a group called Napa Climate
       Now supports the project because it would increase the supply of locally-produced renewable energy
       to the county.85

     ● North Sky River Project (Kern County): In October 2012, Defenders of Wildlife, the Center for
       Biological Diversity, and the Sierra Club filed a lawsuit in federal court to block NextEra’s proposal for a
       100-turbine, 300-MW North Sky River Project due to its proximity to California Condor habitat in the
       Tehachapi Mountains. The lawsuit was unsuccessful, and the project was allowed to proceed. As
       completed, the project has a total capacity of 162 MW.86

     ● Panoche Valley Solar Farm (San Benito County): In 2010, San Benito County approved a 399-MW solar
       facility near the town of Hollister. Shortly thereafter, the Sierra Club, the Santa Clara Valley Audubon
       Society, and Save Panoche Valley sued the county, alleging that the project endangered key
       populations of native species. The environmental groups reached a settlement with the developer in
       2019, reducing the size of the project to 130 MW, less than one-third of the original plan.87

     ● Seguro Battery Storage Project (San Diego County): Plans to construct a 320-MW battery energy
       storage system on 22.5 acres of private land in the North County region of San Diego encountered local
       opposition by residents who raised concerns about fire risk and other issues. In November 2023,
       opponents started a change.org petition, which had received approximately 5,000 signatures by the
       end of 2024.88

     ● Shu’luuk Wind Project, a/k/a Kumeyaay II (San Diego County): In June 2013, the Campo tribe’s
       General Council voted 44-34 against Invenergy’s proposed Kumeyaay II Project (or Shu’luuk Wind
       Project). The project would have generated between 160 MW to 250 MW and included up to 85 wind
       turbines on 4,000 acres of tribal lands. In February 2014, the Bureau of Indian Affairs cancelled the
       final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), effectively ending the project.89

     ● Sienna Solar and Storage (San Bernardino County): In August 2023, Avantus proposed the Sienna Solar
       and Storage project, comprising up to 525 MW of solar energy generation and up to 525 MW of
       battery energy storage to be located on approximately 1,854 acres in Lucerne Valley. In October 2025,
       the San Bernardino County Planning Commission approved a conditional use permit for the project.
       Opponents of the project, including the Morongo Basin Conservation Association (MBCA), appealed
       the Commission’s decision to the County Board of Supervisors. The appeal alleged inconsistencies in
       the information submitted by the developer, including that the plans for the project as approved differ
       from the original proposal in terms of site location and capacity, raising concerns that the project will
       have a negative aesthetic impact and create excessive dust, and that the offsite impacts and
       decommissioning plans had not been properly addressed. [Note: On January 27, 2026, the County
       Board of Supervisors held a public hearing and unanimously voted to deny the appeal and uphold the
       Planning Commission’s approval of the project.]90

     ● Silurian Valley Solar Development (San Bernardino County): Iberdrola proposed a 200-MW solar farm
       in the Silurian Valley in 2014 on about 1,616 acres of BLM land. The site of the farm was directly
       between Death Valley National Park and the Mojave National Preserve, which local citizens and the
       National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) claimed would reduce habitat connectivity between
       the 2 areas. The project faced opposition from environmental groups including the Wilderness Society.
       BLM denied the permit in November 2014, citing the location's ecological, historical, recreational, and
       scenic importance.91

      operational and producing enough energy to power 40,000 homes.93

6.1 State Siting Framework97
Local governments have principal siting authority over electric generating projects, including wind and solar
energy projects, of any size. The local government has 120 days to decide a preliminary application, if required
by the local government’s land use regulations, and 90 days to decide a final application. The Colorado Public
Utilities Commission (CPUC) has authority to review any denial of a project application by a local government.
A certificate of public convenience and necessity is required from the CPUC for public utility facilities.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public engagement on project applications.

6.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Colorado. However, at
least 17 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by 16 counties across the state.98 (Weld County has
adopted at least 2 separate ordinances restricting renewable energy development.) Most of the local
ordinances in Colorado target solar energy development, but there are also restrictions on wind and battery
storage projects. Several of the ordinances impose moratoria on new development, but often only for short
periods of time (e.g., 6 to 12 months). This is notably different from other states, where multi-year moratoria
are more common. Colorado does, however, have several local ordinances imposing restrictive setback,
height, and other requirements that could have longer-term impacts on renewable energy development.

6.3 Contested Projects
     ● Hesperus Solar Project (La Plata County): Primergy Solar’s proposal to build a 155-MW solar project
       with 155 MW of battery storage on 1,900 acres in La Plata County has encountered opposition from a
       local group called Stop Hesperus Solar. Opponents have objected to the placement of panels on
       agricultural land and argued that the project will cause an irreversible loss of wildlife habitat in a major
       migration corridor. In January 2023, the La Plata County Planning Department informed Primergy Solar
       that its application was incomplete, finding that the application did not include a water demand study,
       among other issues. The company likely will need to resubmit its application for the project.99

     ● Invenergy’s Pueblo County Solar Project (Pueblo County): In December 2018, Pueblo County denied
       Invenergy’s application to construct a 700-acre, 100-MW solar energy generation facility with 5 MW of
       battery storage. Local residents opposed the project due to concerns about fire risk, property value
       depreciation, and visual impacts.100

     ● Montezuma Solar Project (Montezuma County): In June 2022, Empire Electric Association (EEA) began
       construction on a 5-MW solar project in Montezuma, Colorado. Residents fought the project, citing
       concerns about impacts to agricultural livelihoods and local wildlife, but they ultimately lost the battle
       to stop construction. Developers made certain concessions to residents, including setting the project
       back 50 feet from property lines, building an 8-foot-tall privacy fence around the project, and
       promising to plant trees when the project is finished.101

      ● Pronghorn Solar Park (Pueblo County): On June 9, 2022, Pueblo County denied Leeward Renewable
        Energy’s application to construct a 150-MW solar project on 831 acres of private land near the
        Comanche power plant. In denying the application, county commissioners cited pushback from
        residents and concerns about property values. County planning and development staff had also
        previously recommended that the application be denied due to impacts on local residents. Residents
        wearing matching t-shirts with stop signs cheered the decision, asserting that the project would have
        impeded their views of mountains and wildlife.102

      ● Sundance Solar and Storage Project (Elbert County): Cypress Creek submitted an application for the
        Sundance Solar and Storage Project, which would include 75 MW of solar energy and 50 MW of battery
        energy storage, approximately 3.5 miles north of the town of Kiowa. On April 22, 2025, the Elbert
        County Planning Commission voted 7-2 to deny a special use permit, citing concerns over property
        values and failure to meet the area’s rural design criteria. On May 14, 2025, with a vote of 2-1, the
        Board of County Commissioners approved the permit allowing the project to move forward. The
        project is expected to power approximately 15,000 homes and increase the county revenue from
        $16,000 to over $9.8 million over the next 40 years. Benefits of the “good neighbor commitment” by
        the developer include $200,000 in scholarships over the project’s lifespan and an additional $300,000
        in community investments during construction.103

      ● Tessera’s Saguache County Solar Thermal Project (Saguache County): In 2011, Tessera Solar withdrew
        its proposal to construct a 1,526-acre, 145-MW solar thermal facility in Saguache County, Colorado.
        The project faced organized opposition from local residents, who complained about noise, wildlife
        impacts, and the industrial nature of the project.104

7.1 State Siting Framework106
The state has principal siting authority over renewable energy projects of at least 1 megawatt (MW) in size. A
certificate of environmental compatibility and public necessity (CECPN) is required from the Connecticut Siting
Council for all projects that may have adverse environmental impacts, and for wind projects that are larger
than 65 MW in size (regardless of their environmental impacts).

Local governments may, within 65 days of the filing of an application for a CECPN with the Connecticut Siting
Council, regulate the siting of the project but any local decision may be overridden by the Council. The


106
   Conn. Gen. Stat. Ann. §§ 16-50i(a), 16-50x, 16-50x(a), 16-50k, 16-50m, 16-50p(a), 16-50x(d); Preston v. Conn. Siting Council, 20
Conn. App. 474, 483-84 (1990).



                                    Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 56
                                                                                                           Connecticut




Appellate Court of Connecticut has held that the Connecticut Siting Council “is empowered to review decisions
from [local] zoning commissions on a de novo basis, applying concerns that transcend those involved in local
zoning decisions, and that review may . . . result in the approval of a particular site although the facility failed
to meet the requirements of local zoning regulations.”

The Connecticut Siting Council must render a decision on an application for a CECPN within 180 days of the
filing of the application. The Council is required to conduct at least 1 public hearing within 150 days from
receipt of the application.

7.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Connecticut. In 2017,
the Connecticut state legislature enacted Public Act No. 17-281, which prohibits solar photovoltaic projects
that are 2 MW or larger on “core forest” or “prime farmland” statewide unless state regulators find that the
project will not “materially affect” the land’s status as core forest or prime farmland. In addition, at least 14
local governments in the state have adopted ordinances restricting renewable energy development,
particularly wind projects. Restrictions in the height of wind turbines are particularly common (included in 13
or the 14 local ordinances).

7.3 Contested Projects
      ● Connecticut Wind Colebrook Project (Litchfield County): In 2011, a community group called
        FairwindCT filed a lawsuit challenging the Connecticut Siting Council’s approval of BNE Energy’s
        petition to construct 6 1.6-MW wind turbines at 2 separate sites in the Town of Colebrook. The trial
        court dismissed the lawsuit, and, in 2014, after 3 years of litigation, the Connecticut Supreme Court
        upheld the dismissal. On January 9, 2020, BNE Energy submitted a request to the Connecticut Siting
        Council to modify the approved plan to allow installation of a different type of wind turbine. On March
        4, 2020, FairwindCT submitted an objection to the proposed modification, but the Executive Director of
        the Council ultimately approved the modification request. On June 1, 2020, FairwindCT and abutting
        landowners filed a petition with the Council for a declaratory ruling to disallow the modification. On
        December 17, 2020, the Council issued a final decision upholding the modification request. FairwindCT
        and the abutting landowners appealed to the New Britain Judicial District Superior Court, which, in
        November 2021, ruled in their favor, vacating the Council’s approval of the requested modification.107

      ● Denslow Hill Road Solar Project (New Haven County): In August 2024, the Connecticut Siting Council
        unanimously rejected a plan for a 1.5-MW solar project, citing concerns over the developer’s plans to
        remove about 7.9 acres of trees. In September 2024, the developer filed an appeal to the decision. In
        the appeal, the developer claimed that the council “exceeded” its authority, arguing that, as the owner
        of the land, the developer could have cleared the trees without local zoning approval and then
        submitted the proposal to the Siting Council, which would have had “no basis” for denying it.108

        comment period. On January 24, 2025, the Connecticut Siting Council issued its final decision

8.1 State Siting Framework116
Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. The Delaware Energy Office
is charged with providing general support for the responsible siting of renewable energy projects but does not
have final decision-making authority over projects.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the project approval
process.

wind energy development and the other targeting solar energy projects – in 2022.117

9.1 State Siting Framework123
Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects less than 75 megawatts (MW) in
size. However, project developers may opt-into a state-level siting process, which is administered by the
Florida Siting Board (described below).

In 2021, Florida enacted legislation preventing local governments from restricting solar energy facilities on
agricultural land. The law provides that “[a] solar facility shall be a permitted use in all agricultural land use
categories in a local government comprehensive plan and all agricultural zoning districts within an
unincorporated area.” The law further provides that, although counties may adopt ordinances specifying

123
   Fla. Stat. Ann. §§ 163.3205(3)-(4), 403.503(14), 403.506, 403.508(f), 403.508(2)(c), 403.510, 403.508(2)(a), 403.508(5),
403.509(1)(b), 403.5066(b), 403.50663



                                   Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 68
                                                                                                                     Florida




buffer and landscaping requirements, any such requirements “may not exceed the requirements for similar
uses involving the construction of other facilities that are permitted uses in agricultural land use categories
and zoning districts.” (There is no equivalent state legislation addressing local regulation of wind facilities.)

The state has principal siting authority over solar projects larger than 75 MW. These larger projects must
generally obtain a certification from the Florida Siting Board. In non-contested cases, a certification may be
issued by the Secretary of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Applications for certification
must be filed with the Department of Environmental Protection’s Siting Coordination Office, which has 40 days
to determine if the application is complete. If the application is contested, a certification hearing must be held
within 265 days of the filing of the application. Within 45 days following the hearing, a Siting Board
Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) must issue a Recommended Order, indicating whether the certification should
be issued and, if so, on what conditions. Following the ALJ’s recommendation, the Siting Board must issue a
decision within 60 days.

9.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Florida. In 2024, the
Florida state legislature enacted legislation prohibiting the construction or expansion of any wind energy
facility offshore, within 1 mile of the coastline or intercoastal waterways, or on any waters or submerged
lands. No local restrictive ordinances have been identified in Florida.

      ● Cubico Solar Farm in West Bibb County (Bibb County): On May 23, 2022, the Macon-Bibb Planning and

        Commissioners voted to deny a permit to the developer Silicon Ranch to construct a 4,700-acre solar
        farm in Kathleen. The proposal faced opposition from local naturalists due to its proximity to the
        13,450-acre Oaky Woods Wildlife Management Area, which hosts a regionally significant population of

11.1 State Siting Framework132
Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. A special use permit
from the relevant county planning commission is required for solar projects that will occupy more than 20
acres or 10% of the parcel of land on which they are to be sited. For solar projects that will occupy more than
15 acres, approval by the Hawaii Land Use Commission is also required. Solar projects are not permitted in
agricultural districts. Wind projects are allowed in agricultural districts without restrictions.

For projects requiring approval by the Hawaii Land Use Commission, the county initially reviews the project
and must send its decision to the Commission, which then has 45 days to issue a decision. The county must
hold at least 2 public hearings for projects to be developed on public lands. Hearings for projects on private
land are at the discretion of the county.

      HRS §§ 171-95.3, 171-95.3(c), 205-6(b), 205-2(d)(6), 205-6(e)

11.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Hawaii. Only 1 restrictive
local ordinance has been identified. In 2024, the City of Honolulu adopted an ordinance, imposing extremely
onerous setback requirements for wind energy facilities (i.e., the greater of 1.25 miles or 10 times turbine
height).

11.3 Contested Projects
      ● Kahuku Na Pua Makani Wind Project (Honolulu County): Local opposition to the planned 24-MW Na
        Pua Makani wind project in Kahuku on the North Shore of Oahu reduced the scope of the project from
        13-15 turbines to 8 turbines. In 2016, Keep the North Shore Country filed a contested case hearing
        petition to challenge the developer’s plan for mitigating impacts to endangered species including the
        Hawaiian Hoary Bat. In 2018, the Board of Land and Natural Resources accepted the developer’s plan
        and issued an incidental take license for the project. Keep the North Shore Country appealed that
        decision. In May 2019, the state Circuit Court upheld the state agency’s decision to grant the license,
        and in February 2022, the Supreme Court of Hawaii affirmed on appeal. While this lawsuit was
        pending, Keep the North Shore Country filed a separate petition challenging the proximity of the
        turbines to schools and homes under Honolulu’s zoning ordinance, and an organization called Life of
        the Land filed a motion to block the project’s power purchase agreement. In addition to legal
        challenges, there were significant protests: in October 2019, approximately 128 protesters were
        arrested while trying to block wind turbines from being delivered to the construction site.133

        Kawailoa Wind LLC, sought to amend its Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) and Incidental Take License

12.1 State Siting Framework136
Local governments have principal siting authority over “electric plant” projects that “facilitate the production,
generation, transmission, delivery or furnishing of electricity” (including wind and solar energy projects).
However, with limited exceptions, electric plant projects also require a certificate of public convenience and
necessity (CPCN) from the Idaho Public Utilities Commission (IPUC). Where a CPCN is issued to a public utility,
that will override any conflicting local government action or order.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no
deadline for the local government or IPUC to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

12.2 Restrictive State Statutes Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Idaho. Of the 44 counties
in the state, at least 10 have adopted restrictive local ordinances targeting wind and/or solar energy
development. At least 6 counties – Gooding, Bannock, Bonneville, Cassia, Elmore, and Twin Falls – have
imposed either temporary moratoria or permanent bans on renewable energy projects.137 Several counties
have also established onerous setback, height, and noise requirements for projects.

12.3 Contested Projects
      ● Blue Ribbon Energy Project (Bingham County): In 2010, Blue Ribbon Energy applied for a permit to
        construct 27 wind turbines near Goshen, Idaho. The Bingham County Planning and Zoning Commission
        denied the request, citing a lack of sufficient information on the turbines’ proximity to residences. The
        developer appealed to the Bingham County commissioners, who reversed the denial and granted
        approval. However, a second phase of the project was rejected in 2012, due to concerns over property
        values, as well as the purported health and safety risks of wind energy.138

      ● Harmon Solar Project (Bannock County): Balanced Rock Power’s planned 300-MW, 2,400-acre solar
        farm is on pause after the Bannock County Public Commission voted to ban large-scale solar
        developments. Residents had opposed the Harmon Solar Project and other projects, citing concerns
        that solar and wind farm developments would negatively impact local wildlife, as well as the natural
        beauty and the safety of the Marsh Valley.139

      ● Lava Ridge Wind Energy Project (Jerome, Lincoln, and Minidoka Counties): The proposed Lava Ridge
        Wind Energy Project would be the largest wind farm in Idaho, with 400 turbines up to 740 feet tall
        producing 1,000 MW of electricity on federal land. However, it has encountered opposition due to its
        size and proximity to the Minidoka National Historic Site where 13,000 Japanese Americans were
        imprisoned during the 1940s. In May 2022, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named the
        Minidoka National Historic Site as 1 of the 11 most endangered historic places in the country due to
        the proposed wind farm, which would be visible from the visitor center. In July and August 2022, all
        three counties in which the project would be located passed resolutions against it. On January 20,
        2023, BLM released a draft environmental impact statement in which BLM stated that its 2 preferred
        alternatives would consist of a reduced number of turbines (269 or 378 turbines rather than the 400
        turbines the developer is seeking to construct), due to concerns raised in the review process. In March
        2023, the Idaho House and Idaho Senate each adopted unanimous resolutions opposing the project. In

13.1 State Siting Framework143
Local governments have principal siting authority over commercial wind and solar energy projects. However, a
local government may not set standards that are more restrictive than state requirements for any commercial
wind energy project that is 50 kilowatts or larger, or for any size commercial solar project.

The state requirements specify maximum setback distances, sound limitations, flicker limitations, and
construction and decommissioning standards. Moreover, state law mandates that counties “may not adopt
zoning regulations that disallow, permanently or temporarily, commercial wind energy facility or commercial
solar energy facilities from being developed or operated in any district zones to allow agricultural or industrial
uses” and “may not require permit application fees for a commercial wind energy facility or commercial solar
energy facility that are unreasonable” (among other things).

The local government must hold a public hearing within 60 days of the filing of a project application and make
a decision within 30 days of the public hearing.

13.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Illinois. In 2023, the
Illinois state legislature enacted Senate Bill 1127, which prohibits solar and wind energy development in the
Lee-Ogle Enterprise Zone, a 2,000-acre area in and around Rochelle in northern Illinois. In addition to this state
action, at least 21 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in 19 counties.144 Two counties – Iroquois
and Moultrie – have each adopted 2 separate restrictive ordinances. Wind energy projects have been the
most common target of local restrictions, but some also target solar and/or battery storage projects.
Ordinances imposing temporary moratoria or indefinite bans on projects have been adopted in at least 15
counties (out of 102 total in the state). Restrictive setback, shadow flicker, and noise rules have also been
adopted in some counties.

    ● Grain Belt Express (Christian, Clark, Cumberland, Greene, Macoupin, Montgomery, Pike, Scott, and
      Shelby Counties): In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of a high-voltage
      direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border to transmit clean
      energy. The Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) first approved it in 2015. Landowner and agriculture
      groups called Concerned Citizens and Property Owners, Illinois Agricultural Association, and
      Landowners Alliance of Central Illinois challenged the approval in state court, and, in 2018, an Illinois
      appellate court overturned the approval on the grounds that regulators improperly allowed the
      company to use an expedited review process. The project was eventually taken over in 2020 by
      Invenergy, but the previous court order still prevented the project from going forward. In 2022, Gov.
      J.B. Pritzker signed the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which enabled construction to proceed despite
      the court’s ruling. The ICC approved the project for the second time in March 2023, allowing Invenergy
      to start building the HVDC power line. In August 2023, an Illinois appellate court enacted a stay on
      implementation of the March 2023 order to decide the project’s constitutionality. In September 2023,
      the court lifted the stay allowing the developer to continue with planning while the appeal moves
      forward. In August 2024, the Illinois appellate court reversed the ICC’s March 2023 approval of the
      project, citing issues with the financing of the project. In November 2024, the state’s Supreme Court
      granted leave to hear the appeal of the appellate court’s ruling. On July 23, 2025 the U.S. Department
      of Energy announced the cancellation of a $4.9 billion conditional federal loan guarantee for phase 1 of
      the project from Ford County, Kansas to Callaway County, Missouri. [Note: In January 2026, the Illinois
      Supreme Court decided the pending appeal and ruled in favor of the developer, allowing the company
      to move forward with construction of the project.]152

14.1 State Siting Framework164
Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. However, state law
dictates that local governments may not unreasonably restrict solar projects, except to protect public health
and safety. There is no similar prohibition on local governments restricting wind projects in state law.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no
deadline for local governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

14.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Indiana. Local
restrictions are fairly widespread, however. At least 36 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by 33
counties (out of 92 total) across Indiana. Three counties – Fulton, Hamilton, and Madison – have each adopted
at least 2 restrictive local ordinances. Most of the ordinances target wind and/or solar energy development.
Only 1, adopted in Boone County, also seeks to restrict battery storage projects. At least 16 counties have
ordinances imposing either temporary moratoria or indefinite bans on wind, solar, and/or battery storage
projects. Caps on the amount of land that can be used for projects are also fairly common in Indiana, as are
restrictive setbacks and noise restrictions.

14.3 Contested Projects
      ● Aypa Solar Project (Jefferson County): In September 2024, the Madison City Council voted to deny a
        rezoning proposal that would have allowed the proposed Aypa Power solar farm to proceed in
        Madison, Indiana. Residents expressed concerns about buffer zones and impacts on the environment
        and wildlife.165

      ● Big Blue Ribbon Wind Farm (Henry County): The Henry County Planning Commission rejected a
        proposal for the Big Blue Ribbon Wind Farm in 2019 amidst community opposition to the project.
        Residents raised concerns about health impacts and property rights, arguing that a 1,500-foot setback
        from homes was not sufficient.166

      ● BrightNight Solar Project (Clark County): In October 2023, the Clark County Board of Zoning Appeals
        denied a special exemption permit for a 3,900-acre solar project proposed by developer BrightNight.
        The permit was necessary because the project would have been built on agricultural land. Residents
        opposed the project on the basis of potential impacts to viewsheds. In 2025, the developer re-
        submitted the application for the project with a modified plan for developing only 1,500 acres and
        expanding the setbacks from 150 feet to 650 feet. At a public meeting on June 18, 2025 the Clark
        County Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) reached a stalemate, voting 2-2 on the application. On August
        20, 2025, the project was rejected by the BZA in a 3-2 vote.167

      ● Carina Solar (Bartholomew County): Plans to construct the 100-MW Carina Solar project on 1,880
        acres of land under Bartholomew County and City of Columbus jurisdiction encountered opposition
        from a local group Nonprofit Bartholomew County Citizens Concerned about Commercial Solar Fields

15.1 State Siting Framework190
Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects that are less than 25
megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting of larger projects (25 MW or larger).
A certificate of public convenience, use, and necessity from the Iowa Utilities Board is required for these larger
facilities. State law provides that “[t]he failure of a facility to meet zoning requirements” established by cities
or counties “shall not preclude the board from issuing the certificate.”

A public hearing is required on certificate applications submitted to the Utilities Board. There is no statutory
deadline for the Iowa Utilities Board to issue a final decision on certificate applications.

15.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Iowa. Local-level
restrictions are common, however. At least 52 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in 43 counties
(out of 99 total) across Iowa.191 Eight counties – Floyd, Henry, Page, Pottawattamie, Ringgold, Scott, Sioux, and
Woodbury – have multiple restrictive local ordinances. Most of the ordinances target wind and solar energy
projects, but there are also a small number of restrictions on battery storage and transmission development.
Onerous setbacks are the most common type of restriction, being included in at least 23 local ordinances. At
least 21 ordinances include moratoria / bans on development and 12 establish size or capacity limits for
projects.
