15.3 Contested Projects
      ●   Arbor Hill Wind Farm (Madison County): In August 2018, the Madison County Coalition for Scenic
          Preservation challenged Madison County’s decision to approve this 52-turbine wind farm. In June 2019
          the state district court dismissed the case and the plaintiffs appealed; the Iowa Court of Appeals
          affirmed the lower court in January 2021. However, in December 2020, Madison County adopted an
          ordinance capping the number of turbines in the county at the current number, effectively preventing
          the project from proceeding. In January 2021, MidAmerican sued the county, and in March 2022, the
          parties reached a settlement allowing the company to construct 30 turbines. However, in July 2022,
          MidAmerican abandoned plans to move forward with the project, due to the reduction in size, among
          other issues.192

      ●   Coggon Solar (Linn County): Beginning in 2019, the developer of Coggon Solar began public outreach
          related to an application for a 640-acre, 100-MW solar project in Linn County. After residents voiced
          opposition to taking farmland out of commission, the Planning & Zoning Commission voted to
          recommend that the County Board of Supervisors deny the project. In January 2022, the Board voted
          2-1 to approve the project. However, a family who lives near the proposed project brought a lawsuit
          against the board of supervisors, and, in July 2022, the Iowa Utilities Board denied Coggon Solar’s
          request for a certificate while the lawsuit was ongoing. On or before February 1, 2023, the court

      ●   Red Rock Wind Energy Center (Emmet County): In 2024, Invenergy proposed the Red Rock Wind
          Energy Center with a total capacity of 300 MW, to be developed in phases on property in Emmet,
          Dickinson, Clay Counties (see entry on Dickinson County). In October 2024, the Emmet County Board of
          Adjustment denied a conditional use permit for the phase of the project in Emmet County. In
          December 2024, the developer filed a lawsuit against the Board of Adjustment alleging that the denial
          was in bad faith as the project proposal was not subject to the 2024 moratorium halting the issuance
          of conditional use permits for wind projects that the county adopted within days of its application. The
          developer asserts that its permit application complies with the requirements of the 2011 ordinance
          regulating wind projects in the county. As of November 2025, the developer and the Emmet County
          Board of Supervisors were negotiating a settlement agreement to resolve the pending lawsuit and
          approve the conditional use permit for the project, subject to the terms and conditions in the
          agreement.198

      ●   Salt Creek Wind (Tama County): In August 2022, a local resident involved with Tama County Against
          Turbines Coalition filed a petition for declaratory judgment that the conditional use permits issued by
          the Tama County Board of Adjustment to Salt Creek Wind were illegal. Two months earlier, in June
          2022, another member of the same group filed a lawsuit against the board for failing to vote on a
          moratorium on wind energy and for readopting the existing wind ordinance without following proper
          procedures. The June 2022 case was dismissed in October 2022. At a public meeting in December
          2022, several residents urged the board to adopt a 6-month or 12-month moratorium. In April 2023,
          Salt Creek Wind, LLC sued Tama County Against Turbines and several of its individual members,
          claiming that the group had “chastised and bullied the [Board of] Supervisors [to] issue a moratorium
          on wind energy projects” and had “filed frivolous lawsuits . . . to frustrate . . . contracts between Salt
          Creek and the local landowners.” Also in April 2023, Southern Natural Resources, LLC (SNR) sued Salt
          Creek Wind, LLC and associated companies, alleging that the development was in violation of SNR’s
          exclusive development rights in the area and that the project misappropriated proprietary and trade
          secret information.199

    ●   Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm (Freemont and Page Counties): In August 2022, the Page County Board
        of Supervisors approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of opposition from
        residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning agreements. Just
        over a month after the approval, residents opposed to the project filed a lawsuit against the county
        and board in state court, which was later removed to federal court. In February 2023, after the
        developer, Invenergy, informed the Board of Supervisors that it would be removing 3 turbines from the
        plan, the Page County Zoning Administrator informed the developer that this was a “material change,”
        which rendered the application “void” and revoked the permit. The developer appealed the Zoning
        Administrator’s decision to the Page County Board of Adjustment. In March 2023, the Board of
        Adjustment upheld the revocation of the permit. A week later, the developer filed a lawsuit against the
        County officials in federal court challenging the revocation. In May 2024, the federal court denied the
        residents’ state claims which had been rendered moot at the time the permit was revoked. In
        November 2024, in a 2-1 vote, the Board of Supervisors approved a resolution to enter into a
        settlement agreement resolving the pending litigation and allowing the developer to proceed with
        construction of the project. In November 2025, construction of the project was completed, and the
        facility began operating with a total of 54 wind turbines and a generating capacity of 214 MW.200

      ●   Siouxland Wind Farm (Woodbury County): The viability of MidAmerican Energy’s plans to construct
          the 90-turbine Siouxland Wind Farm is in doubt due to Woodbury County’s adoption of an ordinance in
          August 2022 that increased the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250

          177 to 1.7. Opponents of the project cited noise and visual impacts, and over 700 residents signed a

          “[MidAmerican] just need[s] to pack up and go somewhere else where it’s more suitable.”

          changes.202

16.1 State Siting Framework204
Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. There is no statutory
requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local
governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

16.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Kansas. Since 2004,
successive state Governors have blocked wind energy development in parts of the Flint Hills region in eastern
Kansas. Since 2009, at least 20 counties (out of 105 total) in Kansas have adopted at least 23 local ordinances
restricting wind and solar energy development.205 Three counties – Douglas, Linn, and McPherson – have each

16.3 Contested Projects
      ● Acciona Barton County Solar Project (Barton County): Local community members opposed a proposed
        300-MW solar project near Cheyenne Bottoms, the largest inland wetland in the United States. Several
        public hearings attracted large crowds of opposition. The County Commission first approved a
        moratorium on all commercial-scale solar in May 2023, then in March 2024, the Commission adopted
        zoning changes that specify a no-build zone within the Cheyenne Bottoms Basin.206

      ● Anderson County Wind Farm (Anderson County): In 2015, Calpine Corporation proposed a 200-MW
        wind project on 30,000 acres on a ridge in Eastern Anderson County. A group called Landowners
        Against Windmills organized in opposition. The group argued that the county’s zoning director
        unlawfully allowed Calpine to construct a 328-foot weather monitoring tower without a special use
        permit, violating public notice requirements. The tower was subsequently destroyed by vandalism at a
        loss of $200,000. The project was apparently abandoned. As of February 2023, there are no Calpine
        projects in Kansas or public plans to build in Anderson County.207

      ● Argyle Creek Wind Project (Sumner County): In January 2017, nearly 60 residents of Sumner County
        filed a lawsuit to challenge the county’s approval of a conditional use permit for the 60-turbine, 150-
        MW Argyle Creek Wind Farm. In September 2017, a judge ruled against the Sumner County
        Commission, thereby blocking the project.208

      ● Neosho Ridge Wind (Neosho County): Plans by Apex Clean Energy to construct a 139-turbine, 300-MW
        wind farm in Neosho County were met with opposition from residents. Objections to the project
        included concerns regarding the cost of the project and potential issues with regulating the wind farm
        due to the lack of a strong zoning ordinance. After Apex Clean Energy received a permit for the project,
        45 landowners filed a lawsuit in federal court to stop the project as an anticipatory nuisance. The court
        denied the developer’s motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that the plaintiffs adequately
        alleged a claim of anticipatory nuisance. In June 2020, the parties voluntarily stipulated to dismissal,
        and the project entered commercial operation in 2021.216

      ● Pretty Prairie Wind Farm (Reno County): A proposed 80-turbine, 220-MW wind farm by NextEra
        encountered local opposition in Reno County. After the Reno County Planning Commission issued a
        negative recommendation, 233 residents submitted protest petitions, which forced a unanimous vote
        of the Reno County Commission. In June 2019, the County Commission voted 2-1 in favor of the
        project, but, without a unanimous vote, the permit could not be issued. In July 2021, the developer
        filed a lawsuit alleging that the protest petitions were invalid, but in May 2020, the court ruled against
        the developer. In August 2022, the state appellate court upheld the decision that the protest petitions
        were legal sufficient to force a unanimous decision.217

17.1 State Siting Framework218
Local governments have principal siting authority over energy generation projects, including wind and solar
energy projects, that are less than 10 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting
of larger energy generation facilities (10 MW or more). These larger projects require a construction certificate
from the Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation but are still subject to local zoning ordinances.

The State Board must make a decision on a certificate application within 120 days of receipt or 180 days if a
hearing is requested. The applicant is required to hold a public meeting prior to filing a certificate application.
The State Board must also convene a public hearing upon the request of 3 or more local residents or certain
local officials.

17.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Kentucky. House Bill
291 of 2013 establishes minimum setbacks for wind energy projects in the state of at least 1,000 feet from
property lines and at least 2,000 feet from any residential neighborhood, school, hospital, or nursing home.
Caldwell County has adopted its own ordinance imposing even more restrictive setbacks for wind projects,
requiring them to be at least 2,500 feet from residential buildings (with certain exceptions). Local ordinances
restricting solar energy development have been adopted in at least 12 other counties. Nine of these
ordinances include restrictive setbacks. Bans / moratoria are less common, but have been adopted in some
counties, as have use and viewshed restrictions.

   ○ Total number of state-level restrictions: 1
   ○ Total number of local restrictions: 13
   ○ Technology targeted Restrictions by type:
        ■ 1 (wind)
        ■ 12 (solar)
   ○ Type of restrictions:
        ■ Kentucky House Bill 291 of 2014: Rule 6a and 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)
           ■ Boyle County: Rule 3: Use Restriction (solar)
           ■ Breckinridge County: Rule 10a and 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
           ■ Caldwell County: Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)
           ■ Calloway County: Rule 10a: Setback Restriction (solar)
           ■ City of Hopkinsville (Christian County): Rule 10a: Setback Restriction (solar)
           ■ City of Villa Hills (Kenton County): Rule 3: Use Restriction (solar) | Rule 5: Viewshed Restriction
               (solar)
           ■ Lyon County: Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
           ■ Mason County: Rule 10a and 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
           ■ McCracken County: Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (solar) | Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
           ■ Meade County: Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (solar)
           ■ Ohio County: Rule 10a: Setback Restriction (solar)

18.1 State Siting Framework226
Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that will occupy less than 75 acres
of land. A permit from the Louisiana Department of Energy and Natural Resources (DENR) is required for solar
facilities that will occupy 75 or more acres of land, with certain exceptions for facilities owned by electric
utilities. A permit from the DENR is also required for all onshore wind facilities.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no
deadline for local governments or the state DENR to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

      La. R.S. §§ 33:106, 33:109, 30:1131 and 1141 through 1145, 30.1154(A), 30.1154(D)

18.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Louisiana. House Bill
459 of 2025 introduced restrictive setback and noise limits for solar energy projects. Both solar and wind
projects have also been restricted under local ordinances. Of the 64 Parishes in Louisiana, 9 – Ascension,
Bossier, Caddo, Iberia, Jefferson, Rapides, Richland, St. James, and Washington – have adopted restrictive local
ordinances. Most (8 of the 9) establish restrictive setbacks for solar or wind projects..

   ○ Total number of state restrictions: 1
   ○ Total number of local restrictions: 9
   ○ Technology targeted:
        ■ 2 (wind)
        ■ 7 (solar)
   ○ Type of Restrictions:

        ■ Ascension Parish: Rule 10a and 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
        ■ Boassier Parish: Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
        ■ Caddo Parish: Rule 8: Shadow Flicker Restriction (wind)
        ■ Iberia Parish: Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (solar) | Rule 10a: Setback Restriction (solar)
        ■ Jefferson Davis Parish: Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)
        ■ Rapides Parish: Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
        ■ Richland Parish: Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
        ■ St. James Parish: Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)
        ■ Washington Parish: Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)

18.3 Contested Projects
   ● Cajun Crescent Energy Center (Calcasieu Parish): In September 2021, local residents of Southeast
     Calcasieu Parish filed a lawsuit against the parish zoning board and police jury to contest the approval
     of a 3,400-acre solar farm that would generate 300 to 400 MW. Opponents of the project stated that
     they have not received sufficient guarantees as to human health and safety, as well as impacts on birds




                         Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 131
                                                                                                                     Louisiana




         and other wildlife. On November 19, 2024, the Calcasieu Planning and Zoning Board rejected a zoning
         exception necessary for construction to proceed.227

      ● St. James Solar (St. James Parish): In June 2024, after more than 2.5 hours of comments at a public
        meeting, the St. James Parish Council denied by 4-3 vote a land use permit for St. James Solar, a 2,200-
        acre, 360-MW solar farm proposed by D.E. Shaw Renewable Investments (DESRI). The Council’s denial
        followed the St. James Parish Planning Commission’s 8-1 rejection of the project in April 2024. DESRI
        had agreed to offer a $4.67 million community benefits package and stated that the solar farm would
        have extensive buffers, fencing, and screening such that it would be virtually invisible and noiseless to
        passerby. The project, however, would have required a special exception from the agricultural and
        residential land use designations in the land use plan, which prohibit solar farms, and that exception
        was denied. DESRI’s original plan for a 3,500-acre version of the project had prompted the Council to
        enact a moratorium and a new ordinance on solar farms in 2022.228

      ● White Castle Solar Farm (Iberville and Pointe Coupee Parishes): Developer NextEra has proposed a
        2,057-acre solar project in Iberville and Pointe Coupee Parishes. Pointe Coupee Parish residents have
        generally not opposed the project, but a contingent in Iberville Parish has stood in strong opposition to
        it. Citing concerns about devalued property, loss of farmland, and impacts to the parishes’ rural
        atmosphere, project opponents held up signs saying “no solar” and “you’re not wanted here” at a
        September 2023 parish meeting. Parish President Mitchell Ourso voiced his opposition to the project,
        saying, “I cannot support this project here in our parish. . . . Before there was industry in our parish,
        everything was agriculture. This has no economic impact, and I think it can be detrimental for years to
        come in White Castle.”229

19.1 State Siting Framework230
All wind and solar energy projects must be approved by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection
(DEP). Solar energy projects require the following permits from the DEP: a stormwater permit if the project
will occupy 20 acres or less; a permit under the Site Location of Development Act if the project is larger than
20 acres; and a Natural Resources Protection Act permit if the project will be sited near protected natural
resources.

Wind project permitting differs depending on the size and location of the project. Grid-scale wind projects that
are to be developed outside an expedited permitting area require a permit from the DEP under the Site
Location of Development Act. A public hearing must generally be held on permit applications, but that
requirement can be waived in certain circumstances. Before issuing a permit, the DEP must determine that the
project meets applicable standards including with respect to noise mitigation, stormwater management, and
protection of groundwater, wildlife and fisheries, and natural areas.

Grid-scale wind projects to be located within an expedited permitting area identified by the Maine Land Use
Planning Commission and small-scale wind projects (non-grid-scale later 0.1 megawatts) that are proposed
outside of an expedited permitting area are regulated under the Maine Energy Act. Under the Maine Energy
Act, the DEP must certify that the wind development will meet the noise control requirements adopted by the
Board of Environmental Protection, will be designed and sited to avoid unreasonable adverse shadow flicker
effects, and will be constructed with setbacks adequate to protect public safety as recommended by a licensed
civil engineer and by a manufacturer of the generating facility.

The DEP must issue a decision on permit applications for wind projects in expedited permitting areas within
185 days of accepting the application, or within 270 days if a public hearing is held.

19.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 2 state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been adopted in Maine. In 2018,
then Maine Governor Paul LePage signed an executive order, imposing a moratorium on wind energy
development in parts of the state. The moratorium was ended by Governor Janet Mills when she took office in
2019. However, in 2021, Governor Mills signed into law L.D. 1619, which permanently banned offshore wind
development in state waters off the Maine coast. In addition to these state-level actions, at least 32 local
ordinances restricting wind, solar, and related transmission projects have been adopted by 29 cities and towns
in Maine.231 Two towns – the Town of Albion and the Town of Dixmont – have each adopted 2 restrictive local

19.3 Contested Projects
   ● Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project (Kennebec and Waldo Counties): The Aroostook Renewable
     Gateway Project is a 150-mile, 1,200-MW transmission corridor designed to transmit energy from the
     proposed 170-turbine King Pine Wind Farm in Aroostook County to consumers in southern Maine and
     Massachusetts. LS Power was initially developing the project. In June 2023, Maine adopted a bill
     approving the project, but the project has been slowed by local opposition and moratoria. Maine
     residents opposing the project have raised concerns about impacts to property and sightlines, formed
     a citizen group called Preserve Rural Maine, and obtained legal counsel. In August 2023, in response to
     this project, the town of Albion imposed a 6-month moratorium on utility lines and corridors, with
     residents expressing concerns that the project would disrupt farmland and that the project’s
     electromagnetic fields would disorient bees. Also, in response to the project, in September 2023, the
     Town of Palermo adopted a transmission line moratorium. In November 2023, the Town of Unity
     adopted a 180-day moratorium on high-voltage power lines. In December 2023, LS Power announced
     that it could no longer proceed with the project at the agreed-upon price. In response, the Maine
     Public Utilities Commission announced that it was terminating its agreement with LS Power and
     delaying development until it could find another developer for the project. However, in October 2024,
     the Department of Energy announced a $425 million capacity contract with Avangrid to restart
     conversations with the Maine PUC on continuing the transmission project. In November 2024, the

      ● Bull Hill Wind Project (Hancock County): In 2011, the local organization Concerned Citizens of Rural
        Hancock County (CCRHC) intervened in a public evidentiary hearing before the Land Use Regulation
        Commission (LURC) to challenge developer Blue Sky East, LLC’s request for a permit to build the 19-
        turbine, 34-MW Bull Hill Wind Project. The opponents argued that the wind farm would ruin the
        landscape and threaten wildlife while generating very little electricity. The LURC approved the project
        after imposing more stringent noise requirements and requiring a community benefits package of
        $4,000 per turbine per year.235

      ● Fox Islands Wind (Knox County): In April 2010, a group of neighbors organized as the Fox Islands Wind
        Neighbors began complaining about noise from the recently completed 4.5-MW Fox Islands Wind
        project. In November 2010, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) commenced
        enforcement proceedings and instructed Fox Islands Wind to submit a revised operation protocol to
        address noise issues. In April 2011, DEP accepted the revised protocol and issued a conditional
        compliance order. In July 2011, Fox Islands Wind Neighbors filed a petition in superior court
        challenging the order. In May 2015, after 4 years of litigation, Maine’s Supreme Judicial Court
        concluded that the order was supported by substantial record evidence and within the agency’s
        discretion.236

      ● Greene Apple Solar (Androscoggin County): At a town meeting on June 18, 2022, residents of Greene
        voted overwhelmingly against a proposal to lease 80 acres of public land to Greene Apple Solar Power
        as part of a 600-acre, 120-MW solar farm. Opponents explained that they wanted the town to develop
        the 80 acres into recreational fields instead. The developer plans to move forward with the parts of the
        project that will be sited on private land.237

      ● Pulpit Rock Road Solar (Cumberland County): A 7-acre, 1-MW solar farm proposed by Allen Solar is
        facing resistance from the town of Raymond. In December 2023, residents expressed their concerns to
        the Raymond Planning Board, and in March 2024, residents advocated for a moratorium to the
        Raymond Select Board. Residents living next to the site stated that they would initiate legal action to
        halt the project if necessary and have hired an attorney to draft changes to the current ordinances.
        Opponents have said that they support renewable energy, but argue that such projects do not belong
        in a residential area, citing concerns about potential negative impacts to the environment, including
        ecosystems and water sources, and to property values. The developer stated that it has worked to
        address these concerns and that the project complies with current ordinances and minimizes
        environmental impact. As of March 2024, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection was
        reviewing the project to determine whether it meets the requirements for the approval of a permit.245

      ● Saddleback Ridge Wind Farm (Franklin County): In 2012, the organization Friends of Maine Mountains
        (“Friends”) filed an appeal with the Maine Supreme Judicial Court challenging the state Board of
        Environmental Protection (BEP)’s February 18, 2012 final order approving the 34-MW Saddleback
        Ridge Wind Project. The BEP’s order affirmed the state Department of Environmental Protection
        (DEP)’s approval of the project. Friends alleged that BEP misapplied the nighttime sound limits and
        argued that certain provisions of the Maine Wind Energy Act were unconstitutional. In March 2013, the
        court unanimously vacated the BEP’s decision and remanded for further administrative proceedings.
        The court found that BEP abused its discretion by allowing 45 dBA of noise during the nighttime after
        having adopted a nighttime limit of 42 dBA. The court, however, found no merit in Friends’
        constitutional challenges to the Maine Wind Energy Act.246

20.1 State Siting Framework248
Local governments have principal authority over the siting of solar energy projects that are less than 5
megawatts (MW) in size. State law preempts local bans on solar projects that are 1 MW or larger and all
energy storage projects (regardless of size).

The state has principal authority over the siting of solar projects that are 5 MW or larger and wind projects
that are 70 MW or larger in size. A certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the Maryland
Public Service Commission (MPSC) is required for projects under state jurisdiction. Solar projects that are
more than 5 MW but less than 25 MW in size and wind projects that are less than 70 MW in size are exempt
from the CPCN requirement but still require MPSC approval.

20.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Maryland. In 2025,
the Maryland state legislature enacted the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, which imposes an acreage cap on
solar energy development on certain farmland classed as “priority preservation areas.” In addition, at least 10
of the 23 counties in Maryland, as well as the City of Baltimore, have adopted restrictive local ordinances,
targeting solar and/or wind development. Four counties – Garrett, Harford, Talbot, and Worcester – have
banned development in certain areas. Others have established size limits for projects, restricted the use of
energy from the projects, and established onerous setback, height, and viewshed requirements.

20.3 Contested Projects
      ● Betterton Halo Solar (Kent County): In 2025, Halo Betterton, LLC proposed the 5-MW Betterton Halo
        Solar project to be located on approximately 30 acres of land in the Town of Betterton. In April 2025,
        the developer applied for the required Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) from the
        Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC). In May 2025, the Maryland Department of Natural
        Resources recommended that the application be deemed administratively complete. In September
        2025, the PSC held a public hearing on the project at which town officials expressed their opposition to
        it, citing concerns about potential impacts to the town’s residential character and public safety risks
        because the project site would block their designated helicopter landing zone. Nearly 2 dozen
        opponents at that hearing also raised concerns over historical preservation, public safety, and impacts
        on property values. In November 2025, a town community meeting was held at which over 50 local
        residents and representatives of regional preservation groups, including the Kent Conservation and
        Preservation Alliance, objected to the project, primarily on the grounds that the proposed project site
        is restricted to residential use. In December 2025, the PSC stayed the proceedings to review the legal
        question of whether the proposed project site is zoned for clean energy development.249

      ● Chaberton Energy Sugarloaf Solar Project (Montgomery County): Chaberton Energy filed an
        application with the Maryland Public Service Commission for a certificate of public convenience and
        necessity for a 4-MW community solar project that would be located in Montgomery County’s
        “Agricultural Reserve” zone. In September 2024, Montgomery County’s Planning Board submitted
        comments to the Public Service Commission, arguing that the project conflicts with the intent and
        requirements of the Agricultural Reserve zone, as well as other local requirements. The Planning Board
        noted that it had received over 140 letters and emails in opposition to the project.250

      ● Chaberton Snow Solar (Worcester County): In May 2024, the Worcester County Commissioners
        rescinded the denial of a proposal for a 30-acre, 4-MW solar farm proposed by Chaberton Snow Solar
        LLC, after previously denying the proposal in November 2023. The rescission, which followed an
        administrative hearing, officially settled an appeal that the developer had filed in the Worcester
        County Circuit Court in December 2023. The initial denial drew upon concerns regarding the project’s
        decommissioning processes, even though the project received a favorable recommendation from the

        2019, the Maryland Environment Secretary denied a permit for the project, citing watershed
        impacts.253

    ● Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project (Baltimore, Carroll, and Frederick Counties): In 2024, a plan by
      PSEG to construct a high-voltage transmission line across 70 miles of land in Baltimore, Carroll, and
      Frederick Counties encountered opposition from local governments in all 3 counties, as well as the
      Maryland Farm Bureau and an organization called Stop MPRP, Inc. While the Maryland Public Service
      Commission will have the authority to make a decision on the project, the opponents are soliciting
      comments against the project and working to block approval.255

    ● Mills Branch Wind and Solar (Kent County): In April 2015, Apex Clean Energy announced that they
      were slowing the application process for the prospective 5,000-acre Mill Branch Wind Farm in
      response to local opposition centered on potential impacts to noise, migratory birds, and property
      values. The project would have spanned 6 miles and included 25-35 turbines with a total capacity of
      100 MW. The developer, Apex Clean Energy, eventually decided to convert the project to a solar
      energy project. Local opposition continued after this decision, and in January 2017, the Maryland
      Public Service Commission published a proposed order denying the developer’s application for a
      Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. The developer then requested to withdraw its
      application, and the request was denied.256

    ● Ripley Road Solar Project (Charles County): In July 2017, Origis Energy USA proposed Ripley Road
      Solar, a 27.5 MW project which would have produced power for the Southern Maryland Electric
      Cooperative (SMECO). The project generated local opposition because it required clearing 190 acres of
      forest. Although the Public Service Commission had conditionally approved the project, in August 2019,
      the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) denied the wetlands and waterways permit,
      finding that the plan failed to provide protection to a nearby stream from potential harm caused by
      clearing the woodlands.257

    ● Shugart Valley Solar Project (Charles County): In October 2018, Origis Energy USA proposed the 32.5-
      MW solar project (also known as “MD Solar 1”), which would have generated nearly half of the
      electricity consumed by Georgetown University. The plan drew fierce and widespread opposition
      because it would have required clearing 210 acres of forest in the Nanjemoy Peninsula. In August 2019,
      the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) denied the nontidal wetlands and waterways
      permit needed for the project, determining that the proposal was not in compliance with Maryland’s
      Nontidal Wetlands Protection Act. The project was then cancelled.258

    ● Skipjack Wind (Worcester County): Skipjack Wind, a proposed 966-MW offshore wind project near
      Ocean City, Maryland has encountered opposition from the city government and the tourism industry
      due to concerns that visual impacts will harm business. In February 2018, the Mayor and Ocean City
      Council unanimously approved a resolution against any project being sited within 30 miles of the city,
      but the Maryland House of Delegates rejected the proposal. The developer of Skipjack Wind
      nonetheless agreed to move the turbines from 19 miles offshore to 22 miles offshore. In September
      2021, after the developer applied for an expansion, several elected officials and business leaders
      expressed concern about turbines ruining beachfront views, jeopardizing tourism, and negatively
      impacting real estate values and the local economy. In January 2024, developer Orsted announced it
      was pulling out of its agreement with the state of Maryland for financial clean energy credits intended
      to help fund the offshore wind development but stated that it would “continue to advance Skipjack
      Wind’s development milestones, including its Construction and Operations Plan.”259

21.1 State Siting Framework262
Local governments have principal siting authority over small-scale wind and solar energy projects less than 25
megawatts (MW) in size. These projects require a consolidated permit (including all necessary municipal,
regional and state permits) from the relevant local government. The local government must make a decision
whether to grant or deny the permit within 12 months of receipt of a complete permit application.

The state has principal authority over larger wind and solar projects of 25 MW or more. These larger projects
require a consolidated permit from the Energy Facilities Siting Board (EFSB). The EFSB must make a decision
whether to grant or deny the permit within 15 months of receipt of a completed permit application. The
developer of a small-scale wind or solar project (less than 25 MW in size) may opt to seek a consolidated
permit from the EFSB, though the required local permits remain under the authority of the relevant local
government.

262
   Mass. Session Laws ch. 239 of 2024; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40A § 3; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164 §§ 69G, 69J1/4, 69K1/2, 69T; Mass.
Gen. Laws ch. 25A § 21; see also Steven Ferrey, Siting Technology, Land-Use Energized, 66 Cath. U. L. Rev. 1, 25 (2017),
https://scholarship.law.edu/lawreview/vol66/iss1/6/.



                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 155
                                                                                                                   Massachusetts




The EFSB is required to conduct a public hearing in at least 1 of the affected cities or towns in which a large
wind or solar project would be located. Local governments are required to establish uniform pre-filing
requirements for small-scale wind and solar projects that shall include provisions for public meetings and
other forms of public engagement.

21.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Massachusetts.
However, at least 21 cities and towns across the state have adopted restrictive local ordinances targeting
wind, solar, and in some cases battery storage projects.263 Eleven of the restrictive local ordinances impose
temporary moratoria or permanent bans on project development. Height restrictions for wind projects are
also quite common, featuring in 8 of the ordinances (i.e., adopted by the Cities of Methuen and Westfield and
the Towns of Andover, Essex, Fairhaven, Hamilton, Ipswich, Rehoboth).

21.3 Contested Projects
      ● Amherst Capped Landfill Solar (Hampshire County): In 2011, the Town of Amherst selected SunEdison
        to build a 2.4-MW solar array on a capped town landfill. In response, citizens filed a lawsuit against
        town officials for allegedly violating an agreement with the state that the landfill site must be used for
        recreational purposes. The lawsuit became moot in February 2012, when the state legislature passed a
        bill allowing all capped municipal landfills to serve as sites for solar projects. In April 2012, plaintiffs
        amended the lawsuit to include potential impacts to habitat of the grasshopper sparrow, which is
        protected under the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act. The lawsuit was dismissed without
        prejudice in December 2015. However, in July 2016 town officials terminated their contract with
        SunEdison after learning from the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries and Wildlife that the landfill
        solar project would likely impact habitat of the grasshopper sparrow.264

      ● ASD Shutesbury MA Solar LLC (Hampshire County): In November 2021, ASD Shutesbury MA Solar LLC
        withdrew an application to build an 11-MW solar farm in Amherst as the Town Council considered
        enacting an 18-month moratorium on large solar arrays.265

      ● Bullard Farm Solar Plant (Middlesex County): The Holliston Planning Board unanimously rejected the
        proposed Bullard Farm Solar Plant in 2012. A local group called Stop Bullard Farm Power Plant claimed
        that the solar array would pose risks to the health of area residents due to toxic chemicals in the panels
        and the output of electromagnetic frequency.266

      ● Cape Cod Solar (Barnstable County): In 2019, PureSky Energy proposed the Cape Cod Solar project on
        approximately 83 acres (out of over 200 acres) of a former country club golf course in the Town of
        Falmouth. The project consists of 3 solar facilities with battery energy storage systems (BESS) and has a
        total capacity of up to 13.5 MW. The project has faced opposition from local residents, who have
        advocated for the preservation of the golf course on the grounds that it is historically significant. A
        Change.org petition garnered over 3,500 signatures to preserve the nearly 100-year-old golf course.
        Other opponents have expressed a preference for the development of housing, rather than the solar
        facility, on the land. In September 2025, the Cape Cod Commission, in a 14-1 vote, approved the
        conversion of the golf course. In November 2025, the Town approved the site conversion plans which
        include donating approximately 137 acres to the town to be protected as permanent open space. The
        solar project will now go before the Falmouth Planning Board for site plan review. 267

      ● Cape Wind (Barnstable County): In 2017, after spending $100 million of his own money, the developer
        of Cape Wind, a proposed 454-MW offshore wind farm, abandoned the project. For years, the project
        was weighed down by costly legal challenges from groups such as the Alliance to Protect Nantucket
        Sound. In addition to the Alliance to Protect Nantucket Sound, which was chaired by William Koch, the
        project faced opposition from fishing groups and Native American tribes. As a result of delays caused
        by opposition, Cape Wind was unable to meet the construction deadlines set out in power purchase
        agreements. In 2015, 2 utilities canceled their contracts with Cape Wind.268

      ● Commonwealth Wind (Barnstable County): Commonwealth Wind is a proposed 1,200-MW offshore
        wind farm proposed for development south of Martha’s Vineyard. In December 2022, developer
        Avangrid requested to terminate power purchase agreements for the project; the power purchase
        agreements were formally terminated in October 2023. Later in October 2023, in response to the
        termination of power purchase agreements for the project, the Barnstable Town Council unanimously
        voted to withdraw authorization for negotiation of a host community agreement for the project. Also
        in October 2023, Barnstable Town Manager Mark Ells expressed reservations about the project’s draft
        environmental impact report (DEIR) and stated: “At this time, given what we’ve seen in the DEIR, we
        do not support the project moving forward.” Residents have opposed plans to bring a transmission
        cable for the wind farm onshore in Barnstable, including at a November 2023 community meeting,
        citing concerns about electromagnetic fields. The citizen group Saver Greater Dowses Beach, which has
        a Facebook page with over 1,200 members, formed in opposition to Avagrid’s plans to install power
        cables in the area. In April 2024, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management reviewed and approved the
        project, which has been combined and rebranded with Park City Wind as New England Wind (see
        below entry for New England Wind).269

      ● Convergent Energy Braintree (Norfolk County): In December 2024, Braintree’s fire chief declined to

        been located 200 feet from a church and 159 feet from the nearest house. In deciding not to support
        the project, the fire chief stated that the project’s proposed evacuation routes in the event of a battery
        fire were “insufficient.”270

      ● New England Wind 1 Transmission (Barnstable County): In July 2024, residents of Centerville, a village
        in the Town of Barnstable, filed a civil suit against the Barnstable Town Council seeking injunctive relief
        to stop the construction of transmission lines for Avangrid’s New England Wind 1 offshore wind
        project. The transmission lines, if constructed, would pass underneath the town’s main street. The
        plaintiff group Save Greater Dowses Beach argued that the Town Council negotiated a side agreement
        with Avangrid without public input. The case was dismissed in August 2024.274

      ● New England Wind 2, formerly known as Commonwealth Wind Project and Park City Wind
        (Barnstable County): In 2017, Avangrid began the development of 2 offshore wind farms south of
        Martha’s Vineyard – Commonwealth Wind (1,200-MW) and Park City Wind (800-MW). In April 2023,
        the developer filed a lawsuit against the Edgartown Conservation Commission after the town denied
        the company’s request to install subsurface transmission cables in town waters (see separate entry for
        New England Wind 1). Avangrid received a favorable ruling from the court, and in September 2023, the
        Commission rescinded its denial of the request. At a November 2023 Town public meeting concerning
        offshore wind, many Barnstable residents opposed plans to bring the cable installation, expressing
        concerns about disruption to public beaches and roads and impacts from electromagnetic fields. The
        citizen group Save Greater Dowses Beach formed in opposition to Avangrid’s plans to install the cables.
        In December 2023, the state Energy Facilities Siting Board voted to permit the landing of underground
        cables for the projects at Craigville Beach in Barnstable. In April 2024, the Department of the Interior’s
        Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) reviewed and approved the projects, which were
        combined and rebranded as New England Wind 2. In May 2025, the group ACK for Whales filed a
        lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia challenging the project alleging that the
        BOEM approval process violated several federal environmental laws, including the Marine Mammal
        Protection Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Outer
        Continental Shelf Lands Act. In September 2025, the Department of Interior filed a motion indicating
        that it is reconsidering its 2024 permit approval for the project. The litigation remains pending.275

      ● Northfield Solar Project (Franklin County): In September 2021, the Northfield Planning Board

        noncontiguous tracts. In November 2022, an abutter and an organization called “RESTORE: The North
        Woods” filed an appeal to contest the issuance of permits. The complaint alleged that the project
        would cause the abutter to “suffer a loss of the rural and agricultural values and aesthetic of the scenic
        country setting” and harm “prime farmland.” In April 2023, a Franklin County Superior Court judge
        ruled that the plaintiffs had standing to pursue their claim, allowing the case to proceed to trial.
        However, the following September, the parties agreed to dismiss the appeal, allowing the project to
        move forward.276

      ● Park City Wind (Barnstable County): Park City Wind is a proposed 800-MW offshore wind project
        owned by Avangrid. In April 2023, the developer filed a lawsuit against the Edgartown conservation
        commission after the town denied the company’s request to install cables in town waters. Avangrid
        received a favorable ruling from the court, and in September 2023, the commission rescinded its denial
        of the request. In October 2023, Avangrid terminated power purchase agreements for the project. The
        same month, in reaction to Avangrid’s termination of the power purchase agreements, Barnstable
        Town Council announced that it was pausing further action on easements necessary for installing
        subsurface transmission cables for the project. At a November 2023 public meeting concerning
        offshore wind, many Barnstable residents opposed plans to bring these cables ashore in Barnstable,
        expressing concerns about disruption to public beaches and roads and impacts from electromagnetic
        fields. In December 2023, the state Energy Facilities Siting Board voted to permit the landing of
        underground cables for the project at Craigville Beach in Barnstable. In April 2024, the Bureau of Ocean
        Energy Management reviewed and approved the project, which has been combined and rebranded
        with Commonwealth Wind as New England Wind (see above entry for New England Wind).277

    ● Petersham Solar (Worcester County): In 2021, Sunpin Energy proposed the 4.3-MW Petersham Solar
      project to be located on approximately 14 acres in Petersham, Worcester County. In November 2021,
      after 4 public meetings, the Petersham Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) voted 2-1 to approve the
      developer’s application for a special use permit for the project. However, as a unanimous vote was
      required, the permit was not issued. The dissenting board member and local residents opposing the
      project, expressed concern that it would require the cross-cutting of forest in a 14-acre parcel and
      harm the character of the community. In December 2021, the developer challenged the ZBA’s decision
      in the Massachusetts Land Court. In August 2023, the Land Court ruled that the ZBA had acted within
      their authority and the denial was reasonable based on public safety, health, and welfare. The
      developer subsequently challenged the Land Court’s ruling in the Massachusetts Appeals Court. In July
      2025, the Appeals Court reversed, holding that the proposed use was allowed with a special permit,
      and that the ZBA had exceeded their discretion in denying the permit. The matter is currently on
      appeal by the ZBA before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court.278

    ● Shutesbury Solar Project (Franklin County): In August 2016, opponents of a proposed 6.2-MW solar
      farm filed a lawsuit in federal court alleging that the 30-acre site contained Native American burial
      grounds and that it was a ceremonial landscape. While the developer, Lake Street Development, had
      already conducted archaeological studies and found no artifacts, opponents argued that additional
      analysis was necessary. In August 2017, the court dismissed the case on jurisdictional grounds, and the
      project was allowed to proceed.279

      landing site. In August 2023, SouthCoast Wind petitioned to terminate the project’s power purchase
      agreements. SouthCoast received new power purchase agreements with Massachusetts and Rhode

22.1 State Siting Framework285
Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 50 megawatts
(MW) in size and wind projects less than 100 MW in size. Localities have the option to retain control over

285
     Mich. PA 233 §§ 222, 223 (3)b, 225 (2), 226(5), 227, 232; Michigan H.B. 5120 of 2023 (effective date Nov. 29, 2024); Matthew
Eisenson, Michigan Court of Appeals Considers Challenge to New Process for Siting Renewables, Climate Law Blog, Apr. 11, 2025,
https://blogs.law.columbia.edu/climatechange/2025/04/11/michigan-court-of-appeals-considers-challenge-to-new-process-for-
siting-renewables/.

                                                                                                                      Michigan




larger projects if they have adopted a “compatible renewable energy ordinance” (CREO), which is not more
restrictive than applicable state law. In October 2024, the Michigan Public Service Commission (PSC) issued an
order with guidance on what local governments can, and cannot, include in a CREO. That order was challenged
in court in November 2024. In May 2026, the Michigan Court of Appeals partially upheld the PSC’s order, but
remanded key sections of it back to the PSC for further consideration.

The state has principal authority over the siting of solar projects that 50 MW or larger in size and wind projects
that are 100 MW or larger. A certificate from the Michigan PSC is required for these larger projects. The PSC
may preempt local restrictions on such projects.

The PSC must determine whether a certificate application is complete within 60 days of receipt and issue a
final decision within 1 year of the filing of the application. Local governments with a CREO must issue a
decision on a project application within 120 days of receipt, otherwise the PSC obtains jurisdiction. A public
meeting is required for projects under PSC jurisdiction.

22.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Michigan. Local
restrictions are widespread across the state, however. At least 98 restrictive local ordinances have been
adopted by 87 local governments in Michigan.286 Nine localities – Beaver Township, Claybanks Township,
Clinton County, Conway Township, Garfield Township, La Salle Township, Montrose City, Tyrone Township,
and Winfield Township – have each adopted at least 2 separate restrictive ordinances. One – Douglass
Township – has adopted at least 3 separate restrictive ordinances. The vast majority of the ordinances restrict
wind and/or solar energy development, with only 3 targeting battery storage projects. Forty-four of the
ordinances impose temporary moratoria or permanent bans on project development. Other common
restrictions include onerous setbacks (included in 38 ordinances), height restrictions (included in 24
ordinances), noise limits (included in 18 ordinances), and limits on shadow flicker (included in 18 ordinances).

22.3 Contested Projects
      ●   45th Parallel Solar (Otsego County): RWE Clean Energy proposed a 200-MW solar farm, called 45th
          Parallel Solar, to be developed on approximately 1,000 acres of private land in Hayes Township. In
          February 2025, the Otsego County Planning Commission, in a 7-1 vote, approved a special use permit
          for the project. The developer had submitted a separate proposal to lease additional public land for the
          project. In May 2025, the Michigan Department of Natural Resources rejected the leasing proposal
          following mass public criticism from both lawmakers and environmental organizations, citing concerns
          over deforestation and a lack of transparency. The development of the project continues on the
          proposed 1,000 acres of private land and commercial operations are estimated to begin in 2027.287

    ●   Beaver Township Wind Farm (Bay County): In 2018, DTE Energy canceled plans to develop a wind farm
        in Beaver Township after the township board “set a sound limit that was so low that it basically would
        not allow any turbine in any 1-mile by-1 mile section.” Opponents of the project had voiced concerns
        about impacts to property value and wildlife, as well as physical safety.288

    ●   Birch Valley Solar (Tuscola County): Ranger Power has proposed to construct a 170-MW solar facility
        called Birch Valley Solar on approximately 1,500 acres of farmland in Arbela Township. If completed,
        the project would net $340,000 annually for the township’s fire, infrastructure, or safety expenses. The
        proposal also includes a host community agreement requiring the developer to pay the township
        $2,000 per MW of installed capacity. Despite the anticipated benefits, the project is facing local
        opposition. Opponents have raised concerns of encroachment on prime farmland and the fact that the
        project’s scale would exceed the local zoning ordinance’s cap on utility-scale solar development of 4%
        of total township acreage. In July 2025, the developer submitted an application for a special land use
        permit. If the Arbela Township Board of Trustees denies the permit, the developer may seek project
        approval from the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) under the Public Act 233 of 2023, which
        allows the PSC to preempt certain local government decisions.289

    ●   Branch County Wind Farm (Branch County): DTE Energy began signing leases to construct a wind farm
        in Batavia, Matteson, Sherwood and Union townships in 2017, eventually spending $250,000 signing
        280 leases on farmland. However, the project faced intense opposition from groups like Concerned
        Citizens of Branch County. In August 2020, Matteson and Sherwood Townships passed restrictive
        ordinances, with another restrictive ordinance pending in Batavia, and the company put the project on
        hold.290

    ●   Crescent Wind Farm (Hillsdale County): A 166-MW wind farm in Wheatland Township of Hillsdale
        County faced backlash from a group called the Concerned Citizens of Wheatland Township, who spoke

      ●   Confluence Solar Project (Genesee County): Opponents of Ranger Power LLC’s plans for a 200-MW,
          1,500-acre solar farm collected over 200 signatures for petition against the development and lobbied

          keep out major commercial projects, including setbacks of 500 feet from any dwelling unit and 300 feet

          Energy claimed that this and a related decision have caused DTE Energy to look elsewhere for future
          renewable energy projects. The secretary of the Huron County Wind Resistance, a local anti-wind

          advertising dollars. But, they showed up, and they said, ‘no.’ Victory for the people is what we’re
          saying.”293

          decision, but a judge dismissed the suit. Invenergy continued to move forward with the project despite
          the Board’s decision, as it had received approval from the 5 other affected townships. Construction on
          the wind farm began in April 2023. The 201-MW, 72-turbine project was operational as of January
          2024, with capacity to power roughly 80,000 homes.296

      ●   Kenowa Ridge Wind Farm (Kent and Muskegon Counties): In December 2019, American Electric
          Power canceled plans to build 31 wind turbines in 2 Michigan townships after 1 of them, Casnovia,
          adopted a restrictive ordinance that requires wind turbines to be set back from property lines by a
          distance of 4 times turbine height. Casnovia Township had previously approved a special use permit for

          sued Casnovia Township alleging that the permit included 32 “capricious and arbitrary” conditions that
          would make it impossible to build the project.301

      ●   Lake Winds Energy Park (Mason County): In April 2013, Mason County residents, supported by
          Citizens Alliance for Responsible Renewable Energy, filed a lawsuit in Mason County Circuit Court,
          challenging the Mason County Planning Commission’s approval of Consumers Energy’s 100-MW Lake
          Winds Energy Park and seeking an injunction to stop the project’s operations. The project, which
          consists of 56 turbines, had been operational since November 2012. The plaintiffs alleged that noise,
          vibrations, and flickering light were causing physical harm as well as economic losses. The developer
          had received 128 complaints within the first year of operation and had faced opposition during
          construction. In September 2013, the Mason County Planning Commission determined that the wind
          farm violated the agreed-upon noise standards and ordered Consumers Energy to bring the facility into
          compliance. In late 2014, the developer reached a confidential settlement that resolved the pending
          lawsuit.302

    ●   Mustang Mile Solar Energy (Lenawee County): In 2017, Invenergy proposed the 150-MW Mustang
        Mile Solar project to be located on approximately 2,777 acres in Macon Township. From 2018 to 2020,
        the township adopted amendments to its solar ordinance to allow large-scale solar facilities as a
        special land use. However, in 2021, the Planning Commission recommended denial of a permit for the
        Mustang Mile Solar project on the basis that it did not meet the required standards for a special land
        use. The Township Board, in a 3-2 vote, approved issuance of a special use permit for the project,
        despite the Commission’s findings and recommendation to deny it. In 2021, local opponents of the
        project filed a lawsuit in the Lenawee Circuit Court challenging the Board’s issuance of the permit. The
        circuit court affirmed the Board’s decision; in its ruling, the court erroneously stated that the
        Commission had recommended approval of the permit. The opponents appealed the circuit court’s
        decision to the Michigan Court of Appeals. In October 2025, the court of appeals vacated the circuit
        court’s decision reasoning that the lower court’s decision was an error unsupported by the record. The
        matter was remanded to the Board for further proceedings.307

    ●   Pegasus Wind (Tuscola County): In June 2019, Pegasus Wind applied for zoning variances to construct
        33 wind turbines near a local airport. The Tuscola Airport Zoning Board of Appeals (AZBA) denied the
        applications for variances, citing concerns about air traffic safety. The developer appealed the denials
        to the Tuscola Circuit Court, which reversed the AZBA’s decision. In October 2019, Pegasus Wind
        submitted applications for 8 additional variances, which the AZBA again denied. Pegasus Wind
        appealed the denial to the Tuscola Circuit Court, which affirmed the denial. In 2022, the Michigan
        Court of Appeals reversed the Circuit Court’s decision, finding that denial was improper. However, in
        April 2024, the Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals’ decision, allowing the AZBA’s
        denial of the variances to stand.308

        Solar project raised concerns pertaining to potential noise, environmental impacts, and impacts to
        agricultural land.309

23.1 State Siting Framework320
Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 50 megawatts
(MW) in size and wind projects less than 5 MW in size. Localities may adopt an ordinance to assume
jurisdiction over the permitting of wind projects between 5 and 25 MW in size.

The state has principal authority over the siting of solar projects that are 50 MW or larger and wind projects
that are 5 MW or larger (unless the local government has an ordinance extending its authority to projects up
to 25 MW in size, in which case the state only has authority over the siting of larger projects (i.e., 25 MW or
more)). The state also has jurisdiction over energy storage systems with a capacity of 50 MW or more. A site
permit from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission (MPUC) is required for projects under state
jurisdiction. Under state law, the issuance of a site permit by the MPSC supersedes and preempts all other
zoning, building, or land use rules, regulations, or ordinances promulgated by regional, county, local, and
special purpose government.

The MPUC must hold at least 1 public hearing before deciding whether to issue a site permit. A final decision
must be made by the MPUC within 1 year of receipt of a complete application and within 60 days of receipt of
a report from an administrative law judge for solar projects and within 180 days of receipt of a complete
application for wind projects.

23.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Minnesota. An
administrative rule adopted by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission in 2009 restricts the development of
wind and solar energy facilities in areas classified as “prime farmland.” In addition to this state-level
restriction, at least 38 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by 34 local governments in
Minnesota.321 Four counties in the state – Aitkin, Pope, Traverse, and Wabasha – have each adopted at least 2
restrictive ordinances. Most of the ordinances target wind and solar energy projects, with only 1 – adopted in
Traverse County – covering battery storage projects. Most ordinances (26) impose temporary moratoria or

23.3 Contested Projects
      ● Big Blue Wind Farm (Faribault County): This 18-turbine, 36-MW wind farm went online in December
        2012. After years of complaints about noise, the PUC intervened in 2017 and discovered that the
        project’s noise protocol had never been approved. Residents then pushed for the farm to be
        completely shut down, but the Public Utilities Commission instead ordered the developer to address
        the problems and issued a warning.322

      ● Gopher State Solar Project (Renville County): In August 2024, Ranger Power submitted an application
        to construct the 200-MW Gopher State Solar Project on approximately 1,667 acres in the townships of
        Kingman, Osceola, and Bird Island. Opponents of the project, including county officials, have
        questioned the estimated costs of decommissioning as insufficient. Local residents also raised concerns
        of potential visual and noise pollution and impacts to property values. In June 2025, an administrative
        law judge recommended approval of the permit by the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) subject to

      ● Lemon Hill Solar (Olmsted County): In 2025, Ranger Power proposed the 180-MW Lemon Hill Solar

        townships. In November 2025, at a Minnesota Public Utilities Commission public meeting, a majority of
        attendees raised concerns about the potential for soil disturbance from the project and its impacts on
        water supply and property values, and called for increased setbacks. The permitting process remains

        October 2020 and implemented a moratorium on solar energy projects while it revised its ordinance to

24.1 State Siting Framework330
The state has principal authority over the siting of all electricity generating projects, including wind and solar
energy projects. Projects require a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the Mississippi
Public Service Commission (MPSC). Prior to requesting a CPCN from the MPSC, the project developer must
first obtain a franchise from the relevant local government where it intends to provide electric services.

330
      Miss. Code Ann. §§ 17-1-3, 77-3-11, 77-3-13, 77-3-13(3), 77-3-19.


                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 193
                                                                                                                    Mississippi




The MPSC must hold a public hearing after receipt of a CPNC application. There is no statutory deadline for the
MPSC to reach a final decision on applications.

24.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Mississippi. Of the 82
counties in the state, only 1 – Harrison County – has adopted a restrictive local ordinance. The ordinance
established size and height limits for wind energy projects.

      ● Minkar Solar Farm (Lamar County): In July 2023, Lamar County residents organized a community
        meeting to express opposition to the proposed 90-MW, 1,700-acre Minkar solar farm. Residents raised
        concerns about property value impacts, destruction of agricultural land, displacement of wildlife, and
        more. Two residents created signs, an online petition, and a social media group in opposition to the
        project; as of February 2024, the petition had 336 signatures. At the time, developer Lighthouse BP
        was conducting studies of the proposed site and was planning on holding a public meeting. The Lamar
        County Board of Supervisors will ultimately decide on whether to approve the project. 331

      ● Soul City Solar (Hinds County): In 2021, Apex Clean Energy began acquiring leases for a proposed
        6,000-acre, 396-MW solar farm and 70-MW battery storage facility. Nearby residents organized in
        opposition to the project, sending a letter to the Hinds County Planning and Zoning Department, along
        with a Change.org petition with over 1,000 signatures. The Hinds County Planning Commission voted
        against recommending the project; however, the Hinds County Board of Supervisors approved the
        project in a 3-2 vote on June 17, 2024. On April 10, 2025, the Circuit Court affirmed the decision of the
        Hinds County Board of Supervisors. On May 9, 2025, a local opponent appealed the Circuit’s Court

25.1 State Siting Framework333

Local governments have principal siting authority over electric generating projects under the Missouri Zoning
and Planning Enabling Act (though renewable energy facilities are not explicitly mentioned).

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no
deadline for the local government to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

        Creek Solar project argued that the Zoning Board of Adjustment erred when it denied the special use
        permit for this solar project, including by focusing only on public opposition and ignoring support for
        the project.340

        Sweet Grass County. Four companies that own neighboring land initiated a legal action alleging
        nuisance. In March 2019, a Montana judge issued a preliminary injunction on construction while the
        case awaited trial. In July 2019, Pattern asserted in a legal filing that the preliminary injunction made it
        impossible to obtain the necessary financing to complete the project and satisfy contractual
        obligations. Pattern further explained that it was compelled to abandon the project.341

        farm east of Livingston, Montana. Local residents formed an opposition group, Friends of Mission

27.1 State Siting Framework345
Local governments may adopt ordinances to encourage wind and solar energy development. However, the
state has principal authority over the siting of renewable energy facilities. All projects must be approved by
the Nebraska Power Review Board. The Board must hold a public hearing within 60 days of receiving an
application for project approval and must make a final decision on the application within 60 days thereafter.
The Board may waive the hearing requirement in certain instances if it finds it unnecessary.

restrictions are widespread, however. At least 46 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by 42 local

      ● Kilgore Wind Farm (Cherry County): In July 2016, the Cherry County Planning Commission formally

28.1 State Siting Framework358
Local governments have principal siting authority over solar and wind projects that are less than 70 megawatts
(MW) in size. The state has principal authority over the siting of solar and wind projects that are 70 MW or
larger in size. Such larger projects must be permitted by the Nevada Public Utilities Commission (NPUC).

The NPUC must make a decision within 150 days of receiving a permit application or, if a federal agency is
required to conduct an environmental analysis of the facility, within 120 days. There is no statutory
requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the permit review process.

State law prohibits local governments from adopting unreasonable restrictions on wind and solar
development on private land and mandates that local zoning regulations must be designed “to promote
systems which use solar or wind energy”.

28.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Nevada. Of the 16
counties in the state, at least 2 – Lander and Nye – have adopted restrictive local ordinances. In 2024, Lander
County imposed a temporary moratorium on wind and solar energy development, which was extended in
2025. Nye County has established restrictive setback requirements for solar energy projects.

      ○ Total number of state restrictions: 0
      ○ Total number of local restrictions: 2
      ○ Technology targeted:

           ■ 1 (solar)
      ○ Type of Restrictions:

           ■ Nye County: Rule 10b: Setback Restriction (solar)

      ● Beatty Energy Center Project (Nye County): Beatty Energy Center is a proposed solar-plus-storage
        project that would include 800-MW of solar capacity and up to 800 MW of battery storage capacity on
        approximately 6,515 acres of federal BLM land in Nye County. In June 2022, the Bureau of Land
        Management sided with local opponents of Beatty Energy Center and 2 other large solar projects
        (Bonnie Clare Solar and Sawtooth Energy Center Project) near Death Valley National Park by giving
        them “low priority” permitting status. If approved, the projects would collectively generate 3,300 MW
        of electricity on up to 25,000 acres of land. The Bureau cited proximity to Death Valley National Park
        and sensitive habitat for the Mojave Desert tortoise as concerns. The projects are opposed by Nevada-
        based Basin and Range Watch, which thanked BLM for its decision.361

29.1 State Siting Framework379

Local governments have principal authority over the siting of wind and solar projects that are less than 30
megawatts (MW) in size. However, the state may choose to exercise discretionary jurisdiction over certain

379
      N.H. RSA §§ 162-H:2:VII, 162-H:2:XII[IN1] , 162-H:7:VI; 162-H:10, 674:17(I)(j), 674:62, 674:63


                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 224
                                                                                                     New Hampshire




projects with a capacity of 5 MW to 30 MW, either on its own motion or by petition. State law prohibits local
governments from adopting “unreasonable” limits on small-scale wind projects (0.1 MW or less) including, for
instance, bans on construction or excessive setbacks (defined as setbacks that are more than 150% of the
system height).

The state has principal authority over the siting of renewable energy facilities that are 30 megawatts (MW) or
larger, as well as projects over which it has exercised discretionary jurisdiction. A certificate from the New
Hampshire Site Evaluation Committee (NHSEC) is required for all such projects. The NHSEC must decide
whether to accept a certificate application within 60 days. If accepted, all state agencies having permitting or
regulatory authority over the project must submit to the NHSEC draft permit conditions within 150 days, and a
final decision on the relevant parts of the application within 240 days. The NHSEC is required to make a final
decision on whether to issue a certificate for the project within 1 year of receipt of the application.

The applicant must hold at least 1 public information hearing 30 days before submitting a certificate
application to the NHSEC. In addition, the applicant must hold at least 1 public information hearing within 30
days of the NHSEC accepting the application. The NHSEC must hold at least 1 public hearing in each county
involved within 90 days of accepting the application.

29.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in New Hampshire. At least
3 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by the City of Keene and the Towns of Fitzwilliam and
Westmoreland, all of which are located within Cheshire County. The ordinances in the City of Keene and Town
of Fitzwilliam both target solar energy development, while the Town of Westmoreland’s ordinance restricts
wind development.

29.3 Contested Projects
      ● Antrim Wind Project (Hillsborough County): In December 2016, the New Hampshire Site Evaluation
        Committee approved the 29-MW Antrim wind farm, which would involve 9 wind turbines on a ridge.
        Project opponents concerned about noise and impacts on wildlife, property values, and scenic views
        appealed the decision to the New Hampshire Supreme Court. In May 2018, the court ruled against the
        project opponents on all counts, allowing the project to move forward. The project began commercial
        operations in 2019.380

      ● Franklin Solar Project (Merrimack County): In April 2024, the New Hampshire Supreme Court
        overturned the City of Franklin Planning Board’s denial of a 6-acre, 1-MW solar farm proposed by GSSG
        New Hampshire. The project met the city’s zoning ordinances but was opposed by residents who were
        concerned about disruptions of the scenery and property values. The court stated that a board cannot
        deny projects that comply with zoning ordinances based solely on subjective views. The court
        essentially approved the project by issuing a builder’s remedy which allows a project to proceed if it
        meets zoning ordinances.381

      ● Granite Reliable Wind Farm (Coos County): In 2010, a 99-MW, 33-turbine wind farm near Groveton
        was proposed. The Appalachian Mountain Club raised concerns that the project might impact sensitive
        high-elevation forest. However, the project was ultimately completed as originally planned in 2012.382

      ● West Portsmouth Street, Concord Solar Project (Merrimack County): In 2018, NextEra Energy’s plans
        for a 10-MW, 54-acre solar farm in Concord were rejected by the local zoning board because there
        would be too much “impervious surface” for a residential open-space zoning lot. The zoning board
        denied the developer’s request for rehearing.383

30.1 State Siting Framework385
Local governments regulate the permitting of small-scale renewable energy projects with a capacity of 0.1
MW or less. State law prohibits “unreasonable” local restrictions on small wind energy systems (i.e., those
consisting of a single turbine and used for onsite consumption), including bans on construction, excessive
setbacks (defined as setbacks greater than 150% of the system height), limits on tower height, and caps on
noise of less than 55 decibels. Additionally, developers of offshore wind projects have the right to appeal to
the state when a local government blocks approvals needed for the project (e.g., for cable landings).

The state has principal authority over the siting of renewable energy facilities that are larger than 0.1MW.
Such projects require a permit from the Office of Permitting and Project Navigation, within the New Jersey
Department of Environmental Protection (NJ DEP). Projects may also require additional permits from other
state agencies depending on the location and nature of the project.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process at
either the state or local level and no deadline for the NJ DEP or local governments to issue a final decision on a
proposed project.


30.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state statutes or ordinances restricting renewable energy development have been identified in New Jersey.

      ● Atlantic Shores South Project (Ocean County): In July 2023, all of the municipalities of Long Beach

        Shores Project, arguing that the project would have detrimental impact on New Jersey’s southern
