        Jersey Board of Public Utilities, seeking to have the Board decrease the value of Atlantic Shores’

31.1 State Siting Framework393
Local governments have principal siting authority over energy generation projects, including wind and solar
energy projects, that are less than 300 megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal siting authority over
larger facilities (i.e., 300 MW or more). Approval by the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission is required
for those larger projects. If the Commission finds that an existing state, county, or municipal land use

393
   N.M. Stat. Ann. §§ 3-18-32, 3-21-1, 62-9-3(B), 62-9-3(C), 62-9-3(G), 62-9-3(K), see also Steven Ferrey, Siting Technology, Land-Use
Energized, 66 Cath. U. L. Rev. 1, 25-26 (2017),
https://scholarship.law.edu/lawreview/vol66/iss1/6/.

regulation is “unreasonably burdensome” as to a proposed project and that “compliance with the regulation is
not in the interest of the public convenience and necessity,” that regulation “shall be inapplicable and void as
to the siting.”

The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission must decide an application within 6 months of filing. A public
hearing is typically required prior to the Commission’s decision, but the Commission may approve an
application without a hearing if no protest is filed within 60 days of the application.

31.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state statutes or ordinances restricting renewable energy development have been identified in New
Mexico.

31.3 Contested Projects
      ● Cenergy’s Two Community Solar Projects (Chaves County): On April 6, 2022, the Chaves County
        Planning and Zoning Commission voted not to recommend permits sought by Cenergy Power for two
        5-MW community solar projects based on objections from neighbors. Local residents expressed
        concern that the solar projects would cause visual impacts, harm property values, cause runoff into
        nearby rivers, destroy wildlife habitats, and take away land that should be used for homes or
        agriculture. On April 14, 2022, the Chaves County Board of Commissioners denied the permit
        applications.394

      ● Chaves Solar 2 LLC Community Solar Project (Chaves County): In October 2021, the Roswell-Chaves
        County Exterritorial Zoning Commission voted against a permit for a 5-MW community solar garden
        just west of Roswell, New Mexico. The commission had received 3 protest letters from nearby property
        owners and comments from 3 other property owners who opposed the project. Opponents did not
        want the project near their homes, small farms, and orchards, and expressed concerns about radiation,
        toxic materials, dust, glare, noise, temperature effects, wildlife effects, and property devaluation. In
        November 2021, the developer and landowners filed an appeal.395

        each 5 MW or smaller, after hearing objections from residents.397

      ● Rancho Viejo Solar Project (Santa Fe County): The Rancho Viejo Solar Project, a 680-acre, 96-MW solar
        farm with a 2-acre, 48-MW battery storage facility proposed by AES, has faced resistance from the
        local community. Residents have established the Clean Energy Coalition for Santa Fe County and New
        Mexicans for Responsible Renewable Energy to fight against the project. The latter started an online
        petition directed at Santa Fe County, asking that officials either deny the project’s conditional use
        permit application or issue a moratorium and amend county codes before considering the project
        further. Residents have expressed distrust toward the company and argued that the county has failed
        to adequately engage the community. A resident submitted in August 2023 a Notice of Violation to
        Santa Fe County and filed in September 2023 a complaint with the New Mexico Attorney General,
        alleging that the County’s meetings with AES violated New Mexico’s Open Meetings Act. The County
        denied the allegations, and the Attorney General responded that no violations occurred. In August
        2024, residents attended a county meeting at which AES presented a revised plan that sought to
        address the community’s concerns. Opponents have stated that the project should not be located near
        residential areas, due to the risk of fires and environmental contamination. Supporters have stated
        that the technology has become much safer and emphasized the importance of addressing climate
        change.398

32. NEW YORK

32.1 State Siting Framework400
Local governments have principal siting authority over renewable energy facilities, including wind and solar
energy projects, that are less than 25 megawatts (MW) in size.

The state has principal siting authority over larger renewable energy facilities (25 MW or larger). Approval by
the state Office of Renewable Energy Siting (ORES) is required for those larger projects. Additionally, project
developers may elect to have smaller projects, with a capacity of 20 to 25 MW, approved by ORES rather than
the relevant local government. ORES also has jurisdiction over projects previously under the jurisdiction of the


400
   N.Y. Public Service Law, Art. 8 §§136-148; N.Y. Town Law §261 et seq.; N.Y. Village Law §7-700, 19 N.Y.C.R.R. §§ 900-1.1 to 900-
15.2, 900-5.1, 900-1.3; see also Michael B. Gerrard & Edward McTiernan, New York’s New Statute on Siting Renewable Energy
Facilities, New York Law Journal, Vol. 263, No. 93, May 14, 2020, https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/3026/.


                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 240
                                                                                                                   New York




state siting board pursuant to Article 10 of the New York Public Service Law and over co-located energy
storage systems and associated electric transmission systems less than 10 miles in length.

Project developers are required to consult with local governments about local laws prior to applying for
project approval from ORES. However, ORES “may elect not to apply, in whole or in part, any local law or
ordinance which would otherwise be applicable if it makes a finding that, as applied to the proposed major
renewable energy facility, it is unreasonably burdensome in view of the [state’s climate] targets and the
environmental benefits of the proposed major renewable energy facility.”

ORES must decide whether an application is complete within 60 days of its filing. ORES must issue draft permit
conditions within 60 days, and issue a final permit decision within 1 year, after determining that the
application is complete. The applicant must hold a public meeting with the local government and with
community members at least 60 days before filing a permit application.

32.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state law restricting renewable energy development has been adopted in New York. In 2023, the
state enacted legislation prohibiting the New York Power Authority from developing renewable energy
projects on “land used in agricultural production” and “lands located upon any Native American territory or
reservation” (with limited exceptions). In addition, at least 86 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted
by 81 local governments in the state.401 Five New York towns – Clifton Park, Duanesburg, Enfield, Fremont,
and Vestal – have each adopted at least 2 restrictive local ordinances. (It should be noted that, given New
York’s system of state siting for large-renewable energy projects, any local ordinance that purports to apply to
projects larger than 25 MW is invalid.)

Notably, as well as having many local restrictions on wind and solar projects, New York also has the largest
number of ordinances restricting battery storage projects of any state (15). All of those ordinances impose
either temporary moratoria or permanent bans on battery storage projects. Moratoria and bans targeting
wind and/or solar projects are also common (included in 52 local ordinances), as are project size caps (17
ordinances), and restrictive setbacks (14 ordinances).

32.3 Contested Projects
      ● Alle-Catt Wind Farm (Allegany, Cattaraugus, and Wyoming Counties): In November 2021, the Fourth
        Department of the Appellate Division of the New York Supreme Court affirmed the State Siting Board’s
        approval of the 340-MW Alle-Catt Wind Farm in Western New York. The approval had been challenged
        by a group called the Coalition of Concerned Citizens.402

      ● Bay Breeze Solar Project (Jefferson County): AES has proposed a 150-MW solar energy facility called
        Bay Breeze Solar Project to be located outside the Village of Chaumont and within the Town of Lyme in
        Jefferson County. A group called “Concerned Citizens for Responsible Solar” was formed to lead the
        local opposition to this project, as well as the Riverside Solar Project (see separate entry on Riverside
        Solar), and has raised concerns about property value impacts, fire safety, and impacts to wildlife. In
        December 2024, the Town of Lyme adopted a 12-month moratorium on all solar energy systems
        and/or battery energy storage systems, which suspended further work on the project.403

      ● Bear Ridge Solar Project (Niagara County): Bear Ridge Solar is a project proposed by Cypress Creek
        Renewables in the towns of Cambria and Pendleton. The project was originally planned to be 100 MW,
        covering 900 acres of land. In February 2023, the Town of Cambria argued before an administrative law

         contested acres. As of January 2024, Cypress Creek Renewables believed that everything was in line to
         build a 88-MW version of the project, with groundbreaking possible before 2025.404

      ● Black Oak Wind Farm (Tompkins County): The Black Oak Wind Farm, a proposed 7-turbine, 16-MW
        project, was first conceived in 2006. However, in December 2017, the developer canceled the project.
        The developer blamed the Town of Enfield’s moratorium and other actions, which effectively held up
        the project for 2 years and drove the company into bankruptcy.405

      ● Bliss Solar 1 Project (Schoharie County): In June 2019, Bliss Solar 1, LLC, a subsidiary of Borrego, filed
        an application with the Schoharie Town Board to install a 5-MW solar system and a 2-MW solar system
        on 41.55 acres of land just outside the Village of Schoharie. The proposal was later reduced to a single
        5-MW project. In March 2021, the Town Board voted against the project. In June 2021, the developer
        filed an appeal in state court, alleging that the Board’s decision was arbitrary and capricious. In
        February 2022, the trial court ruled in favor of the Board, and the developer filed a notice of appeal to
        the appellate division.406

      ● Bluestone Wind Farm (Broome County): In October 2021, the Third Department of the Appellate
        Division of the New York Supreme Court denied a petition by Broome County Concerned Residents and
        others challenging the state Siting Board’s approval of the 125-MW Bluestone Wind Farm in Sanford,
        New York. The petitioners alleged that the Siting Board failed to adequately consider local laws and
        impacts on locally endangered golden eagles, along with other claims.407

      ● Cape Vincent Wind Project (Jefferson County): In 2014, after a 10-year battle to develop a 200- to
        285-MW wind project in the Town of Cape Vincent, BP Wind Energy formally withdrew its application.
        Seasonal residents opposed the project due to concerns about impacts to property values, while many
        year-round residents supported the project because of the revenues it would bring.408

      ● Carson Power’s Pulvers Corners Solar 1 and 2 Projects (Dutchess County): In November 2023, the
        Town of Pine Plains’ Planning Board unanimously approved permits and site plans for Carson Power’s
        Pulvers Corners Solar 1 and 2, each of which would have a capacity of roughly 5 MW, and which
        together would take up 42 acres of land on a 172-acre property. A coalition of neighbors formed an
        unincorporated association called Preserve Pine Plains to oppose further development of the project.
        In December 2023, Preserve Pine Plains filed a lawsuit in New York state court challenging the Pine
        Plains Planning Board’s approval of the project and negative declaration (i.e., finding of no significant
        adverse environmental impacts). The suit alleges that the board’s environmental review and
        permitting of the project violated Pine Plains’ zoning laws and State Environmental Quality Review Act
        (SEQRA), along with the town’s comprehensive plan, which emphasizes the importance of “preserving
        the community’s rural character and natural beauty.” In June 2024, a state judge dismissed the
        lawsuit.409

      ● Cassadaga Wind Project (Chautauqua County): The group Concerned Citizens of Cassadaga Wind
        Project intervened in a statewide Siting Board proceeding under Article 10 of the Public Service Law to
        oppose the 126-MW Cassadaga Wind Farm. The project was ultimately approved by the Siting Board in
        January 2018.410

      ● Chapman Road Community Solar (Oneida County): In February 2025, U.S. Light Energy proposed the
        5-MW solar project called Chapman Road Community Solar to be developed on approximately 23 acres
        of a 70-acre parcel in the town of New Hartford. On February 12, 2025, the New Hartford Town Board

      ● Chenango Solar (Broome County): In September 2025, Cipriani Energy Group proposed a 4.9-MW solar
        energy facility to be developed on approximately 74 acres in the Town of Chenango. The proposal
        includes clearing approximately 22 acres of trees on the hillside near Smith Hill Creek to install the
        facility. On September 29, 2025, the Town’s Planning Board held a public hearing at which dozens of
        local residents expressed opposition to the project. The opponents raised concerns about increased
        risk of flooding due to land clearing, potential damage and loss to surrounding nature, reduction in
        property values, and disruption as a result of construction activities.412

      ● Columbia Solar (Herkimer County): EDF Renewables has proposed a 2,200-acre, 350-MW solar farm in
        the Town of Columbia. Local residents have put up signs that read “Oppose Columbia Solar.” An
        organizer for a group called Protect Columbia reported in January 2023 that he was consulting with
        legal counsel about options to challenge the project.413

      ● Empire Wind 1 and 2 (Kings and Nassau Counties): Empire Wind is an offshore wind project proposed
        by Equinor, which consists of the 810-MW Empire Wind 1 project and the 1,260-MW Empire Wind 2
        project. The project would be approximately 14 miles from Long Island, New York and 19.5 miles from
        South Branch, New Jersey at its closest point. Plans for a cable landing for the Empire Wind 2 project
        on state parkland in Long Island, New York encountered local opposition. The state legislature enacted
        a bill allowing the alienation of parkland for the project. In October 2023, however, Governor Kathy
        Hochul vetoed that bill. In her veto message, Governor Hochul stated that “[i]t is incumbent on
        renewable energy developers to cultivate and maintain strong ties to their host communities.” In
        February 2024, despite the uncertainty over the site of the cable landing for Empire Wind 2, BOEM
        approved the Construction and Operations Plan for both Empire Wind 1 and 2. In April 2025, BOEM
        imposed a stop-work order on the Empire Wind 1 project on the basis that “the project was rushed

      ● EWT Portland Community Wind (Chautauqua County): Dutch developer EWT proposed constructing a
        7-MW, 7-turbine community wind project in Portland, New York as part of New York State’s
        Community Distributed Generation Program. However, in October 2020, the Town of Portland adopted
        a restrictive wind energy ordinance that threatens the viability of the project. In 2021, the developer
        filed a lawsuit against the town and a motion for a preliminary injunction; the court denied the motion.
        The project has not been built.416

      ● Florida Wind 1, LLC Wind Turbine Project (Montgomery County): In 2021, New Leaf Energy LLC
        submitted a proposal to build a single 4.5-MW wind turbine, standing 650 feet tall, on a 135-acre
        vacant property in the Town of Florida, New York. In October 2024, after several years of review, the
        Florida Planning Board unanimously denied approval. Local opponents had raised concerns about
        visual impacts, community character, shadow flicker, and noise.417

      ● Flint Mine Solar (Greene County): A 100-MW solar project proposed in the towns of Coxsackie and
        Athens in Greene County faced opposition from the Town of Coxsackie. In 2019, Coxsackie passed an
        ordinance that would have blocked the project. However, on August 4, 2021, the state Siting Board
        approved the project over the town’s objection. On March 28, 2023, the Siting Board approved an
        amendment to the project.418

      ● Freepoint Solar (Greene County): In September 2021, the Athens Town Board denied a use variance
        application for the Freepoint Solar project. The developer filed a lawsuit against the town, claiming
        that the town incorrectly applied town law in reviewing the use variance application. The Court found
        in favor of the developer. The developer then applied a second time, at which point the town again
        denied the use variance on the grounds of “failure to establish the public necessity.” The developer
        commenced a new lawsuit, and in December 2024, the court again found in favor of the developer.419

      ● Galloo Island Wind Project (Jefferson County): In February 2019, Apex abandoned plans to construct a
        108-MW wind farm on Galloo Island. The project faced opposition from residents concerned about

      ● Garnet Energy Center (Cayuga County): On October 27, 2022, the state Siting Board approved

      ● Gate of Heaven Solar Farm (Westchester County): On September 2, 2021, the Mount Pleasant

      ● Gravel Road Solar (Seneca County): Delaware River Solar is seeking to develop a 128-MW solar energy
        facility across 675 acres in the town of Tyre. The project is under the jurisdiction of the New York State

        expressed opposition to a 125-MW solar project being developed by Delaware River Solar. Residents
        have claimed that they have not been allowed a voice in the process and have not been properly
        informed as to developments. Residents have formed a group called Tyre United to oppose the project.

        scheduling meetings with local and state representatives. In December 2023, Tyre Supervisor Elizabeth

    ● Hardscrabble Wind Power LLC (Herkimer County): In November 2012, dozens of Herkimer County
      residents filed a lawsuit in the Albany County Supreme Court against Iberdrola Renewables, the
      developer of the 74-MW Hardscrabble Wind Power farm, which had been operational since January
      2011. The lawsuit alleged that the 37 turbines were bigger and noisier than described during the
      planning stage, and alleged health problems, property value impacts, and a significant loss of use and
      enjoyment of their properties. In August 2018, following years of litigation and motion practice, the
      lawsuit was settled out of court for an undisclosed amount, and the wind farm remained in
      operation.424

    ● Harrison Project (Westchester County): The Harrison Solar Project is a proposed 5-MW battery energy
      storage project in Harrison, New York. Local officials raised concerns about potential flooding, visual
      impacts and decommissioning plans. At a public hearing on the project in April 2024, an overflow
      crowd of concerned residents voiced opposition to the proposed project.425

    ● Kirkville Solar (Onondaga County): In 2025, New Leaf Energy proposed the 5-MW Kirkville Solar

      ● Lighthouse Wind Project (Niagara and Orleans Counties): In January 2018, the Somerset Town Board
        passed restrictions that would effectively prevent approval and construction of the proposed 201-MW,
        70-turbine Lighthouse Wind project, unless the state were to override those restrictions under Article
        10 of the New York Public Service Law. In September 2022, after 8 years of contentious public hearings
        and lawsuits, the developer formally abandoned the project.427

      ● Mad River Wind Farm (Jefferson and Oswego Counties): The proposed 88-turbine, 350-MW Mad River
        Wind Farm in the Tug Hill region of upstate New York encountered opposition from the Tug Hill
        Tomorrow Land Trust due to potential ecological impacts. In June 2019, supporters of the project
        accused the Worth town board of secretly passing a law that severely restricted wind farm
        construction in April and then claiming the next month that they would table a vote on the law. In
        December 2020, the developer abandoned the project.428

      ● Madrid Solar Farm (St. Lawrence County): In February 2022, the St. Lawrence County Planning Board
        rejected a plan for a 4.4-MW solar farm in Madrid, New York, citing concerns that the project would
        use too much of the county’s prime agricultural land.429

      ● Meade Road Solar Project (St. Lawrence County): Plans for a 5-MW solar project on 25 acres of land in
        the town of Canton encountered public opposition. The plan was first proposed in 2020 and not
        approved until November 2022. In the meantime, the cattle farmer who owns the land where the
        project will be sited reports that he has lost money due to delays in the planning process.430

    ● Oneida groSolar Project (Madison County): Residents of Oneida sued the city in August 2015 to stop
      construction of a 2.8-MW solar farm by groSolar on 13 acres of city-owned land. A Madison County
      judge rejected the petition as untimely. Nonetheless, the developer worked with the city to find an
      alternative location. A 1.5-MW project was completed at the new location in December 2017.435

    ● Orangeville Wind Farm (Wyoming County): An organization called Clear Skies Over Orangeville (CSOO)
      was formed as early as 2006 to fight the 75-turbine Orangeville Wind Farm when the developer was
      still buying up leases. CSOO brought 2 lawsuits against the town in 2010 and 2012 to stop the project.
      However, a New York State Supreme Court judge dismissed both cases in 2018. Meanwhile, 60
      Orangeville residents brought a $40 million nuisance action against the developer Invenergy after the
      project was completed in 2014. In July 2022, a federal district court denied Invenergy’s motion for
      summary judgment, allowing the nuisance action to proceed to trial. In September 2022, the parties
      stipulated to dismissal upon reaching a settlement.436

    ● Oyster Shore Energy Project (Nassau County): Oyster Shore Energy Storage project is a proposed 275-
      MW battery energy storage project. In April 2024, the Town of Oyster Bay approved a moratorium on
      battery energy storage construction, which was extended by 6 months in November 2024. Town
      officials cited concerns about fires and public safety.437

    ● Quiogue Solar Project (Suffolk County): The Quiogue Solar Project is a proposed 2-MW solar array in
      Westhampton Beach. In April 2024, more than 100 people signed a petition opposing the project and
      opposing the Village of Westhampton Beach’s approval of the project in February 2024. In August
      2024, local residents filed a lawsuit against Westhampton Beach Village to block the proposed solar
      farm, citing concerns about the facility’s proximity to homes, potential noise, negative impacts to the
      environment and wildlife.438

    ● Raquette Lake Microgrid Battery Project (Hamilton County): In February 2024, National Grid and REV
      Renewables canceled plans to build a 20-MW battery storage microgrid facility in the town of Long

      by Raquette Lakers Against Lithium Battery Facility received over 27,000 signatures.439

      They have placed road signs around the town stating “no commercial solar farm here.” In September
      2025, the developer put the project on hold after local officials requested a study on potential visual
      impacts of the solar panels. [Note: In January 2026, it was reported that the project had been
      cancelled, but at a February 5, 2026 meeting, the town’s Planning Board Chairman stated that the
      developer was reviewing the proposal and that the project remained active.]440

      ● Shepherd’s Run Solar Project (Columbia County): In the Town of Copake, the developer Hecate LLC

        February 2024, ORES reversed its decision and denied the permit without prejudice because the

    ● South Fork Wind Project (Suffolk County): The South Fork Wind project, a 132-MW offshore wind farm
      developed by Orsted (and previously Eversource), has faced concerted opposition. Although the
      project has been complete and operational since March 2024, multiple lawsuits are still pending
      against the project. A group called Citizens for the Preservation of Wainscott opposed the project’s
      cable landing in filings before the New York Public Service Commission. In January 2021, the same
      group filed a lawsuit against the East Hampton Town Board for approving an easement for the cable to
      land on Wainscott Beach and town-owned roads. The Public Service Commission granted the cable a
      key permit in March 2021. On February 24, 2022, the Supreme Court of New York, Suffolk County,
      dismissed the lawsuit after determining that extensive environmental review had been undertaken.
      That same month, a solar developer filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging the federal
      government’s approval of the offshore wind farm, alleging insufficient review of environmental
      impacts, including impacts to whales; in March 2022, a second group of plaintiffs filed a separate
      lawsuit in federal court alleging insufficient consideration of PFAS contamination in connection with
      burying a cable in Wainscott. In November 2023, the Preservation Society of Newport County and
      Southeast Lighthouse Foundation each filed lawsuits under NEPA and the NHPA against Secretary Deb
      Haaland, the Department of the Interior, and the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management over their
      review and permitting of South Fork Wind. Meanwhile, in April 2023, an anti-offshore wind group
      called Save Long Beach Island filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey,
      challenging the National Marine Fisheries Service’s pending incidental take authorizations for several
      offshore wind farms, including the South Fork Wind project. The lawsuit alleged that these projects
      would disrupt endangered whale populations and that the cumulative impacts of noise pollution were
      not properly assessed. In February 2024, the court dismissed Save Long Beach Island’s lawsuit without
      prejudice for lack of standing and because the claims were unripe. In January 2024, another anti-
      offshore wind group called Green Oceans filed a complaint against BOEM and other federal agencies
      alleging violations of NEPA and other environmental statutes in deciding to permit South Fork Wind
      and other projects. In light of the fact that the project has been operational since March 2024, it is
      unclear what relief would be available to the plaintiffs of the pending lawsuits.447

      ● SUN8 PDC Dryden Solar Project (Tompkins County): In September 2017, the Willow Glen Cemetery

        known as Hecate Grid) proposed to install a 650-MW battery energy storage system (BESS) in
        Richmond County. At the time, it was the largest battery storage project to be proposed in New York
        State. In June 2024, the Public Service Commission issued a permit for the project.However, in August

        City mayoral candidate Curtis Sliwa, was reported to have played a role in the developer’s decision to
        cancel the project.451

      ● Union Energy Center Project (Putnam County): The Union Energy Center Project was a proposed 116-
        MW battery-energy storage project. Hundreds of local community members expressed strong
        opposition to the project at a Carmel Town Board public hearing in June 2024, citing concerns about
        fire safety and potential environmental impacts. The Carmel Town Board subsequently enacted a 6-
        month moratorium on battery storage facilities. In March 2025, the project developer formally
        withdrew its project proposal.452

      ● Williams Street Solar (Chautauqua County): In 2019, Solar Liberty Energy Systems proposed the 3.75-
        MW Williams Street Solar project to be located on approximately 45 acres in the Residential Zoning
        District in the Town of Dunkirk. The Zoning Board granted a variance request, enabling the project to
        proceed. However, in September 2025, the Town Board rejected, by a 3-1 vote, the project. Board
        members who voted against the project expressed concern that it would be inconsistent with the
        residential and agricultural character of the town.453

33.1 State Siting Framework454

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar and wind energy projects, except for wind
projects that are 1 megawatt (MW) or greater.

The state has principal siting authority over those larger wind projects (1 MW or greater). A certificate of site
compatibility and a permit from the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) are required
for projects under state jurisdiction.

The applicant must request a pre-application site evaluation meeting with the DEQ within 180 days, but no
less than 120 days, prior to filing an application with the Department. The applicant must also request a
scoping meeting with the DEQ no less than 30 days prior to filing the application. The DEQ must hold public
hearings in each county in which the project will be located within 75 days after a complete permit application
is filed.

33.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in North Carolina. In
2017, the state legislature enacted the Competitive Energy Solutions for North Carolina Act, which imposed an
18 month moratorium on permitting new wind energy facilities. In addition to this state restriction, at least 24
restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in 23 counties across North Carolina.455 Hertford County has
adopted at least 2 restrictive local ordinances. Most of the local restrictions target wind and solar energy
projects. Only 1 ordinance targeting battery storage projects has been identified in Cleveland County,
Moratoria / bans on new development are the most common type of restriction, included in 15 local
ordinances. Wind projects are often also subject to restrictive height limits (included in 8 ordinances),
restrictive setbacks (4 ordinances), and noise limits (4 ordinances).

33.3 Contested Projects
      ● Bacon’s Castle Solar Farm (Surry County): On June 16, 2022, County Supervisors rejected plans for a
        20-MW solar farm that would have been situated across the street from a historic 17th century
        homestead. The Surry County Planning Commission previously found that the proposal conflicted with
        the county’s 2040 Comprehensive Plan due to visual impacts on scenic and cultural resources and the
        county’s ordinance, which requires that solar projects “avoid important historic, archaeological or
        cultural sites. Eight out of the 10 residents who spoke about the application at a public hearing
        advocated against the project.”456

        allowed progress to begin on the solar farm. The commissioners pointed to local community
        opposition as justification for their votes.457

34.1 State Siting Framework463

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 50 megawatts
(MW) in size and wind projects that are less than 0.5 MW. The state has principal siting authority over larger
solar (50 MW or greater) and wind (0.5 MW or greater) projects. A certificate from the North Dakota Public
Service Commission is required for projects under state jurisdiction. The Commission must make a decision
within 6 months of receiving a completed application. A public hearing is required in each county in which the
project will be located.

      N.D. Cent. Code §§ 49-22-03(5), 49-22-03(5), 49-22-07, 49-22-08(6), 49-22-13.

34.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in North Dakota. Restrictive
local ordinances have been adopted in at least 13 (out of 53 counties) in the state.464 Grant Forks County has
adopted at least 2 separate restrictive local ordinances. Most of the local restrictions target wind energy
development. Only 2 counties – Bowman and McKenzie – have adopted ordinances restricting solar energy
development. Across both technologies, onerous setback requirements are the most common type of
restriction, included in 9 of the local ordinances.

        officials who supported the project in August 2019. Opponents organized an anti-wind organization,
        North Dakota Visionkeepers, to block the project. The new project owner, Burke Wind, stated in May
        2019 that they intended to move the project to elsewhere.467

35.1 State Siting Framework473

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 50 megawatts
(MW) in size and wind projects that are less than 5 MW. The state has principal siting authority over larger
solar (50 MW or greater) and wind (5 MW or greater) projects. These larger projects require a certificate of
environmental compatibility and public need from the Ohio Power Siting Board (OPSB). However, even where


473
   Ohio Rev. Code §§ 303.58(A), 303.62(A), 303.213, 4906.01(B)(1), 4906.13(A), 4906.07, 4906.10, 4906.13(B); Ohio Admin. Code §§
4906-3-03(B), 4906-3-0


                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 275
                                                                                                                        Ohio




projects are under state jurisdiction, local governments may (i) establish restricted areas where wind and solar
projects are prohibited or (ii) veto individual projects.

The applicant for a state certificate must hold at least 1 public informational meeting no more than 90 days
prior to submitting the application to the OPSB. The OPSB must make a determination of completeness within
60 days of receiving the application. The OPSB must then schedule a public hearing at least 60 days, but no
more than 90 days, after receipt of the complete application.


35.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 2 state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been adopted in Ohio. House Bill
482 of 2014 establishes restrictive setback requirements for wind energy facilities (i.e., there must be at least
1,125 feet between the turbine tip and the nearest adjacent property line). Senate Bill 52 of 2021 authorizes
counties in Ohio to veto specific renewable energy projects and designate “restricted areas” in which certain
projects (i.e., wind projects that are 5 MW or larger and solar projects that are 50 MW or larger) are
prohibited. Following the enactment of Senate Bill 52, at least 30 counties (out of 88 total) in the state have
designated restricted areas, most of which cover both wind and solar projects. At least 1 county – Crawford
County – has adopted 2 ordinances establishing restricted areas. Additionally, 1 other county – Portage
County – imposed a temporary moratorium on large wind and solar projects but, after it expired,474 declined
to establish restricted areas pursuant to Senate Bill 52.

35.3 Contested Projects
   ● Alamo Solar I (Preble County): In June 2021, the Ohio Power Siting Board granted a construction
     certificate for Alamo Solar I in Gasper and Washington Townships. The group Concerned Citizens of




                        Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 277
                                                                                                                                  Ohio




         Preble County opposed the project and appealed the decision to the Ohio Supreme Court, which
         upheld the certificate in October 2023.475

      ● Alpin Sun Solar Project (Mahoning County): In November 2023, Mahoning County commissioners
        unanimously approved Green Township’s ban on large wind and solar projects in unincorporated parts
        of the township. A public hearing was held in Green Township at the end of October 2023, in which
        residents were largely supportive of banning wind and solar. The ban had the effect of blocking the
        planned 150-MW Alpin Sun solar project. 476

      ● Angelina Solar I (Preble County): In June 2021, the Ohio Power Siting Board granted a construction
        certificate for Angelina Solar I in Israel and Dixon Townships. The group Concerned Citizens of Preble
        County opposed the project and appealed the decision to the Ohio Supreme Court, which upheld the
        certificate in October 2023.477

      ● Birch Solar (Allen and Auglaize Counties): On October 20, 2022, the OPSB rejected an application for
        the 300-MW Birch Solar Farm, the first time the OPSB ever denied an application for a large solar
        project. The project would have put solar panels on 1,410 acres out of a total project area of 2,345
        acres, the majority of which was then in agricultural use. Because the project met the criteria for
        grandfathering, it was not subject to county veto under S.B. 52. In rejecting the project, however, the
        OPSB focused largely on the fact that the two counties and 4 townships where the project would have
        been located opposed the project. The Board found that the project satisfied all criteria except the
        public interest standard and cited “universal opposition from local government and residents” as a
        “determining component” for failure to meet the public interest standard. The developer appealed the
        decision to the Ohio Supreme Court, arguing that public opposition does not equate to public interest.
        In January 2025, the developer withdrew its appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court due to continued
        opposition to the project.478

      ● Chestnut Solar (Marion County): Plans to construct Chestnut Solar, a 404-acre, 68-MW solar farm in
        Pleasant Township, encountered intense local opposition and were ultimately abandoned. In February
        2023, the Marion County Board of Commissioners issued a resolution in opposition to the Project. In
        April 2024, the staff of the Ohio Power Siting Board recommended that the Board deny the application,
        upon finding that the project would not serve the public interest, convenience, and necessity due to
        “overwhelmingly one-sided” opposition “from the local government agencies and the citizens.” That
        same month, the Ohio Power Siting Board held a public hearing at which the majority of commenters
        expressed opposition to the project. Opponents cited concerns about aesthetic impacts, drainage
        issues, farmland loss, and property values. In May 2024, the developer withdrew its application for the
        project.482

      ● Chipmunk Solar (Pickaway County): On March 2, 2022, EDF Renewables submitted an application for
        construction of the 400-MW Chipmunk Solar project on approximately 3,684 acres in Pickaway County.
        However, on December 22, 2022, the developer withdrew the application amidst intense local
        opposition. The project would have provided $3.6 million per year in local tax revenue (mostly to fund
        public schools) and $3 million per year in lease payments to participating landowners.483

        application process for a Certificate of Environmental Compatibility and Public Need with the Ohio
        Power Siting Board (OPSB). CFFF and Walnut Township government intervened in the proceeding in
        opposition to the project. On August 21, 2025, the OPSB approved the application, allowing the project
        to move forward. In October 2025, the OPSB denied the opponents motion for rehearing and affirmed
        the approval of the project. In December 2025, the opponents filed a notice of appeal in the Ohio
        Supreme Court.485

      ● Fountain Point Solar Farm (Logan County): The proposed Fountain Point Solar Farm, which would span
        3,800 acres in Bokescreek, Rushcreek, and Perry Townships, is currently being considered by the OPSB.
        The group No Solar in Logan County (Ohio) has opposed the project, and around 100 residents
        opposed the project at a March 2022 public meeting.487

      ● Frasier Solar Project (Knox County): Frasier Solar, an 800-acre, 120-MW solar farm proposed by Open
        Road Renewables in Knox County has encountered organized opposition. In November 2023, an
        anonymously funded group called Knox Smart Development (KSD) was formed to oppose the project.
        KSD has hosted events with speakers from the Heartland Institute and natural gas-associated groups,
        including the Empowerment Alliance. In December 2023, KSD published an op-ed laying out points in
        opposition to the project and advising residents on means to oppose it. In January 2024, KSD and a
        second opposition group called Preserve Knox County (PKC) intervened in a proceeding in front of the
        Ohio Power Siting Board to oppose the project. The Ohio Environmental Council, the Ohio Chamber of
        Commerce, the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, and a participating landowner
        intervened in support. In April 2024, the Ohio Power Siting Board held a public hearing which was
        adjourned after 6.5 hours of testimony, with the OPSB deciding to hold 2 additional public hearings to
        accommodate the remaining speakers. At the hearings, opponents raised concerns about loss of
        farmland and agricultural production, as well as noise and other disruptions surrounding properties,
        while supporters emphasized property rights, economic benefits, and plans to include sheep grazing as
        part of the project. In August 2024, the Board held an adjudicatory hearing. On June 26, 2025, the
        OPSB approved the project, finding that opposition from local government officials was not unanimous
        and that the project served the public interest. On August 21, 2025, the OPSB denied a motion for
        rehearing and upheld the approval of the project. In October 2025, the opponents filed a notice of
        appeal in the Ohio Supreme Court.488

      ● Hillclimber Solar (Champaign County): In 2025, RWE proposed the Hillclimber Solar project,
        comprising 116.5 MW of solar energy generation and 40 MW of battery energy storage, to be located
        on over 900 acres in Urbana Township. Although Champaign County has an active ban on new utility-
        scale solar projects in its townships and unincorporated areas, the project is reportedly exempt
        because the developer had signed agreements with the regional electric grid operator (PJM) that pre-
        dated the ban. In September 2025, the developer filed a pre-application notice with the Ohio Power
        Siting Board (OPSB) for state level approval of the project. At a November 2025 Champaign County
        public hearing, opponents of the project raised concerns about its potential environmental impacts,
        changes in viewshed, and a lack of local benefits. The opponents have placed “no solar” lawn and field
        signs in properties near the area where the project would be sited. The developer had already
        decreased the size of the project by 200 acres after opposition at the initial public meeting a month
        prior. The project is estimated to generate roughly $30 million in tax revenue over the project’s
        lifespan. The permitting process remains pending before the OPSB.491

      ● Honey Creek Wind (Crawford County): On May 5, 2022, the Crawford County Commissioners adopted
        a resolution pursuant to S.B. 52 prohibiting large wind farms in all unincorporated areas of the county,
        which effectively barred construction of the 300-MW Honey Creek Wind Farm proposed by Apex Clean
        Energy. Apex Clean Energy successfully petitioned to have the project put to a vote in a referendum in
        November but ultimately lost in the referendum when voters opted to uphold the restrictions.492

36.1 State Siting Framework506

Local governments have siting authority over wind and solar energy projects of any size. The state has
concurrent siting authority over wind energy facilities that are 0.5 megawatts (MW) or larger in size. Those
wind projects must be approved by both the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (OCC) and the relevant local
government.

The applicant of a wind project under state jurisdiction must hold a public meeting within 60 days of
publishing the required notice of intent to build the project. There is no statutory permitting timeline for
project approval at either the state or local level.

      Okla. Stat. tit. 19 § 863.24; Okla. Stat. tit. 17 §§ 160.2, 160.14, 160.20, 160.21

36.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least two state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been adopted in Oklahoma, both
targeting wind energy projects. The Oklahoma Wind Energy Development Act of 2015 established restrictive
setback requirements for wind energy facilities, requiring them to be at least 1.5 miles from public schools,
hospitals, and airports. In 2019, additional setback requirements were adopted, requiring individual wind
turbines to be at least 1.5 nautical miles from military airspace. In addition to these state restrictions, at least
3 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in Oklahoma. All 3 ordinances establish restrictive height
limits for wind turbines and 1 – adopted in Ponca City – also imposes density limits on wind projects.

Total number of state restrictions: 2
   ○ Total number of local restrictions: 3
   ○ Technology targeted:
          ■ 5 (wind)
   ○ Type of Restrictions:
          ■ Oklahoma House Bill 2118 of 2019: Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)
          ■ Oklahoma Statutes § 17-160.20(A): Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)
          ■ City of Owasso (Tulsa County): Rule 9: Height Restriction (wind)
          ■ City of Yukon (Canadian County): Rule 9: Height Restriction (wind)
          ■ Ponca City (Kay County): Rule 2: Density Cap (wind) | Rule 9: Height Restriction (wind)

37.1 State Siting Framework515

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind projects of less than 100 megawatts (MW), solar
thermal projects of less than 25 MW, and solar photovoltaic (PV) projects that occupy less than 240 acres of
high-value farmland, less than 2,560 acres of land that is predominantly cultivated, or less than 3,840 acres of
any other land. Local governments must make a decision on a project application within 150 days of receipt.



515
   Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 215.427(1), 469.300(11), 469.300(12)(a)(A), 469.300(12)(a)(K), 469.320, 469.504, 469.370(2), 469.370(5),
469.370(9)(d)



                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 297
                                                                                                                Oregon




The state has principal siting authority over all other solar and wind projects. Developers of projects that
typically fall under local jurisdiction may also opt-in to the state siting process. A certificate from the Oregon
Energy Facility Siting Council (EFSC) is required for projects under state jurisdiction. However, under House Bill
4031 (2026), a certificate from the EFSC is not required for facilities producing power exclusively from solar
(photovoltaic or thermal), wind, geothermal, or marine energy, provided that: (1) the developer receives
approval from the local government by December 31, 2028, (2) construction has begun in a manner that
qualifies for specific federal tax credits, and (3) the facility is placed in service by December 31, 2030, unless a
later date is allowed by an IRS exception.

The EFSC must hold a public hearing after the Oregon Department of Energy issues a draft proposed order on
the certificate application and must also hold a contested case hearing on any issues raised at the public
hearing. The EFSC must make a decision within 12 months from the filing of the application.


37.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Oregon. In 2019, the
Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development adopted regulations, which prohibits solar energy
projects covering more than 20 acres of prime farmland or 20 acres of other farmland (with limited
exceptions). In addition to this state prohibition, at least 5 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in 4
counties. Wallowa county has adopted at least 2 restrictive local ordinances, 1 banning certain wind
development, and the other establishing size limits for solar projects. Curry and Polk Counties have each
adopted ordinances limiting the size of solar projects and Umatilla County has an ordinance establishing
restrictive setbacks for wind projects.

   ○ Total number of state restrictions: 1
   ○ Total number of local restrictions: 5
   ○ Technology targeted:
        ■ 2 (wind)
        ■ 4 (solar)
   ○ Type of Restrictions:
        ■ Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development solar Siting Rules: Rule 1:
            Ban/Moratorium (solar)
        ■ Curry County: Rule 2: Size Cap (solar)
        ■ Polk County: Rule 2: Size Cap (solar)
        ■ Umatilla County: Rule 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)
        ■ Wallowa County: Rule 1: Ban / Moratorium (wind) | Rule 2: Size Cap (solar)

        those lawsuits, allowing the project to move forward.517

      ● Echanis Wind Farm (Harney County): In 2007, Columbia Energy Partners (“CEP”) proposed Echanis
        Wind Farm, a 104-MW wind farm to be developed on approximately 10,500 acres of private land. The
        project met immediate opposition from the Oregon Natural Desert Association (“ONDA”) due to its
        proximity to the federally-protected Steens Mountain. Despite opposition, Harney County granted a
        conditional use permit. CEP then proposed 2 additional 104-MW wind projects with a potential third
        proposal, which prompted increased public opposition. In 2009 CEP withdrew the additional proposals
        but obtained approval for its initial project, which required approval from the Bureau of Land
        Management (BLM) and submission of an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) because the
        transmission lines needed to cross over 40 miles of federal lands. Opposition continued throughout the
        EIS process garnering about 250 public comments. In 2011, BLM approved the project. ONDA and the
        Audubon Society of Portland challenged the decision in federal district court, which dismissed their
        lawsuit. In 2016, the opponents appealed the district court’s dismissal to the Ninth Circuit, which
        partially reversed the dismissal of the lawsuit and remanded BLM’s approval, concluding that the EIS
        was inadequate. No significant progress has been made on the project since the Ninth Circuit’s
        decision to reverse and remand.519

      ● Mountain Meadow Solar Project (Clackamas County): Mountain Meadow Solar, LLC applied to
        Clackamas County for permission to construct a 10-acre solar farm on a parcel then used for growing

      ● Nolin Hills Energy Project (Umatilla County): In September 2017, Capital Power proposed a 350-MW

        transmission line passing through commercial, industrial and agribusiness zones, on a total of to 48,000
        acres. In January 2022, the developer filed its application for a site certificate with the Energy Facility
        Siting Council (EFSC) instead of seeking local land use approval with the county’s Board of
        Commissioners. In July 2022, the county amended its Development Code to require a 2-mile setback
        from rural homes. In August 2023, the EFSC unanimously approved the project. The county
        government challenged the EFSC’s decision in the state’s Supreme Court alleging that the project does
        not comply with the local setback restrictions. On April 18, 2024, the court affirmed the EFSC’s decision
        allowing the project to proceed as long as it otherwise complies with the state’s land use goals. The
        court held that the EFSC has the ultimate decision-making authority over large energy facilities that
        comply with statewide planning goals. Development of the project is ongoing.522

38.1 State Siting Framework528

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar and wind energy projects of any size. However, an
environmental permit from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection is required before a
project can be approved at the local level.

There is no statutory requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no
deadline for the local government to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

38.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Pennsylvania. In 2018,
the Pennsylvania Game Commission adopted a resolution prohibiting wind energy development on 1.5 million

38.3 Contested Projects
      ● Atlantic Wind Project (Carbon County): In 2016, Atlantic Wind submitted a proposal to construct 37
        wind turbines in Penn Forest Township on lands owned by the Bethlehem Municipal Authority. The
        2016 proposal was “deemed approved” when Penn Forest Township defaulted on deadline during the
        review process. Township residents filed a lawsuit challenging the deemed approval, but the approval
        was upheld in December 2017 by a Carbon County judge. In 2018, with the litigation on the first
        application still pending, Atlantic Wind submitted a modified application, this time seeking permission
        for only 28 turbines located farther from homes.529

      ● Brookfield Solar Energy Center (Lancaster County): During a series of 21 public hearings between
        January 2020 and March 2021, residents protested a 75-MW solar energy project proposed by
        Brookfield Solar I LLC that would span 1,000 acres across 26 different parcels of land in Mount Joy
        Township. At 1 hearing in August 2020, protestors argued that the town supervisor should be fired
        because he owns a solar lease. In June 2021, Mount Joy Township supervisors rejected the developer’s
        request for a conditional use permit to build a 391-acre stretch of the project along a major highway.
        On September 2, 2022, the Court of Common Pleas of Adams County, Pennsylvania upheld the denial
        of the permit, finding that the developer failed to provide sufficient analysis of adverse impacts on
        surrounding property owners, including stormwater runoff and glare. 530

      ● Brookview Solar 1 (Lancaster County): In November 2023, the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court
        affirmed the denial of a permit for the Brookview Solar 1 project in Mt. Joy Township. Project
        neighbors had opposed the development, collecting 950 signatures for a petition against the project.531

      ● Cuffs Run Pumped Storage Project (York County): York Energy Storage LLC plans to construct a 1.8-
        mile-long dam and flood 580 acres to create a hydroelectric facility designed to feed power into the
        regional grid. The project is named the Cuffs Run Pumped Storage Project and will have an estimated
        1,000-acre footprint. In July 2023, a coalition of 17 nonprofits and local governments, along with
        Republican State Senator Kristin Phillips-Hill of York, signed a letter urging federal regulators to reject

      ● Laurel Hill Wind (Lycoming County): In January 2005, Laurel Hill Wind Energy, LLC applied for a special
        exception to construct a 69-MW wind energy facility on land primarily within the County’s Resource
        Protection (RP) Zoning district. The county Zoning Administrator granted the special exception by
        classifying the project as a “public service use,” prompting a nearby property owner to appeal. After
        multiple hearings, the Lycoming County Zoning Hearing Board (ZHB) ultimately denied the special
        exception, citing potential adverse impacts and inconsistencies with the RP’s purpose. Laurel Hill
        Energy appealed the denial to the Court of Common Pleas. In May 2007, the Court affirmed the ZHB’s
        denial. In November 2007, the Lycoming County Commissioners amended the zoning ordinance to
        permit wind energy facilities in certain districts, including the RP. In February 2008, Laurel Hill Energy
        applied for a zoning permit under the new ordinance, and its application was approved with conditions
        in May 2008. A month later, 2 local residents Arthur and Elke Plaxton, filed a substantive validity
        challenge against the ordinance amendments as invalid, arbitrary and unreasonable. In December
        2009, the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania found no error in the ZHB’s decision and affirmed the
        denial of the challenge to the amendments. The project was allowed to proceed and was
        commissioned in October 2012.540

39.1 State Siting Framework551
Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects that are less than 40
megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal siting authority over larger energy facilities (40 MW or
greater) (known as “major” facilities). A license from the Energy Facility Siting Board (EFSB) is required for
these larger projects.

The EFSB has 30 days to determine whether an application is complete. Within 60 days of docketing an
application, the EFSB must hold a preliminary hearing to determine any issues to be considered, and identify
the state agencies to provide advisory opinions. Under state law, the local governments where the project is
proposed are also expected to render advisory opinions as part of the siting process. However, the EFSB has
sole and final decision-making authority over projects. The advisory opinions are due within 6 months of the
preliminary hearing.

The EFSB must hold a final hearing within 45 days after the preliminary hearing and must issue a final decision
on the application within 60 days after the final hearing. The EFSB must also hold at least 1 public hearing in
each locality involved.


39.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in Rhode Island. House
Bill 5853 of 2023 prohibits certain solar energy development in “core forest” areas, defined as “unfragmented
forest blocks of single or multiple parcels totaling two hundred fifty (250) acres or greater unbroken by
development and at least twenty-five (25) yards from mapped roads.” In addition to this state restriction, at
least 3 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in Rhode Island. Two of the local ordinances – adopted
by the City of Cranston and City of Warwick – prohibit certain solar energy projects. A 3rd local ordinance –
adopted by the Town of North Kingstown – prohibits wind energy development.

39.3 Contested Projects
      ● Block Island Wind Farm (Washington County): The 5-turbine, 30-MW Block Island Wind Farm,
        completed in 2016, was the first offshore wind project to be constructed in the United States.
        However, the project encountered opposition during the planning and construction stage. In particular,
        the Rhode Island Manufacturers Association filed a lawsuit in 2015, alleging that National Grid’s deal to
        purchase power from the wind farm violated federal law and would result in a significant increase to
        their electric bills. A federal district court found that the statute of limitations had run on the plaintiff’s
        claim and dismissed the lawsuit.552

      ● Green Development’s Town of Johnston Solar Farm (Providence County): Between October 2021 and
        November 2021, Green Development submitted applications for a 300-acre, 24-MW solar farm in the
        Town of Johnston. The project encountered opposition from residents who argued that a large-scale
        solar farm should not be sited in a residential area. Local opponents formed a group called Stop
        Johnston Solar, and Town Council member Robert Civetti pushed for an ordinance banning solar farms
        in residential areas. In April 2022, the Zoning Board narrowly rejected the initial proposal, after a public
        hearing that was reportedly so raucous that officials called several police officers. In June 2022, the
        developer appealed the Zoning Board’s decision to the Providence County Superior Court. In July 2024,
        the court found that the Zoning Board had failed to explain its reasoning for rejecting the project and
        remanded the decision to the Zoning Board “to issue detailed and appropriate written decisions.”
        Meanwhile, the developer submitted a revised proposal for a 160-acre, 24-MW solar, which the Zoning
        Board unanimously rejected in January 2024, after a public hearing at which no residents spoke in
        favor of the project. In March 2024, the developer appealed that decision to the Rhode Island Superior
        Court.553

40.1 State Siting Framework562
Local governments have principal siting authority over solar and wind energy facilities that are less than 75
megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal siting authority over larger solar and wind energy facilities (75
MW or greater). These larger projects require a certificate of environmental compatibility and public
convenience and necessity from the South Carolina Public Service Commission (PSC). Under state law, when
evaluating a certificate application, the PSC “may refuse to apply any local law or local regulation if it finds
that, as applied to the proposed facility, such law or regulation is unreasonably restrictive in view of the



562
      S.C. Code Ann. §§ 6-29-310 et seq., 58-33-20, 58-33-20(2)(a), 58-33-110, 58-33-130, 58-33-160(1)(e)



                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 324
                                                                                                                  South Carolina




existing technology, or of factors of cost or economics or of the needs of consumers whether located inside or
outside of the directly affected government subdivisions.”

The PSC must hold a public hearing no less than 60 days, and no more than 90 days, after receipt of a
certificate application.


40.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development in South Carolina. Of the 46 counties in the
state, at least 4 – Calhoun, Darlington, Edgefield, and Marlborough – have adopted local ordinances restricting
wind and/or solar energy projects. The restrictions take various forms, including caps on the size of projects,
onerous setback requirements, and height limits.

           ■ Marlboro County: Rule 2: Size Cap (solar) | Rule 2: Size Cap (wind)

40.3 Contested Projects
      ● Gallivants Ferry Solar Project (Horry County): Southern Current, a Charleston-based solar farm
        developer, submitted a proposal to build a 138-MW, 1,500-acre project near the unincorporated
        community of Gallivants Ferry in western Horry County. During meetings in 2020, members of the
        County Council raised concerns about leaching of cadmium telluride, questioning what would happen if
        the solar panels were damaged in a hurricane. County Council members also raised concerns about
        decommissioning and whether landfills would accept solar panels. Although the developer agreed not
        to use solar panels that include cadmium telluride, the project was never built.563

41.1 State Siting Framework567
Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects that are less than 100
megawatts (MW) in size. The state has principal siting authority over larger solar and wind energy facilities
(100 MW or greater). These larger projects require approval from the South Dakota Public Utilities
Commission (PUC). A public hearing must be held within 30 days of the PUC’s receipt of the permit
application. The PUC must make a final determination within 9 months of receipt of the application.

41.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in South Dakota. At least 9
restrictive local ordinances have been adopted. One of the ordinances, adopted by Pennington County,
imposed a 1-year moratorium on wind and solar energy development. The other 8 ordinances – adopted by
Letcher Township in Sanborn County and the Counties of Brookings, Deuel, Edmunds, Hugest, Miner, Roberts,
and Sully – established onerous setback requirements for wind and sometimes solar energy projects. The Sully
County ordinance also included noise and shadow flicker limits for wind projects.

41.3 Contested Projects
   ● Crocker Wind Farm (Clark County): In 2017, Geronimo Energy proposed a 400-MW wind farm in Clark
     County. Public hearings on the project featured significant opposition from local residents. The Clark
     County Commission approved the project but required that turbines be set back 3,960 feet (0.75 miles)
     from residences, far more than the 1,000 feet required by the county zoning ordinance. Geronimo
     Energy challenged the setback requirements in court, but the court ruled in favor of the commission.




                        Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 329
                                                                                                                South Dakota




         South Dakota’s Public Utilities granted a construction permit in June 2018. The final project, completed
         in 2019, was 200 MW, half the size originally proposed.568

      ● Crowned Ridge Wind (Codington and Grant Counties): The Public Utility Commission’s permit for the
        132-turbine Crowned Ridge Wind project was appealed by opponents to the South Dakota Supreme
        Court, which upheld it in 2022. One of the landowners who brought the appeal later filed suit about
        the noise level from the operating wind farm. In October 2023, that complaint was dismissed after the
        plaintiff failed to attend a hearing.569

      ● Dakota Power Community Wind Project (Lincoln County): In 2014, the Dakota Power Community
        Wind proposed a 1,000-MW wind farm in rural Lincoln County with up to 500 turbines. Local residents
        organized an opposition group, We-Care SD, to advocate for stricter setbacks. The Lincoln County
        Board of Commissioners increased the setback requirement from 0.25 miles to 0.5 miles from
        habitable dwellings. Voters upheld the setbacks in a July 2017 referendum. In November 2017, the
        developer relinquished 122 easements it had secured for the project, signaling an intent to cancel the
        project.570

      ● Davison County Wind LLC (Davison County): In April 2018, the Davison County Commissioners
        unanimously voted to reject a conditional use permit application for the construction of 9 wind
        turbines in Beulah Township. It marked the second time in 3 years that the Commission had rejected a
        wind energy project. Several Commissioners expressed concern about potential impact on property
        values, whereas several participating landowners expressed surprise at the amount of opposition to
        what they saw as a beneficial project.571

      ● Juhl Energy’s Letcher Township Wind Project (Sanborn County): In 2016, residents of Letcher
        Township preemptively mobilized to block Juhl Energy from developing a wind project in the township.
        Although Juhl Energy had not yet submitted an application, residents were concerned that Juhl Energy
        would look to Letcher Township after nearby Davison County rejected the company’s application for a

42.1 State Siting Framework576

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. However, a certificate
of public convenience and necessity from the Tennessee Public Utility Commission is also required for wind
projects that are more than 1 megawatt (MW) and at least 200 feet high.

A public hearing is required within 60 days of receipt of a complete permit application. There is no statutory
deadline for local or state authorities to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

42.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 2 state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been adopted in Tennessee. House
Bill 1021 / Senate Bill 1336 of 2017 imposed a 1-year moratorium on the construction, operation, expansion,
or redevelopment of wind energy facilities in Tennessee (subject to limited exceptions). Upon expiry of the
moratorium, the Tennessee state legislature enacted House Bill 1731, which requires wind energy projects to


576
      Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 65-17-101(12)(A), 65-17-104, 65-17-105, 65-17-105(d)(3).


                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 333
                                                                                                                  Tennessee




comply with restrictive setback requirements (i.e., requiring facilities to be 3.5 times the total height of the
wind turbine from non-participating landowners property lines) and noise limits (i.e., limiting turbine noise to
35 dBA as measured at the site of non-participating dwellings). In addition to these state restrictions, at least 6
counties (out of 95 total) in Tennessee have adopted restrictive local ordinances targeting wind and/or solar
projects.577 Two counties – Greene and Shelby – have adopted ordinances imposing temporary moratoria on
solar energy projects. A 3rd county – Franklin – has permanently banned both solar and wind energy
development. Other restrictions on renewable energy projects in the state include onerous setbacks (adopted
in Dyer and Haywood counties) and height restrictions for wind turbines (adopted in Robertson County).

43.1 State Siting Framework579

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. There is no statutory
requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local
governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

      Tex. Loc. Gov’t Code §§ 211.003, 231.001 et seq.

43.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Texas. At least 30
restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by 30 cities spread across 22 counties (of out 254 total) in the
state. All of the local ordinances restrict wind energy development; 2 also restrict solar energy projects. At
least 14 cities have adopted temporary moratoria or permanent bans on wind energy development. Wind
energy projects are also commonly subject to restrictive height limits (included in 15 ordinances), energy use
limits (included in 13 ordinances), noise limits (included in 7 ordinances), size caps (included in 5 ordinances),
setbacks (included in 2 ordinances).

     energy in Henrietta, Texas. One meeting sought to recruit the support of fighter pilots stationed at a
     nearby air force base by focusing on potential interference with radar systems. In June 2018, under

      ● Buffalo Meadow Energy Center (Robertson County): In 2022, Savion Energy proposed the Buffalo
        Meadow Energy Center with 200 MW of solar energy generation and 150 MW of battery energy
        storage, to be constructed within the Franklin Independent School District in Robertson County. In
        December 2022, the Franklin Board of Trustees approved the Agreement for an Appraised Value
        Limitation on Qualified Property requested by the developer. [Note: In March 2026, the Robertson
        County Commissioners held a public hearing at the county courthouse to discuss a tax abatement
        agreement for the project. Local residents packed the room and largely opposed the project, raising
        concerns about potential impacts on property values, water resources pollution, and fire safety. The
        County Commissioners have not made a decision on the tax abatement for the project as of June
        2026.]581

      ● Byers Wind Project (Clay County): The proposed 200-MW Byers wind project encountered the same

        the project. Greer helped co-found Clay County Against Wind Farms, which held informational sessions
        against wind energy in Henrietta, Texas. One meeting sought to recruit the support of fighter pilots
        stationed at a nearby air force base by focusing on potential interference with radar systems. In June

      ● Hopkins Energy LLC’s Solar Project (Hopkins County): In June 2021, a local resident filed a lawsuit
        against the French energy company Engie, seeking to halt construction of an 1,850-acre solar project in
        the unincorporated community of Dike, Texas and to obtain $250,000 in damages, alleging that the
        project would cause increased runoff onto neighboring properties. Local opponents have purportedly
        contemplated the possibility of incorporating Dike as a city to block the project.584

      ● Horse Hollow Wind Energy Center (Nolan and Taylor Counties): In June 2005, a local resident group
        called Protect Our West Texas Landscape (POWTL) sued developer FPL Energy to prevent the
        construction of the 735.5-MW Horse Hollow Wind Energy Center. POWTL alleged that the wind farm
        would drastically disrupt the local scenery. The court ruled that no law in Texas regulates aesthetics,
        prompting the plaintiffs to amend the complaint to assert public and private nuisance claims and to
        seek injunctive relief. In December 2006, a trial jury found against the plaintiffs. The case was
        dismissed, and the plaintiffs appealed. In August 2008, the Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment of
        the trial court on all respects except for the allocation of costs and remanded for further
        determination. While that appeal was pending, the same plaintiffs sued the Taylor County
        Commissioners, alleging that the tax abatements given to the wind farms in the area were unlawful;
        that lawsuit, however, was withdrawn within a couple of months for procedural reasons. The Horse
        Hollow Center has been operational since its commissioning in 2005.585

      ● Lane City Wind Project (Wharton County): The Lane City Wind Project is a 203-MW wind energy
        facility with approximately 59 wind turbines on 14,000 acres of land in Wharton County. Construction
        of the project began in the summer of 2024. In February 2025, a local ranch, Blue Creek Real
        Properties, sued the Department of Treasury and the developer, Lane City Wind, LLC seeking to halt
        construction and permanently block federal funding for the project. The lawsuit, filed in the United
        States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, alleges violations of the Endangered Species Act
        (ESA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) due to potential risk to protected birds,
        including the Bald Eagle and Whooping Crane. In April 2025, the district court denied the defendant

      ● Lazy U Solar 1 (Hardeman County): In 2023, OCI Energy proposed the 200-MW Lazy U Solar 1 facility to
        be located on farmland. The project has faced local opposition by residents who have voiced concerns
        over tax subsidies, threats to protected wildlife, and the decommissioning of solar panels. In November
        2025, Hardeman County officials approved a tax abatement for the project following a public meeting,
        despite the voiced opposition. The developer is in the process of relocating protected wildlife from the
        project site.587

      ● Mustang Wind Project (Fayette County): Apex Clean Energy proposed a 250-MW wind farm within a
        50,000-acre area north of Schulenburg. The development would include between 40 to 80 turbines,
        some up to 600 feet tall. Local opponents organized a Facebook page called “Fayette County Texas -
        Stop The Wind Turbines” and an opposition group called “FayCoSaysNo.” The groups were active at
        town hall meetings and recruited hundreds of residents to join in opposition. In June 2024, the County
        Commissioners held a public meeting at which over 140 local residents attended, with 10 speaking in
        opposition and none speaking in support. The leader of the opposition raised questions about fire
        safety, negative impacts on livestock and wildlife, and plans for disposal of the turbines. She also raised
        concerns with red flashing lights, humming sounds and moving shadows from the turbines. On August
        8, 2024, the Fayette County Commissioners Court signed a non-binding resolution opposing
        commercial wind energy development. In October 2024, the developer issued a statement stating that
        “Fayette County is not a focus at the moment.”588
