    ● Oneida 2 Solar (Potter County): In 2025, Xcel Energy proposed the 254-MW Oneida 2 Solar project to
      be located on approximately 1,300 acres in the Rolling Hills neighborhood, north of Amarillo in Potter
      County. In October 2025, Xcel Energy officially withdrew the proposal after more than 60 complaints
      were filed with the Texas Public Utility Commission and following a heated community meeting during
      which opponents of the project raised concerns about flooding, noise, wildlife displacement, and
      property values.589

    ● Ranchland Wind Project (Callahan and Eastland Counties): In May 2020, a group of 365 residents and
      landowners signed a petition urging county commissioners of Callahan and Eastland Counties to reject
      requests for tax abatements associated with the proposed Ranchland Wind Project. A group called
      Callahan County Land Owners Against Wind Turbines issued a statement online claiming that
      developers would be digging into and potentially damaging local aquifers. As of March 2023, the 267-
      MW wind project and 87-MWdc battery storage system is under construction.590

    ● Rio Lago Solar (Bandera County): In 2022, Pine Gate Renewables proposed a 123-MW solar farm on
      privately-owned land, which was projected to generate over $20 million in tax revenue for the county.
      In October 2023, opposing landowners filed a lawsuit in state court alleging environmental damage
      and contamination on their nearby properties and seeking a temporary restraining order to halt
      construction. In December 2023, the trial court issued a temporary restraining order pausing several
      components of the project. In February 2024, the court issued an order temporarily enjoining the
      developer from clearing trees and preparing the leased land unless the developer complied with
      specific requirements including developing a stormwater pollution prevention plan and obtaining
      construction permits approved by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. Several disputes
      over potential violations of the injunction followed. In September 2024, a federal court again
      temporarily enjoined construction, but construction subsequently resumed.591

    ● Solar Proponent LLC (Bastrop County): In October 2022, the Elgin Independent School District voted
      unanimously to reject an application for a 3,000-acre solar farm from Solar Proponent LLC. A local
      group called Friends of the Land had opposed the project, expressing concern that clearing the land of

    ● Stockyard Solar a/k/a Saddle House Solar (Franklin County): Enel Green Power proposed a 210-MW
      solar farm with a 70-MW battery energy storage site to be developed on approximately 2,350 acres.
      The project has faced significant local opposition. More than 1,100 residents signed a petition against
      any solar projects in the county. Opponents created the website “Citizens for Reasonable Regulation of
      Renewable Energy” to host blogs and campaigns against solar development in the county. The county
      commissioners voted to impose a countywide 180-day moratorium on commercial solar development,
      which was later rescinded, as there were questions as to the county’s authority to adopt and enforce
      it. At a local school board meeting held on October 6, 2022 to decide whether to provide tax credits to
      the developer, opponents of the project voiced concerns over fire safety as well as water and soil
      contamination. In November 2022, although the school board rejected the tax credits, the developer
      proceeded with the project. In June 2023, 2 landowners filed a lawsuit in the County District Court
      seeking an injunction to stop the project. In July 2023, the defendants removed the case to the Texas
      Federal District Court, and the plaintiffs moved to remand. In March 2024, the Texas Federal District
      Court denied the motion to remand, dismissed the claims against one defendant, and allowed the
      remaining claims to be heard in federal court. In December 2025, the Texas Federal District Court
      granted the plaintiffs’ unopposed motion to dismiss without prejudice.593

44.1 State Siting Framework595

Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects. There is no statutory
requirement for public hearings or other public involvement in the siting process and no deadline for local
governments to issue a final decision on a proposed project.

44.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Utah. Of the 29 counties
in the state, at least 5 – Beaver, Duchesne, Kane, Utah, and Weber – have adopted local ordinances restricting
renewable energy development. The ordinance adopted in Kane County targets solar energy development,
while the other counties have only restricted wind projects. The restrictions take various forms including
outright bans, onerous setback requirements, and height and shadow flicker limits.

45.1 State Siting Framework596
The state regulates the siting of all electric generating facilities, including all solar or wind projects. A
certificate of public good must be obtained from the Vermont Public Utility Commission (PUC) prior to the
construction of a solar or wind project. In deciding whether to issue a certificate, the PUC must give due
consideration to the recommendations by the local government(s) involved, and in specific instances, grant
substantial deference to the local land-use policies.

Before making a decision on a certificate application, the PUC may hold a non-evidentiary hearing on its own
motion. Such a hearing must be held if requested and an evidentiary hearing(s) must be held if contested issues
remain. Local and regional planning commissions and municipal legislative bodies may to appear as parties in
PUC proceedings. Generally, there is no statutory deadline for the PUC to issue a final decision on a proposed
project.

The Supreme Court of Vermont has held that when the Public Utilities Board has issued an order approving a
facility, “[a]ny attempt at municipal regulation is pre-empted.”


45.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development were identified in Vermont. However, at least 5
restrictive local ordinances have been adopted. Two of the ordinances – adopted by the Northeast Vermont
Development Association (a regional planning commission) and the Town of Stockbridge – ban wind energy
development in certain areas. The Town of Milton and Town of Woodstock have also sought to restrict wind
energy development by establishing height limits for turbines. The Town of Shelburne has established
viewshed restrictions applicable to solar energy projects.

               Ban / Moratorium (wind)

45.3 Contested Projects
      ● Apple Hill Solar and Willow Road Solar, f/k/a Chelsea Solar (Bennington County): Allco Renewable
        Energy’s plans for the 2-MW Apple Hill project and 2-MW Willow Road project in Bennington, Vermont
        have faced opposition from neighbors for close to a decade. The state Public Utility Commission (PUC)
        initially approved the Apple Hill project in 2018, but opponents of the project appealed the decision,
        and the PUC reversed its own decision on remand in May 2020. In addition, in June 2019, the PUC
        denied a certificate of public good for the Willow Road project, finding that the Willow Road project
        and the Apple Hill project were in fact a single 4-MW solar plant and therefore ineligible under a state
        program for solar projects of 2.2 MW or less; the Vermont Supreme Court upheld that determination
        in January 2020. In June 2020 the PUC issued a temporary restraining order after Vermonters for a
        Clean Environment filed comments alleging that the developer was clearing trees on the proposed
        sites and that endangered plant species were being disturbed. On May 16, 2022, the PUC once again
        denied a permit for Apple Hill solar. In January 2023, the Bennington Planning Commission
        unanimously recommended against finding that the revised Willow Road (f/k/a Chelsea) solar project
        was within a preferred site for solar facilities, and in June 2023, the Bennington Select Board rejected
        the proposal. In July 2023, Allco filed a lawsuit in state court against the town of Bennington seeking to
        force the town to declare the proposed site a preferred location for solar under the town’s Energy Plan
        guidelines. This lawsuit was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, and Allco responded by stating that it
        would bring the lawsuit in federal court instead. In October 2023, the Vermont Supreme Court
        affirmed the PUC’s 2020 denial of a certificate of public convenience and necessity. On December 12,
        2023, the Vermont Supreme Court denied Allco’s request for reargument. On June 3, 2025, in a special
        Town of Bennington Select Board meeting, the board voted 5-1 to ratify a settlement agreement in
        support of the project. The board agreed that the project site is a “preferred area,” not prominently
        visible on a hillside, does not violate the town plan and does not have “adverse regional impact.”597

        legal fees over 3 years. In March 2020, the PUC dismissed the developer’s petition to build the project.

46.1 State Siting Framework610

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 5 megawatts
(MW) in size and that disturb less than 10 acres of land, as well as wind projects that are less than 5 MW in
size. State law requires that any local ordinance addressing the siting of renewable energy facilities must be
consistent with the state’s clean energy policy, “provide for the protection of the locality in a manner
consistent with the goals of the Commonwealth to promote the generation of energy from wind and solar
resources,” and establish “reasonable requirements” for renewable energy facilities (e.g., with respect to
setbacks and noise).



610
   Va. Code Ann. §§ 10.1- 1197.5, 10.1-1197.6, 10.1-1197.8, 15.2-2288.7, 45.2.1708, 56-265.1, 56-265.2; 9 Va. Admin. Code §§ 15-
40-30, 15-60-20, 15-60-30, 15-60-130.



                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 358
                                                                                                                          Virginia




The state has siting authority over larger solar (5 MW or larger) and wind (5 MW or larger) projects. Solar
energy projects that are 5 MW to 150 MW in size and disturb more than 10 acres, and wind projects that are 5
MW to 150 MW require a permit from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ). All projects
larger than 150 MW require a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the State
Corporation Commission.

The DEQ must make a final decision within 90 days after receipt of the permit application. A public meeting,
followed by a 30-day public comment period, is required for DEQ permit applications. The State Corporation
Commission must similarly hold a hearing and provide due notice to interested parties before issuing a CPCN.


46.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state level-restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Virginia. However, at
least 39 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in the state.611 At least 1 city and 34 counties have
adopted local ordinances restricting solar energy projects. Restrictions on wind projects are less common,
having been adopted by 1 city and 4 counties. Only 1 county has restrictions on battery storage projects.
Project size / acreage caps are the most common type of restriction, included in at least 26 ordinances. At
least 22 ordinances impose temporary moratoria or permanent bans on projects.

46.3 Contested Projects
      ● 7 Bridges Solar Project (Mecklenburg County): In 2016, Longroad Energy proposed a 105-MW solar
        project to be located on approximately 799 acres near Chase City. In September 2021, the
        Mecklenburg County Planning Commission unanimously voted against permitting construction of the
        project as proposed, mainly because of the county’s 500-acre maximum for solar projects. In response,
        the developer scaled down the project to 80 MW on 500 acres, expanded setbacks from 150 feet to
        250 feet (or more), and proactively coordinated with the Virginia Departments of Environmental
        Quality and Wildlife Resources to add wider buffers from aquatic resources. In August 2024, the Board
        of Supervisors voted 7 to 2 to reject the developer’s proposed siting agreement despite its pledge to
        donate $500,000 to Chase City in addition to the anticipated financial benefits to the county.612

      ● Almeda Solar Grazing Center (Fauquier County): In 2023, Open Road Renewables proposed the 90-
        MW Almeda Solar Grazing Center (also known as Almeda Solar I) which included an agrivoltaics
        component to be developed on approximately 941 acres of farmland spanning 14 parcels. In April
        2023, the Fauquier County Planning Commission rejected the proposal on a 4-1 vote citing concerns
        over the project scale, potential to disrupt or destroy historic resources, and inconsistency with
        Fauquier’s agrarian character. In 2025, the developer re-submitted a modified version of the proposal
        for the project to be located on 3 separate parcels of land, plans for 200-foot setbacks with vegetation
        buffers as well as decommissioning plans. The project would occupy less than 0.4% of the county’s
        farmland and less than 0.25% of its rural lands and is expected to generate $20 million in local tax
        revenue. In February 2025, following a public hearing, the Commission unanimously rejected the
        proposal finding it to be inconsistent with the county’s comprehensive plan. The majority of public
        comments heard by the Commission were from opponents of the project, who argued that farmland
        was being targeted and that the project was incompatible with the character of the county, and
        questioned the developers claims about job creation.613

      ● Antlers Road Solar Farm (Mecklenburg County): In December 2022, the County Planning Commission
        rejected an application for a 90-MW solar farm on private land. The project would be developed across
        1,000 acres, including approximately 489 acres of prime farmland. In January 2023, the Mecklenburg
        County Board of Supervisors similarly rejected the application for the project. In reaching their
        decision, the Board cited the loss of 489 acres of prime farmland as a chief concern. The majority of the

      ● Axton Solar Project (Henry County): In November 2021, the Henry County Board of Zoning Appeals
        rejected Axton Solar LLC’s request to add 484 acres to a previously approved 1,203-acre solar project
        on agricultural land in the unincorporated community of Axton. The request was denied due to
        concerns about aesthetic impacts and an ordinance that mandates that no more than 2.5% of the land
        area within a 5-mile radius may be used by solar. In December 2022, after the developer reduced the
        total project size to about 1,000 acres, with only 434 acres covered in panels, the Henry County Board
        of Zoning Appeals approved the project. However, on April 25, 2023, the Henry County Board of
        Supervisors rejected the project on finding that it would exceed the 2.5% cap by 93 acres.615

      ● Bakers Pond Solar Farm (Prince George County): In October 2023, the Prince George County Planning
        Commission determined that RWE Clean Energy’s proposed 100-MW, 505-acre solar farm was not in
        substantial accord with the county’s comprehensive plan, as it would exceed the county’s limit for the
        size of a solar farm. Some residents have opposed the project, expressing concerns about impacts to
        farming and hunting.616

      ● Bealeton Solar Farm (Fauquier County): In April 2021, Fauquier County planning officials rejected an
        application for a 40-acre solar farm in Bealeton. This application was the first to be considered since
        Fauquier County passed a restrictive solar development ordinance in October of 2020. Officials
        rejected the application because the project would have been located on prime farmland, which they
        claimed was incompatible with the County’s comprehensive plan.617

      ● Blackwater Solar Project (Sussex County): A 5,000-acre, 600-MW solar farm proposed by Blackwater
        Solar LLC has sparked significant objections from local residents. In May 2023, the developer began the
        application process for a conditional use permit for the project. In March 2024, the Sussex County
        Board of Supervisors and Planning Commission heard opinions on the project at a public meeting
        attended by over 300 people, with many opponents raising concerns about erosion, loss of woodlands,
        damage to wetlands, contamination of runoff, and the risk of battery fires. On June 3, 2024, the Board
        of Supervisors voted to deny the permits.618

      ● Caledon Solar (King George County): In 2024, Sun Tribe proposed the 22 MW, 215 acre Caledon Solar
        Project on private land owned by State Senator Richard Stuart who is also the King George County
        attorney. Project opponents, primarily conservationists, have argued that construction of a commercial
        solar facility would violate a perpetual open-space conservation easement that covers the property
        held by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR). Nevertheless, in November
        2025, the King George County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the request for a special
        exception permit for the project, disregarding the County Planning Commission’s recommendation to
        deny it. In December 2025, the DCR approved an amendment to the conservation easement, allowing
        construction of the Project. Opponents allege that Sen. Stuart only received the DCR approval after
        interventions by political allies, including Governor Glenn Youngkin. 619

      ● Cape Solar Project (Page County): The 100-acre Cape Solar project was first proposed in 2018. The
        project faced intense opposition from Page County Citizens for Responsible Solar, and the Page County
        Board of Supervisors denied the application. The developer submitted a new application in December
        2020. However, in March 2022, the Page County Planning Commission recommended denial of the
        revised application due to the anticipated loss of agricultural land, visual impacts, and environmental

      ● Carver Solar (Isle of Wight County): On February 23, 2023, the Isle of Wight County Supervisors

        commission voted to recommend that the county supervisors establish a cap on the cumulative

      ● Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project (City of Virginia Beach): IIn 2020, Dominion Energy proposed
        the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project, a 2,600-MW offshore wind farm. In March 2024, the
        Committee for a Constructive Tomorrow, Heartland Institute, and National Legal and Policy Center
        filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to halt the project. The lawsuit
        alleged that the construction would threaten the endangered North Atlantic right whale and that
        Dominion had not taken sufficient steps to protect right whales. The lawsuit further alleged that, when
        it approved the project, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) failed to consider the
        cumulative impacts of offshore wind farms on the right whale population in violation of the
        Endangered Species Act. The plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction to halt the project’s
        construction until the National Marine Fisheries Service issues a new biological opinion. In May 2024,
        the court denied the request for preliminary injunction, stating that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate
        that they would suffer irreparable harm and to account for the extensive measures to protect whales
        already in place. Separately, residents of Virginia Beach have raised concerns about vibrations, scenic
        disruptions, and environmental harm from the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project. Dominion has
        stated that it has provided multiple opportunities for residents to engage with the company and that it
        is implementing measures to address their concerns. On December 22, 2025, the Bureau of Ocean

      ● Cunningham Springs Solar (Orange County): In March 2024, the Orange County Board of Supervisors
        unanimously rejected plans for a 17-acre community solar project proposed by RWE Clean Energy,
        after the planning commission had previously recommended approval. In voting to deny the project,

      ● Deltaville Solar (Middlesex County): In 2025, KDC Solar submitted a request to the Middlesex Planning
        Commission for a Special Exception for a 20-MW solar energy facility it planned to build on
        approximately 77 acres in Deltaville. In April 2025, the Middlesex Planning Commission unanimously
        recommended denial of the request to the County Board of Supervisors, noting that the project was
        not in accord with the county’s comprehensive plan. Opponents of the project had garnered over 440
        signatures on a petition in opposition to the project. Over 100 local residents attended the April public
        meeting and the majority of those who spoke raised concerns about the project, including the
        potential for it to decrease property values, cause environmental hazards, and change the rural
        character of the area. In June 2025, following a 4-hour public hearing, the Board of Supervisors’ vote
        was split, 2-2, and thus the motion to approve the Special Exception for the project failed.627

      ● Gabriel Solar Project (Prince Edward County): Energix Renewables proposed the 80-MW Gabriel Solar
        Project, which would include a 120-MW battery energy storage component on approximately 539
        acres, by far the largest such project proposed in the county. At a planning commission public hearing
        in December 2024, landowners who support the project spoke about the short- and long-term benefits
        of the project, including significant revenue for the county. Residents who opposed the project raised
        concerns primarily related to fire safety planning and training for local firefighters. In January 2025 the
        county planning commission recommended approval. In March 2025, the Board of Supervisors rejected
        the project in a 7-1 vote, citing fire safety concerns and inconsistencies in the application
        documents.628

    ● Hillendale Solar (Halifax County): In September 2023, the Halifax County Planning Commission
      recommended that a permit for the 102-MW Hillendale Solar project be denied. One of the planning
      commissioners stated that the project would not be a good fit with initiatives meant to preserve the
      nearby Staunton River. Residents voiced both support and opposition to the project, with some
      residents questioning the environmental impacts of solar energy.629

    ● James City County Solar Project (James City County): In March 2023, the James City County Board of
      Supervisors rejected Pivot Energy’s application to develop a 4.75-MW solar farm. Opposition to the
      project—including from the Colonial Soil and Water Conservation District—had centered on impacts to
      prime farmland. The James City County Planning Commission had recommended approval of the
      project in November 2022.630

    ● Kitty Hawk Wind Project Cable Landing (City of Virginia Beach): The Kitty Hawk Wind Project, a 3,500-
      MW offshore wind farm proposed by Avangrid Renewables, has encountered significant community
      resistance around the proposed site of a cable landing. In 2017, the company secured the rights to
      develop a lease area off the coast of the Outer Banks. The neighborhood of Sandbridge in Virginia
      Beach was selected as the site for the project’s cable landing. In November 2023, the City Manager and
      Mayor informed the developer that the city could not support the landing due to the amount of
      community pushback. Local opponents include an organization called Protect Sandbridge Beach
      Coalition, which has met with City Council members and sought an independent assessment of the
      landing. Opponents have expressed concerns about potential economic impacts, including tourism and
      property value impacts; environmental impacts, including hindrances on efforts to renourish beaches;
      and construction-related noise disruptions and road blockages. Many of the opponents claim that they
      do not oppose offshore wind farms in general but object to the site selection for the landing. In March
      2024, the developer provided a new economic impact report to the Council, emphasizing the benefits
      of the project. As of December 31, 2024, the City had not made a decision to approve the cable
      landing.631

47.1 State Siting Framework652
Project developers in Washington may elect to have their facilities permitted at the local or state level. At the
state level, developers of wind and solar energy facilities can elect to obtain a permit from the Washington


652
   Wash. Rev. Code §§ 35A.63.100; 36-70-750; 43.148 et seq.; 43.158 et seq.; 80-50-020; 80.50.060; 80.50.090; 80-50.090(4)(b);
RCW 80.50.100; Don Jenkins, Yakima County solar moratorium eclipsed by state council, Capital Press, Dec. 6, 2022,
https://www.capitalpress.com/ag_sectors/rurallife/yakima-county-solar-moratorium-eclipsed-by-state-council/article_1de9a3fa-
7591-11ed-9593-af0ab3e4fafd.html; 2022 Wash. Laws, ch. 183, Sec. 9(4)(b) (allowing topic of public hearing to be limited to
preemption for projects with insignificant environmental impacts), Sec. 10(2) (requiring state, when approving project, to include


                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 376
                                                                                                                    Washington




Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC), or apply to have their project designated as a “clean energy
project of statewide significance” by the Department of Commerce and approved via a “clean energy
coordinated permitting process” that is overseen by the Department of Ecology. The permitting timelines and
public involvement requirements depend on which process the developer has opted into.

The state can preempt local laws when approving a project as long as the project will have no significant
environmental impact or the impact will be mitigated to an insignificant level. The EFSEC has set aside county-
level moratoria blocking solar energy projects in several instances when approving projects.

47.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Washington state. At
least 8 restrictive local ordinances have been adopted in 7 counties.653 Grant County has adopted 2 separate
restrictive ordinances: 1 imposing a temporary county-wide moratorium on wind energy development and the
other permanently banning solar energy development on certain agricultural land in the country. Similar
moratoria / bans have also been adopted in at least 3 other counties – Kittitas, Pacific, and Yakima. There are
also 3 local ordinances – in Klickitat, Okanogan, and Whitman counties – that include restrictive setback
requirements.

    ○ Total number of state restrictions: 0
    ○ Total number of local restrictions: 8
    ○ Technology targeted:
         ■ 5 (wind)

47.3 Contested Projects
      ● Badger Mountain Solar Project (Douglas County): The Badger Mountain Solar Project is a 200-MW
        solar project proposed by Aurora Solar, LLC, a subsidiary of Avangrid Renewables, LLC. Wenatchi-
        P’squosa people indigenous to the area have objected to the planned construction, citing concerns
        that the project threatens cultural resources including foodways and sacred sites on the mountain. In
        May 2023, the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation formally registered their opposition to
        the project. In January 2024, ProPublica and High Country News published the results of an
        investigation that found that Washington State Department of Natural Resources’ process for assessing
        cultural resources had been inadequate. In August 2024, the developer announced that it was pausing
        project planning for 2 to 3 months as it re-evaluated public comments, including from project
        landowners and affected tribal nations.654

      ● Carriger Solar Project (Klickitat County): The proposed 160-MW Carriger Solar Project drew opposition
        from a group called Citizens Educated About Solar Energy (CEASE). In August 2021, the founder of
        CEASE was ejected from a public meeting about the project for causing a disruption. On January 10,
        2023, the Klickitat County Commission adopted a 6-month moratorium on solar projects in the area
        where the project has been proposed. In August 2023, the Washington Energy Facility Site Evaluation
        Council (EFSEC) indicated that it was considering issuing a determination that the project would have
        “significant impacts” on the environment. Under Washington law, “significance” is defined as a
        “reasonable likelihood of more than a moderate adverse impact on environmental quality.” EFSEC
        identified 2 reasons for the adverse impacts: cultural impacts and visual aesthetics. On cultural
        impacts, EFSEC emphasized objections from the Yakama Nation centered on impacts to Traditional
        Cultural Properties (TCPs). The EFSEC also found it unlikely that mitigation efforts to lessen visual
        impacts would be effective. On June 26, 2025, the EFSEC issued a decision recommending that the
        Governor approve the project.655

    ● Columbia Solar Project (Kittitas County): Tuusso Energy applied to the State Energy Facility Site
      Evaluation Council (EFSEC) for permission to construct a 25-MW, 200-acre solar project across 5
      parcels of private property. Neighbors of the site started an organization, Save Our Farms, to advocate
      against the project. In early 2017, the Kittitas County Commission enacted a temporary moratorium
      that prohibited major solar projects. In July 2018, the EFSEC overrode the County by voting to approve
      the project. In October 2018, Governor Inslee gave final approval, allowing the project to move
      forward.656

    ● Goldendale Energy Storage Project (Klickitat County): The Yakama Nation has been fighting the
      proposed Goldendale Energy Storage Project on its ancestral land for 5 years due to concerns that the
      pumped storage project could destroy tribal cultural property. The project is planned to be constructed
      on a 680-acre site with the capacity to generate 1,200-MW of energy. On July 28, 2022, 17 of
      Washington State’s 29 federally recognized tribes sent a letter to Governor Inslee asking that he deny
      permits for the project. In February 2024, FERC released its final environmental review for the project,
      recommending the project move forward subject to certain conditions. Tribal nations have argued they
      were not properly consulted for the project and that the lack of consultation undermined FERC’s
      review of the project’s cultural impacts.657

    ● Goldeneye Energy Storage (Skagit County):In June 2024, Tenaska submitted a proposal for a 200-MW
      battery energy storage system to the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) rather than seeking
      approval from Skagit County. The project is proposed to be located on approximately 16 acres zoned
      for agriculture in the outskirts of Sedro-Woolley. At a public hearing held in August 2024, local
      residents raised concerns of fire and environmental hazards. The Skagit County Commissioners, the
      Sedro-Woolley mayor and council, and District 39 state legislators all voiced their opposition to the
      project. In November 2024, the Skagit Board of County Commissioners amended the county
      development code to prohibit new electrical energy generation and storage on agricultural and
      resource land. In January 2025, District 39 Senator Keith Wagoner introduced Senate Bill 5283 to

      ● Horse Heaven Wind Farm (Benton County): Scout Clean Energy has proposed a 600-MW wind project
        on 24 miles of ridgeline on the Horse Heaven Hills. The project has garnered local opposition from
        groups such as Save Our Ridges, which maintains a website tracking the project. Construction was
        supposed to be finished by 2022, but the project was still under review as of August 2023. In August
        2023, a hearing was scheduled for public comment about the proposed project. In September 2023,
        the Board of Benton County Commissioners published a resolution formally opposing the project.
        Opponents of the project have raised concerns about impacts to ferruginous hawks, as well as
        concerns about the cultural and historical significance of the Horse Heaven Hills to the Confederated
        Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation. The community group Tri-Cities C.A.R.E.S (Community Action
        for Responsible Environmental Stewardship) has also argued that the project will reduce property
        values and could obstruct emergency planes or hospitals in the event of wildfires. The state Energy
        Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) voted in April 2024 to recommend the Horse Heaven Project for
        approval over objections from the Yakama Nation. The EFSEC’s recommendation halved the Horse
        Heaven project’s size due to concerns that the facility would impact local endangered hawk
        populations. In May 2024, however, Governor Inslee rejected the proposal to halve the size of the
        project. In September 2024, the EFSEC approved a version of the project with mitigation measures that
        did not involve reducing the size of the project. Governor Inslee approved this version of the project in
        October 2024. In November 2024, Benton County, Tri-Cities CARES and the Yakama Nation each filed a
        separate lawsuit in the Thurston County Superior Court seeking judicial review of the approval by the
        state and the regulators and alleging irregularities and errors in the environmental impact study
        process.661

      ● Skykomish River Hydroelectric Project (Snohomish County): A hydroelectric dam project on the
        Skykomish River was abandoned in 2018, 7 years after it was proposed, due to local opposition.
        Residents had opposed the project on the ground that the project would divert up to 90% of the water
        from a scenic waterfall.663

      ● Whistling Ridge Energy Project (Klickitat County): In 2002, SDS Lumber Company, dba Whistling Ridge
        Energy, LLC (“Whistling Ridge”) proposed the Whistling Ridge Energy Project as a 70-MW wind farm,
        with up to 85 wind turbines on both public and private land near the City of White Salmon in Klickitat
        County. The project faced immediate opposition from local residents, a conservation organization
        called Friends of the Columbia Gorge (“Friends”), and tourism groups, who raised concerns about poor
        project design and harm to scenic and wildlife resources. Over 400 public comments were submitted to
        the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC), largely by opponents. In 2012, the Washington
        Department of Natural Resources denied the original project proposals but ultimately authorized a 10-
        year permit from 2012 to 2022 for up to 35 wind turbines. The Governor accepted the EFSEC’s
        recommendation and approved the project. In 2013, Friends challenged the approval in state court,
        which rejected their claims and affirmed the approval. In 2018, Friends filed a challenge in federal
        court, which also failed. However, the project was on hold until 2023, 1 year after the permit had
        expired. Whistling Ridge’s corporate successor, Twin Creeks Timber LLC filed a request to transfer
        ownership and extend the permit to 2026. However, in 2023, the EFSEC denied the requests, and the
        project was officially terminated.664

48.1 State Siting Framework665

The state has principal siting authority over renewable energy projects. Those projects require a certificate of
public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the Public Service Commission of West Virginia (WV PSC).
Developers of solar energy projects that are less than 200 megawatts (MW) in size may opt-in to an expedited
certification process overseen by the WV PSC.

For non-expedited projects, the WV PSC must make a decision within 270 days of receiving a CPCN application
and within 90 days from submission of the final application after a public hearing is held. For projects that opt-
into the expedited certification process, the WV PSC must hold a public hearing within 90 days of public notice
of the filing of the application, and must issue a decision within 150 days of the filing of the application. The
WV PSC may waive the public hearing requirement under either permitting pathway if there are no objections
to the application.

48.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
At least 1 state-level restriction on renewable energy development has been adopted in West Virginia. Senate
Bill 583 of 2020 imposes various restrictions on utility-scale solar energy development. Most notably, the law
prohibits any single solar facility from having a generating capacity greater than 200 MW, and sets a
cumulative generating capacity limit of 400 MW for all solar facilities “operating at any given time, and for
which rate recovery is provided by the” WV PSC. No restrictive local ordinances have been identified in West
Virginia.

48.3 Contested Projects
      ● Beech Ridge Wind Farm (Greenbrier County): The Beech Ridge Wind Farm, a 100-MW wind project in
        Greenbrier County, was met with local opposition when it was proposed in 2005. Opponents including
        the Animal Welfare Institute and Mountain Communities for Responsible Energy challenged the
        project before the Public Service Commission (PSC), and then in federal court. During the pendency of
        the federal lawsuit, the developer agreed to continue construction on only 40 out of the planned 124
        turbines until a decision on the merits. In 2009, a federal district court found flaws in analysis of
        impacts on the endangered Indiana bat and imposed severe restrictions on the project. The court
        allowed the developer to complete the 40 turbines under construction but enjoined the operation of
        those wind turbines at all times except winter, unless the parties could agree otherwise. The project
        was completed in 2010 with the construction of 67 turbines.666

        reading “Stop Solar Farms.” In December 2023, the West Virginia Public Service Commission approved
        Tyr Energy Development Renewables’ plan for the project.669

49.1 State Siting Framework670
Local governments have principal siting authority over wind and solar energy projects that are less than 100
megawatts (MW) in size. Local governments must determine whether an application is complete within 45
days of filing and must make a final decision within 90 days thereafter.

The state has principal siting authority over larger wind and solar projects (100 MW or greater). These larger
projects require a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) from the Wisconsin Public Service
Commission (PSC). The Wisconsin PSC must determine whether an application is complete within 30 days of
filing and must make a final decision within 180 days thereafter.

At least 1 public hearing must be held for projects under local review and for projects with a pending CPCN
application.

State law prohibits local governments from placing any restrictions on wind or solar facilities, unless those
restrictions: (a) protect health or safety; (b) do not significantly increase the cost or decrease efficiency of the
project; or (c) allow for an alternative system of comparable cost and efficiency. Moreover, in the case of wind
facilities, local governments may also not impose more onerous restrictions on those facilities than the
restrictions imposed at the state level. In addition, state law provides that “[i]f installation or utilization of a
facility for which a [CPCN] has been granted is precluded or inhibited by a local ordinance,” the local ordinance
is preempted.

49.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been identified in Wisconsin. At least 20
restrictive local ordinances have been adopted by 16 towns and 3 counties.671 One of the counties – Sawyer
County – has adopted at least 2 separate restrictive ordinances. Wind is the technology most commonly
targeted in restrictive ordinances. Of the 15 ordinances restricting wind, 12 include onerous setback
requirements and noise limits. Only 5 ordinances impose restrictions on solar and/or battery storage projects.

49.3 Contested Projects
      ●   Beautiful Hill Wind Farm (Manitowoc County): Residents expressed concerns regarding “setbacks,
          low-frequency noise, location, and issues with the process” surrounding this proposed 7-turbine
          project. In 2013 the Manitowoc County Board passed a wind ordinance that was as restrictive as state
          law would allow. It appears the project was not completed.672

      ●   Cardinal-Hickory Creek Transmission Line Project (Grant County): The Cardinal-Hickory Creek
          Transmission Line is a 125-mile, 345-kilovolt transmission line that is planned to stretch from Dubuque
          County, Iowa to the Town of Middleton, Wisconsin. The transmission line is expected to support the
          interconnection of renewable energy generation in the upper Midwest region. The project has faced
          significant opposition. In 2021, the National Wildlife Refuge Association, the Driftless Area Land
          Conservancy, the Wisconsin Wildlife Federation, and the Defenders of Wildlife filed a series of lawsuits
          in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin. The lawsuits, which were consolidated,
          challenged the project under NEPA, the National Wildlife Refuge System Improvement Act, the Clean
          Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. In November 2021, the federal district court granted a
          preliminary injunction preventing development of the project that would impact wetlands in southern
          Wisconsin’s Driftless Area. In January 2022, the federal district court held that federal approval of the
          project violated NEPA and the Refuge Act. Then, in July 2023, the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals
          vacated the preliminary injunction and remanded the case for dismissal. In December 2023, the
          eastern half of the transmission line entered into service. In March 2024, the Driftless Area Land
          Conservancy, the National Wildlife Refuge Association, and the Wisconsin Wildlife Federation sued to
          block a federal land exchange necessary for the line’s crossing of a wildlife refuge along the Mississippi
          River. The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin issued a preliminary injunction
          suspending federal approvals for the land exchange in March 2024, but in May 2024, the Seventh
          Circuit reversed the order, holding that the district court had not made the required finding that the
          movants were “likely to succeed on the merits.” The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service completed the land
          exchange in May 2024. The transmission line completed construction and entered into full operation in
          September 2024, with the federal lawsuit against the project still pending.673

      ●   Vista Sands Solar (Portage County): In January 2024, Vista Sands Solar, LLC (Vista Sands), an affiliate of
          Doral Renewables, proposed Vista Sands Solar, a 1,300-MW solar farm with a 300-MW battery energy
          storage system which would be the largest solar farm in the state. The project would be located on
          approximately 9,500 acres of privately-owned agricultural land in the Village of Plover and towns of
          Grant, Plover and Buena Vista. An alliance of opponents including hunters, birdwatchers and public

          400 comments on their draft EIS. In December 2024, after reviewing the developer’s detailed report of
          the public health, ecosystem and economic benefits of the project, the PSC unanimously approved the
          scaled down version of the project and described it especially valuable for the state. The developer
          agreed to restore up to 7,900 acres of agricultural land in the vicinity of the wildlife area, to seed the
          area under development with a beneficial wildflower mix, and not to construct within 500 feet of
          important habitat for the great prairie chicken. Construction is expected to begin in late 2025 and the
          project is expected to produce enough electricity to power about 200,000 homes.681

50.1 State Siting Framework684

Local governments have principal siting authority over solar energy projects that are less than 30 megawatts
(MW) in size, solar energy projects that disturb less than 100 acres, and wind projects with less than 20
turbines. Local governments must determine whether an application is complete within 30 days of filing. A
public hearing on a project must be held no less than 45 days, and no more than 60 days after the application
is deemed complete.


684
      Wyo. Stat. §§ 18-5-502, 18-5-503, 18-5-505, 18-5-506, 35-12-102, 35-12-106.



                                  Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 398
                                                                                                                      Wyoming




The state has principal siting authority over solar energy project that are 30 MW or greater, solar projects that
disturb more than 100 acres, and wind projects with more than 20 turbines. A permit from the State Industrial
Siting Council is required for projects under state jurisdiction.

50.2 Restrictive State Statutes and Local Ordinances
No state-level restrictions on renewable energy development have been adopted in Wyoming. Of the 23
counties in the state, at least 7 have adopted restrictive local ordinances. Most of the local ordinances (6)
target wind energy development and impose restrictive setback requirements. Only Sheridan county has
imposed restrictions on solar energy development.

      ○ Total number of local restrictions: 7
      ○ Technology targeted:

           ■ 1 (solar)

           ■ Fremont County: Rule 6a and 6b: Setback Restriction (wind)

50.3 Contested Projects
      ● Haystack Solar (Natrona County): EG Haystack Solar LLC proposed the 199-MW Haystack Solar and
        battery energy storage facility on a 2,000-acre private ranch 30 miles west of Casper. In February 2025,
        dozens of area residents spoke out against the project during a 7.5 hour public meeting. The Natrona
        County Board of Commissioners voted 3-2 to reject the project in the face of heated public
        opposition.685

      ● Laramie Range Wind Project (Laramie County): In 2018, Repsol Renewables North America began the
        development of the 650-MW Laramie Range Wind Project, comprising 170 wind turbines on

   Dale Killingbeck, Casper-Area Solar Farm Killed After Dozens Of Residents Speak Out Against It, COWBOY STATE DAILY, Feb. 10,

         approximately 56,000 acres 20 miles northwest of Cheyenne. The proposal faced strong local
         opposition, mostly from adjacent non-participating landowners. On September 16, 2025, after several
         weeks of public hearings, the Board of County Commissioners rejected the project with a 3-1 vote.
         During the public hearings, opponents of the project raised concerns about threats to wildlife,
         excessive noise, vibrations becoming a nuisance, obstruction of views and a decrease in property
         values. In November 2025, the developer sued the Laramie County Board of Commissioners in the
         Wyoming First Judicial Court challenging the rejection of the project on the basis that the county acted
         “arbitrarily and capriciously.”686

      ● Pioneer Wind Parks I and II (Converse County): In 2011, Wasatch Wind proposed a 66-turbine wind
        farm in Converse County. The project was opposed by local residents due to concerns about potential
        impacts to scenery, recreation, property values, and the Laramie Range wilderness. The opponents
        formed the Northern Laramie Range Alliance (NLRA) to organize against the project, including by
        advocating for zoning regulations that would prohibit wind development above an elevation of 6,000
        feet; when this failed, the group appealed state and county permitting decisions and eventually took a
        case to the Wyoming Supreme Court. Although these efforts failed, Converse County did enact slightly
        stricter wind regulations. Construction was completed in 2016.687

      ● Pronghorn Wind and Solar (Converse County): In 2022, Focus Clean Energy proposed the “Pronghorn
        H2” project, comprising a roughly 300 MW wind farm and 280 MW solar farm, to power a hydrogen
        production facility. The project is to be located on public and private lands spanning a total of
        approximately 40,000 acres near Glenrock. The project has faced strong opposition from local
        ranchers, landowners, and a group called “Taxpayers Against Pronghorn H2 Project.” The opponents
        have raised concerns over public safety, water use, viewshed impacts, impacts on wildlife migration,
        and interference with private property rights. In April 2025, the Wyoming State Board of Land
        Commissioners, in a 4-1 vote, approved a lease for the project. With the same vote, the Board also
        approved a lease for another project by the same developers in neighboring Niobrara County (see
        Sidewinder Wind). In July 2025, a local rancher filed a lawsuit in the district court challenging the state
        approval of the Pronghorn project. In December 2025, the district court ruled that the Board had
        violated its own rules by approving the lease for the project. [Note: In January 2026, the developer

      ● Rail Tie Wind Project (Albany County): The Rail Tie Wind Project, a 26,000-acre, 504-MW wind farm
        proposed by ConnectGen (which was acquired by Repsol in March 2024), has experienced delays after
        becoming embroiled in legal controversies. At a meeting in February 2020, residents urged the county
        planning and zoning commission to place a moratorium on wind development to block the project,
        citing concerns about the potential for aesthetic changes to the classic western landscape, effects on
        local wildlife, and the potential for groundwater contamination during the installation of turbine
        foundations. An attorney representing landowners opposed to the project also lobbied the county to
        impose aggressive setback requirements that would effectively block wind energy projects. However,
        neither the moratorium nor the setbacks were implemented. While the State Board of Land
        Commissioners initially denied the developer’s lease application on 4,800 acres of state land in
        November 2020, the Board reversed its decision and approved the lease in January 2021. The Albany
        County Board of Commissioners then granted final approval in July 2021. Local residents and
        businesses challenged the permit, and, in May 2022, the Albany County district court upheld the
        permit. Over 45 residents signed onto an appeal to the Wyoming Supreme Court, and the Wyoming
        Supreme Court affirmed, upholding the permit on April 18, 2023. In December 2023, the Wyoming
        Department of Environmental Quality’s Industrial Siting Council approved the project, drawing a
        lawsuit. On December 23, 2024, the Albany County Conservancy and other plaintiffs filed a lawsuit in
        federal court to stop the project, alleging violations of the NEPA, the National Historic Preservation Act,
